Isaiah then describes how his sin was atoned for in Isaiah 6:7. “With it he touched my mouth and said, ‘See, this has touched your lips; your guilt is taken away and your sin atoned for.’” (Isaiah 6:7) God has no choice but to punish sin and those who sin. It is God’s nature, apart from sacrifice for sin, that he must be fully holy and just. He would fail to be holy and just if he did not give the proper punishment for sin and evil actions. To do less than this would require God to be less than himself. To impose the punishment of eternal separation on sinful, rebellious people, who do not receive the sacrifice of Jesus for sin, is the only option for a just and holy God. The word often used to describe this punishment is “hell.” English Bibles translate various Greek words into our English word “hell.” In the teachings of Jesus, the word most commonly used is a translation of the Greek word “Gehenna.” Most likely, Gehenna was originally a valley southeast of Jerusalem where garbage, dead bodies, and other refuse was thrown. An analogous description of judgment is found in Isaiah 66:24: “And they will go out and look on the dead bodies of those who rebelled against me; the worms that eat them will not die, the fire that burns them will not be quenched, and they will be loathsome to all mankind.” It is the imagery that Gehenna brought to the minds of the early disciples that served as a symbol of the eternal state of the enemies of God. It was just as frightening then as it is now. 43

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES Second, hell is the destination of those whose sins are not removed by the sacrifice of Jesus. The judgment of unbelievers in eternity will show the ramifications of the sin and rebellion against God in their decisions made in this life. Before I (Bobby) became a disciple of Jesus, I used to hear that I would go to hell if I did not believe in Jesus. That statement sounded wrong to me. I thought to myself, I am doing fine. I’m a basically good person. But they’re saying if I don’t believe in Jesus (for my own good reasons), then God is going to punish me?! Not only did I have trouble understanding why he would punish me, but I also couldn’t get why he was also going to punish all those sincere people in other religions just because they would not turn to Jesus. Yet my problem was grounded in a false framework. I assumed God’s love—and that’s about it. How could a loving God send anyone to hell? I thought. I only have a few minor flaws, like most other people I know. On a grading curve, there are a lot of people worse than me. Furthermore, I thought of hell only as a punishment for those who rejected Jesus, not considering the depth of my sins apart from God’s grace. But here is the framework given to us in God’s Word. God is holy and just, and because of that, our sin (and our ongoing sinfulness) keeps us from being in relationship with him. This is the case even though he loves humanity. From this perspective, a more appropriate question than “How can a loving God send people to hell?” is “How can a holy God not give sinners over to the separation from God that they have chosen?” We struggle with the Bible’s teaching of hell insofar as we struggle to see sin as that big of a deal. And then, for the same reason, we struggle to appreciate his love as deeply as we should. Because God is also loving, he offers to take away our sin through the sacrifice of Jesus. Those who see their sin as a big deal are the most likely people to see their own need for Jesus’ sacrifice; when we don’t see sin as utterly sinful, it’s easy to view Jesus’ sacrifice as less-than necessary. It is for those aware of the sinfulness of their sin that the gospel of Jesus is the best news ever. First John 2:1-2 resonates with people who have this awareness: 44

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES “My dear children, I write this to you so that you will not sin. But if anybody does sin, we have an advocate with the Father—Jesus Christ, the Righteous One. He is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world.” A careful reading of the context of John 3:16 also teaches this truth. Many people know what John 3:16 says, but it’s easy to miss the sober context given in the verses that come after verse 16: “For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save the world through him. Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe stands condemned already because they have not believed in the name of God’s one and only Son. . . . Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life, but whoever rejects the Son will not see life, for God’s wrath remains on them.” (John 3:16-18; 3:36) So, the fundamental human problem is that we are all separated from God and deserving punishment because of our sin. Apart from Jesus, we stand condemned (John 3:18), and God’s wrath (judgment and punishment) remains on us. We need the cleansing, forgiveness, and mercy for our sins that is only provided by Jesus and his sacrifice for our sins. Again, because our sin remains with us, and we thus deserve punishment by a holy God, Scripture teaches that those who do not possess the Son of God do not have life (1 John 5:12). Unbelievers will be punished according to their sins, and for this they have no one to blame but themselves (Romans 2:5ff). The Bible makes it abundantly clear, however, that God doesn’t want anyone to be lost (2 Peter 3:9). What God really wants is for all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4). Scripture teaches that God will save only the people who turn in faith to Christ. “He will punish those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus. They will be punished with everlasting destruction and shut out from the presence of the 45

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES Lord and from the glory of his might on the day he comes to be glorified in his holy people and to be marveled at among all those who have believed.” (2 Thessalonians 1:8-10a) Theologian Adrio Konig puts all this into perspective: “God . . . determines to abandon the unbeliever, who refuses his help and will not tread the path back to happiness opened by God in his goodness. In this way God remains the king, the sovereign Lord, but the lost have no one but themselves to blame for their condition. This is in complete harmony with the New Testament preaching of damnation, according to which the damned are in every case themselves responsible for their state, never able to ‘answer God back’ (Romans 9:20).”29 Either our sins are taken away through Christ’s sacrifice, or we must go into eternity to pay the penalty ourselves. According to the explicit teaching of the Bible, these are the only two options left to us.30 If God has another plan, he has not revealed it to us. Third, the fate of the unrighteous in eternity will be worse than any fate that can be experienced in this life. There are situations in this life often described as “hell on earth.” But none of these situations, as bad as they may be, are comparable to hell. Jesus warned people about hell with words such as these: “If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut if off and throw it away. It is better for you to enter life maimed or crippled than to have two hands or two feet and be thrown into eternal fire. And if your eye causes you to stumble, gouge it out and throw it away. It is better for you to enter life with one eye than to have two eyes and be thrown into the fire of hell.” (Matthew 18:8-9) 29 Adrio Konig, The Eclipse of Christ in Eschatology, 221-22. 30 Many of us hope and pray that God will find a way to apply Christ’s sacrifice to seekers and God-fearing people who did not hear the gospel in their lives. But we have a responsibility to not go beyond Scripture on this point. So, we cling to the sure teachings of Scripture, working and reaching out to everyone who will listen. And all the while, we trust in God’s justice, goodness, and love, knowing that there may be more than what has been revealed and that the Judge of all the earth will do right (Genesis 18:25). See the wise warning by Robertson McQuilkin, The Great Omission (Grand Rapids: Baker Book House, 1984) and a discussion of related issues in Dennis Okholm and Timothy Phillips, More Than One Way? (Grand Rapids: Zondervan Publishing House, 1995). 46

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES “I tell you, my friends, do not be afraid of those who kill the body and after that can do no more. But I will show you whom you should fear: Fear him who, after your body has been killed, has authority to throw you into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear him.” (Luke 12:4-5) According to Jesus, to be maimed, crippled, or killed cannot compare with the horror of hell. Jesus hoped that this kind of warning would cause people to seriously consider their lives and repent. In the book of Revelation, John uses graphic language to describe the fate of those who chose to follow the dragon (Satan) instead of the lamb (Jesus). He says that their place is the fiery lake of burning sulfur—where the smoke of their torment rises forever and ever (Revelation 14:8-12; 20:11-15; 21:8). Fourth, the Bible teaches that there will be different degrees of punishment in hell. The unrepentant will be separated from God for eternity and punished, but not all will be punished to the same degree. As we mentioned earlier, the Bible teaches that God will be fair in his judgment (Romans 2:5ff; 1 Peter 1:17). God will punish people according to how they have lived, and some people have lived more corrupt lives than others. Some people have had also more opportunity to come to know Jesus than others. God will consider all of these factors. God knows everything about our lives and will judge us accordingly. Jesus put it this way: “The servant who knows the master’s will and does not get ready or does not do what the master wants will be beaten with many blows. But the one who does not know and does things deserving punishment will be beaten with few blows. From everyone who has been given much, much will be demanded; and from the one who has been entrusted with much, much more will be asked.” (Luke 12:47-48) This also explains why Jesus said that unrighteous religious leaders who make a show of their position and mistreat widows will be “punished most severely” (Mark 12:40). And it also explains why Jesus said that it would be more bearable for the people of Sodom on the day of judgment than it would be for the people of Chorazin and Bethsaida (Matthew 11:20-24). 47

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES God is fair; he will punish people according to what they have done and what they deserve. The Bible teaches that there are eternal consequences to our actions. Eternal punishment is an eternal state that negatively parallels the joys of eternal life. It is the final place of universal justice— where everyone gets exactly what they deserve. Again, the seriousness of this truth should lead us to turn to God, who wants instead to shower us with love and the joys of eternal life. Lastly, punishment in eternity of the unrepentant in hell is the mirror opposite of the blessings in eternity of the righteous in the new heaven and new earth. Those who are blessed by their salvation will be blessed for eternity; those who are punished because of their sin will receive a punishment that has effects for eternity. Jesus pointed this out in his discussion on the final judgment in Matthew 25. He compared the righteous to sheep, who dedicated themselves to loving one another, and then he compared the unrighteous to goats, who did not. At the end of the parable, Jesus announced the final verdict for the two groups of people. Both went into eternity according to their actions, but they went in two entirely different directions. “Then he will say to those on his left [the unloving “goats”], ‘Depart from me, you who are cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you gave me nothing to eat, I was thirsty and you gave me nothing to drink, I was a stranger and you did not invite me in, I needed clothes and you did not clothe me, I was sick and in prison and you did not look after me.’ . . . Then they will go away to eternal punishment, but the righteous to eternal life.” (Matthew 25:41-43, 46) The Bible often speaks of the destiny of the righteous as “eternal life” (John 3:16), and the destiny of the unrighteous as “everlasting destruction” or “eternal punishment” (2 Thessalonians 1:9). In Mark 9, Jesus described hell, using imagery out of Isaiah, as the place where “their worm does not die, and the fire is not quenched.” Jesus quotes from this passage in Mark 9:43-48: “If your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life maimed than with two hands to go into hell, where the fire never goes out. And if your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life crippled than to have two feet and 48

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES be thrown into hell. And if your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than to have two eyes and be thrown into hell, where ‘the worms that eat them do not die, and the fire is not quenched.’” In contrast to the promise of blessings that last forever, Jesus warned the unrighteous that the consequences of their punishment would also last forever.31 The only appropriate way to end this chapter is by urging us all to turn to Jesus so that we can have eternal life. And let’s urge everyone else we can to turn to Jesus, so that they will experience eternal life in the new heaven and new earth. 31 There are complex issues related to some of the details here. See William Crockett, Four Views on Hell (Grand Rapids, Michigan: Zondervan Publishing House, 1992). 49

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES 8 THE NEW HEAVEN AND NEW EARTH Christians long for our eternal home in heaven. When we look at the scene of the final judgment in Revelation, we notice that the most important consideration that will determine our eternal destiny is whether our names are written in the lamb’s “book of life.” This is a record of all true Christians, those whose sins have been forgiven by Jesus described in Revelation 20:12-15. “And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. Another book was opened, which is the book of life. . . . Anyone whose name was not found written in the book of life was thrown into the lake of fire.” The next thing God inspired John to write after those words is a description of the destination of those whose names are written in the book of life in Revelation 22:1: “Then I saw ‘a new heaven and a new earth,’ for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and there was no longer any sea.” In this way, God paints a beautiful picture of what eternity will be like for those who have been saved by the grace of Jesus because of their faith in him. We were created for an eternal relationship with God. Our ultimate hopes, dreams, and desires can only find their true fulfillment in the eternal kingdom with God after death. When the Bible speaks of our lives in eternity after death, it speaks of a glorious existence—a close, intimate relationship with God. Christians often speak of life after death as a life in “heaven.” To a large degree, this is accurate because that is where our citizenship is held (Philippians 3:20), where our hopes are stored (Colossians 1:5), and where our inheritance is kept (1 Peter 1:4-5). However, in the Bible, the term “heaven” can mean many things, but it mostly refers to the abode of God.32 So, in this 32 Erickson, Christian Theology, 1226. 50

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES sense, it is hopeful to think of life after death as life in heaven, even though this concept alone falls short of the full biblical picture. The biblical teaching is that God will create an entirely new mode of existence for his people where he will dwell among them in “the new heaven and the new earth.”33 The vision of the new heaven and new earth is eloquently described by N.T. Wright in his book Surprised by Hope34 and Randy Alcorn in his book Heaven.35 These two wonderful books present the depth of the teaching from God’s Word on our eternal destiny as Christians. The pictures given in Scripture are so inspiring, and we encourage everyone to read these two books in order to be able to anticipate the joy toward which we are heading. Most Christians do not focus enough time on the love, joy, and peace that await us. For the purposes of this short chapter, we can best understand our wonderful destination and the eternal life God will give to us in eternity if we grasp four related concepts. First, we will dwell in God’s presence. We believe that the most core concept when thinking about our destiny as those who trust and follow Jesus is that God himself will personally and intimately dwell among us in eternity. “And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, ‘Look! God’s dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God.’” (Revelation 21:3) “The throne of God and of the Lamb will be in the city, and his servants will serve him. They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. There will be no more night. They will not need the light of a lamp or the light of the sun, for the Lord God will give them light. And they will reign for ever and ever.” (Revelation 22:3b-5) Again, the central joy in eternity is that we will be God’s sacred dwelling place. We will experience his full and direct presence. This core facet of eternal life should also make it clear 33 See Lee Wilson and Joe Beam, The Real Heaven (Webb City: Covenant Publishing, 2006), and Randy Alcorn, Heaven (Wheaton: Tyndale House Publishers, 2004). 34 N.T. Wright, Surprised by Hope: Rethinking Heaven, the Resurrection, and the Mission of the Church (New York: HarperOne, 2009). 35 See and Randy Alcorn, Heaven (Wheaton: Tyndale House Publishers, 2004). 51

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES why it’s wrongheaded to see it as a destination everyone will naturally want to experience. Many people do not love God at all and have no desire to live where he rules. In this way, all the hopes and dreams of the Old Testament (where God wanted to have a people to dwell among; see Exodus 19:5-6) and the New Testament (where God, in the form of his Spirit lives in Christians; see 1 Corinthians 6:19) find their ultimate fulfillment. God will no longer dwell in the physical Holy of Holies in the tabernacle/temple as in the Old Testament (1 Kings 6:20). I. Howard Marshall puts it this way: “The fellowship between man and his Creator, which was broken by sin, is now fully restored. God’s presence among his people is no longer confined to his temple, as in the imagery of the Old Testament (but see also Isaiah 57:15), or to his unseen presence among believers (Matthew 18:20); he is visibly in the midst of them, and they can see his face. Both the Father and the Son are the light of the new Jerusalem, and the Spirit of God summons men to enter the city (Revelation 22:17). Thus, finally, redeemed men and women enter into that fellowship of love which binds Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together, and the holy love of God becomes a final and full and victorious reality (1 Corinthians 13:13). God is at last all in all (1 Corinthians 15:28).”36 The original goal of creation will be fulfilled in eternity. God will be our God and we will be his people. Second, God will live with us in a new heaven and new earth. In the end, heaven and earth become one. Creation itself has been subjected to frustration through the fall (Romans 8:19ff), and in eternity all things will be re-created. God’s people have always looked forward to a renewed life where toil, difficulty, and death will be removed. This was the future for which the Israelites longed (Amos 9:11-15; Isaiah 11:6-9; etc.).37 Now, in the new heaven and the new earth, all of the hopes of God’s people will see their ultimate fulfillment. Note the following passages that refer to the new heaven and new earth: 36 I. Howard Marshal, Pocket Guide to Christian Beliefs (Downers Grove: InterVarsity Press, 1978), 138-39. 37 Anthony Hoekema does a good job in showing how these promises find their ultimate fulfillment in the new heaven and new earth, not in a millennial state. See The Bible and the Future, 274-87. 52

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES “See, I will create new heavens and a new earth. The former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind. But be glad and rejoice forever in what I will create.” (Isaiah 65:17-18a) “But in keeping with his promise we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells.” (2 Peter 3:13) “Then I saw ‘a new heaven and a new earth,’ for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.” (Revelation 21:1a) This existence will not be subject to decay (Revelation 22:3-5), and we will live in new bodies—physical bodies that are powerful, imperishable, and glorious (1 Corinthians 15:42-44). Third, we will live without the curse of the fall. Life in the new heaven and new earth will be life minus the trials of this world, life without the curse of sin and death.38 Gone too will be the animosity that separates groups of people by language and region; for it will be a dwelling of people from “every nation, tribe, people and language” (Revelation 7:9). According to metaphors used throughout the Bible, we will be God’s “Holy City,” the “new Jerusalem,” and the “bride of Christ.” Because God will dwell among us, we will live through eternity in sheer happiness. We will not experience pain, crying, mourning, or death, for everything will be made new. “They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the old order of things has passed away. He who was seated on the throne said, ‘I am making everything new!’” (Revelation 21:3b-5a) We will not be subject to Satan (Revelation 20:10), demons, false prophets, or ungodly governments. There will be a separation, so that those who have rejected God and remained 38 Although most Christians think that Revelation 21:1-22:6 is describing a place, it is likely more accurate to say that it is describing the church in eternity. See Robert Gundry, “The New Jerusalem: People as Place, Not Place for People,” Novum Testamentum XXIX, 3 (l987): 254-264. 53

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES unrepentant will not enter (Revelation 21:8, 27; 22:15). We will be a people living in absolute and eternal security (Revelation 21:10-17). We will be constantly rejoicing with each other and praising God. We will experience the peace and joy of God’s presence and God’s rest throughout eternity (Hebrews 4:1, 6, 9-11). Fourth, the new heaven and new earth will be like the Garden of Eden. Once again, humans will have access to the “tree of life,” and this access will ensure endless living and endless healing. The tree of life itself will bear fruit all the time, for all the people. Everything will be made new. “Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, as clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb down the middle of the great street of the city. On each side of the river stood the tree of life, bearing twelve crops of fruit, yielding its fruit every month. And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations.” (Revelation 22:1–2) We will experience a Garden of Eden-like existence and God himself will ensure that it will never end. Nothing will ever destroy it. In summary, we look forward to eternal life because we know that it will bring with it the fullness of a close intimate relationship with God, where God will actually dwell among us, as we live in a new heaven and new earth. We will experience the bliss of sheer happiness in a Garden of Eden-like state. It will be a state of ultimate peace, joy, and love—the ultimate fulfillment of our decision to trust and follow Jesus. 54

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES 9 FIVE END-TIME FRAMEWORKS So far in this this eBook, we have reviewed what Scripture teaches about clear and core end-times teaching. These teachings are emphasized in Scripture and are reflected in the beliefs of the earliest Christians.39 By way of review, here are the five core, orthodox elements we have looked at up to this point: The second coming The resurrection of the dead The final judgment Hell The new heaven and new earth Again, they are the focus of what Scripture teaches about end things and should be foundational to our beliefs. When it comes to other end-times teaching, however, there are multiple issues that can come up which are not core or essential to one’s salvation. Faithful, thoughtful Christians can respectfully disagree on these secondary - and third - level issues without it affecting the integrity of their Christian faith. Recall the following diagram we at Renew.org use to help delineate between the essential elements of the faith and other elements that might be important (second bucket) or personal (third bucket). Again, some describe the different levels of belief using the metaphor of how things can be written—in blood, ink, or pencil. 39 Dayton Hartman does a good job in showing how these five elements are key. He demonstrates their connection to the early creeds as a key benchmark. See Jesus Wins: The Good News of the End Times (Bellingham, WA: Lexham Press, 2019). 55

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES In case you missed it in chapter 2, we believe the following five end-time elements are best categorized as important and/or personal. But again, they are not essential elements. We can be saved without a correct understanding of them. The Millennium – a 1000-year reign of peace described in Revelation 2040 The Antichrist (and other evil leaders) – an evil figure possibly described in 2 Thessalonians 2 and Revelation 1341 The Rapture – the possibility that all Christians will rise up to meet Christ before he returns, often seen as a way of separation so that Christians avoid the judgment of the tribulation42 The Tribulation – the possibility of a set, 7-year period of cosmic disasters, persecution, and evil before the final end43 The restoration of ethnic Israel – the restoration of Jewish people and Jerusalem into God’s final plans44 As a case in point, one of the most prominent nonessential issues which should interest students of the Bible is what to do with the 1,000 years (the “Millennium”) of Revelation 20. Here is how the apostle John describes it: 40 See Robert Clouse, The Meaning of the Millennium: Four Views (Downers Grove: InterVarsity Press, 1977). 41 See Kim Riddlebarger, The Man of Sin: Uncovering the truth about the Antichrist (Baker, 2006), and Robert Gundry, First the Antichrist (Grand Rapids: Baker Books, 1997). 42 See Gleason Archer, Paul Feinberg, Douglas Moo, and Richard Reiter, The Rapture: Pre, Mid, or Post-Tribulational? (Grand Rapids: Zondervan, 1984) and Dave MacPherson, The Incredible Cover-Up (Medford: Omega Publications, 1975). 43 See Cornelius P. Venema, The Promise of the Future (The Banner of Truth Trust, 2000), George Ladd, Last Things (Grand Rapids: Wm. B. Eerdmans Pub. Co., 1978), and Louis Berkof, Systematic Theology (Grand Rapids: Wm B. Eerdmans, 1939). 44 See Bock and Glaser, To the Jew First: The Case for Jewish Evangelism in Scripture and History (Kregel, 2008), Hans K. LaRondelle, The Israel of God in Prophecy (Berrien Springs: Andrews University Press, 1983) and Louis Berkof, Systematic Theology (Grand Rapids: Wm B. Eerdmans, 1939). 56

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES “And I saw an angel coming down out of heaven, having the key to the Abyss and holding in his hand a great chain. He seized the dragon, that ancient serpent, who is the devil, or Satan, and bound him for a thousand years. He threw him into the Abyss, and locked and sealed it over him, to keep him from deceiving the nations anymore until the thousand years were ended. After that, he must be set free for a short time.” (Revelation 20:1-3) Is this millennium meant to describe a time period of 1,000 365-day years? Or is it meant to be symbolic for something else? And when will this millennium occur? Or has it occurred already? There are faithful, intelligent Christians who hold varying views on the millennium. There are five major models or paradigms of end-time teachings to which true disciples of Jesus hold, and they largely center on how to conceptualize the millennium of Revelation 20. As long as we agree on the five key end-time teachings (described throughout the previous chapters), we want to be careful to work with and not divide from those who hold each of these five secondary views. As you read the summaries, you might take note of how each one incorporates the five essential beliefs described in the previous chapters. You will be able to find out more about how we (Bobby and Anthony) understand these points of view if you check out season 4 of our podcast on YouTube called, “Scripture in Black and White.” 1. Preterist Amillennialism (pronounced ah-millennialism) The big idea here is that the vast majority of prophecy is complete. The events in Revelation are by and large symbolic imagery about events in the past. The book of Revelation is written using ancient symbols and imagery of things that were fulfilled in the first century or two. Preteristic amillennialists (as with historic amillennialists) believe that Jesus is currently reigning in heaven and on earth, through the church. The 1000 years are symbolic of a long, undefined time which began when Jesus rose from the dead, bound Satan, and the church was unleashed. The only outstanding expectation is the second coming of Jesus, the resurrection of the dead, the final judgment, and heaven and hell. The majority of Old Testament prophecy has been fulfilled in the past in ancient Israel or in the church. The book of Revelation was written to describe events in the first century, and all references to the tribulations, the Antichrist, and Israel were symbolic or metaphorical images to things already fulfilled in the past. 57

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES The following diagram is a summary of this view. You can find out more about this view in R.C. Sproul’s book, The Last Days According to Jesus: When Did Jesus Say He Would Return (Baker, 2015). 2. Classic Amillennialism These Christians believe that Jesus is currently reigning in heaven and on earth, through the church. The 1000 years are metaphorical years, used for a long, undefined time which began when Jesus rose from the dead, bound Satan, and the church was unleashed. Again, this understanding holds that the 1,000 years are not literal but symbolic (similarly to how Plato used the figure in literature which would have been widely known in the ancient world). Because Satan is bound and demonic influence is somewhat limited, he cannot stop the church from expanding into the whole world. This reign will last until just before the end, when Satan is unleashed for a time. Augustine, the famous Christian writer in the A.D. 400s, championed this view—and it was adopted by Roman Catholics and initially by most Protestants. Christ is ruling in heaven—with the dead—and through the church. At the same time, because the world itself is full of turmoil and evil, there will be growing wickedness and tribulation in the world. Jesus’ return will save his followers from annihilation at the hands of evil forces. His second coming will usher in the final judgment and then the full consummation of his kingdom. 58

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES The following diagram is a summary of this view. This is Bobby’s personal viewpoint. You can find out more about this view in Cornelius P. Venema, The Promise of the Future (The Banner of Truth Trust, 2000). 3. Historic Premillennialism These Christians believe that when Jesus returns to the earth, he will personally usher in a literal 1000-year period of peace and prosperity on earth. Before the return of Jesus and his 1000-year reign, there will be decline, conflict, and a great tribulation. There will be cosmic disruptions, as well as false teachers and an Antichrist figure. But then Jesus will return and reign on earth for 1,000 years. Yet, after the 1000-year reign, again, there will be growing wickedness, as Satan is once more allowed to deceive the nations. But then God intervenes and institutes the final judgment, and Satan is finally defeated. This view was popular in the early church and is a widely held view by many evangelical scholars today. The following diagram is a summary of this view. 59

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES You can find out more about this view in Craig Blomberg and Suny Wook Chung, The Case for Historic Premillennialism (Grand Rapids: Baker Academic, 2009). 4. Dispensational Premillennialism Starting around 1830, there was a group of Christians who heavily stressed a distinction between God’s dealings with Israel and the Church. They advocated that history should be divided up into different periods called “dispensations.” In each of these dispensations, God deals differently with people. Thus, many Old Testament promises were never meant to apply to the church (as the other perspectives typically believe), but they will apply to Israel at the end of time, when God focuses back on that dispensation. Based upon a unique and recent understanding of Daniel 9, they came to believe that seven years before the full second coming of Jesus (they believe the second coming will be in two parts), there will be a partial coming where Jesus secretly removes (raptures) Christians before the tribulation that will come. After the rapture, God’s attention will be focused on Israel. There will be a short, but terrible, period of tribulation that stops when Jesus returns. Jesus will then personally usher in a literal 1000-year period of peace and prosperity on earth, which again will be followed by an apostasy. God intervenes and brings about the final judgment, after which people will face an eternal destiny in hell or in the new heaven and new earth. This view became popular among many evangelicals in the USA because of the Scofield Reference Bible (first published in 1909), Dallas Theological Seminary, and books such as Hal Lindsey’s Late Great Planet Earth and the Left Behind series by LaHaye and Jenkins. The following diagram is a summary of this view. 60

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES You can find out more about this view in a book by Craig Blaising and Darrell Bock, Progressive Dispensationalism (Grand Rapids: Baker Academic, 2000). 5. Postmillennialism These Christians believe we will experience a golden age of earthly peace in the future before Jesus returns. It may be 1000 years, but that number likely is symbolic and signifies a long period of “good times on earth.” The condition of the world gets better and better. Despite setbacks along the way, the Church will gradually convert the world through the preaching of the gospel, most people in the world will become Christians, there will be peace on earth, and life will get better and better. At the end of this “golden age,” Christ will return, the dead will be raised, the final judgment will be pronounced, and the new heavens and the new earth will be revealed. This is the favorite view of liberal Protestants, but it was also the view of early Puritans such as Jonathan Edwards. The following diagram is a summary of this view. You can find out more about this view in a book by Douglas Wilson, Heaven Misplaced: Christ’s Kingdom on Earth (Canon Press, 2008). Did you read anything in the five descriptions which you did not agree with? Likely, you did. Yet did you read anything which disagrees with the essential beliefs of Christianity? No, 61

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES everything you read is in line with Christianity’s essentials, even though there are significant differences between the millennial views. Contrast the essential agreement shared by the five views above with a radical version of the fifth view (Preterist Amillennialism) called Extreme Preterism: Extreme Preterism A small number of amillennialists are hyper-preterists. They take the view that Jesus’ second coming and the resurrection of the dead have already occurred. The second coming and final resurrection were actually spiritual events tied to the destruction of the temple in Jerusalem in A.D. 70. Extreme preterism is heretical because it denies the natural biblical and historic understanding of three key essentials: a future second coming, a future resurrection of the dead, and a future final judgment. Again, these three doctrines are embedded in the essentials of New Testament teaching, and they are imbedded in early Christian faith statements: 1) the rule of faith45 and 2) the Apostles’ and Nicene creeds. Conclusion As we saw from the first five positions, discussing end times is often a matter of agreeing on the essentials but disagreeing on the nonessentials. Such disagreements are meant to be mutually sharpening and to encourage us to study the text more carefully, even as we reaffirm our fellowship with each other. Yet, as we see from the Extreme Preterist position, end-times views can drift far enough away from the essentials of the Bible that they become dangerous to the person who holds them. It takes discernment to know the difference, and in order to develop this discernment, we need to be humble and serious students of the Bible. Reflecting on the Bible’s end-times teachings can engage many of our emotions: urgency, fear, and excitement, to name a few. But above all, the Bible’s end-times teachings are meant to 45 Everett Ferguson, The Rule of Faith: A Guide (Eugene: Wipf and Stock Publishers, 2015). 62

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES fuel our hope, because they remind us of where our ultimate hope lies and that our hope is on its way. This is why the Bible’s final verses end on a shining note of hope, as we eagerly await the return of King Jesus: “He who testifies to these things says, ‘Yes, I am coming soon.’ Amen. Come, Lord Jesus. The grace of the Lord Jesus be with God’s people. Amen.” (Revelation 22:20-21) 63

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES 10 PLACE YOUR FAITH IN JESUS The subtitle of this eBook ends with the phrase “why it matters.” The title promises that we’ll explore What the Bible Says About the End Times: What’s to Come and Why It Matters. As you’ve no doubt noticed, the topic of end times brings with it a tremendous sense of personal urgency. These are matters of ultimate concern with the highest stakes imaginable. With that being the case, the most appropriate way to end this eBook is to invite you to put your trust and allegiance in Jesus as Savior, Lord, and King. That’s what this chapter is about. I (Bobby) vividly remember an experience one fall evening when I was sixteen. For some reason, a group of us got together and went down to the river and became heavily involved in a discussion about God. Although we did not attend church, both my sister Lori and I were intensely interested in this conversation. We somehow thought that it was very important to believe in God and that anyone who did not believe in God was morally suspect. There was one girl there that night (a close friend to both of us) who said she did not believe in God. I can still remember the discussion. She stated that many people believe at a deep level. And she understood that faith can be important. But then she stated, in a matter of fact way, that “it doesn’t really matter what you believe, as long as you believe in it deeply.” Her words stood in the air. None of us knew how to respond. Her words sounded both right and wrong at the same time! In fact, although I did not like her statement, it took me awhile before I understood why I thought her comment was wrong. You might think that these were just the muddled thoughts of a sixteen-year-old, but I have found that more adults think this way about faith than you might imagine. Many Christians tell others how important it is to have faith. Then, in response to questions they cannot answer, they say, “I just accept it by faith.” This sounds good and pious, but it is also confusing. 64

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES When someone talks like this, we can find ourselves wrestling with the whole concept of faith. Such statements naturally make us wonder about the validity of Christian beliefs. Couldn’t someone else with as much validity say, “I just accept the Great Pumpkin by faith.” How can it be virtuous—in and of itself—to “just accept something by faith”? Faith in Jesus Biblical definitions and teachings can help us understand what biblical faith actually is. Hebrews 11 gives us examples of people who had faith. Abel had faith: God told him to provide an offering and he did it (Hebrews 11:4). Noah had faith: God warned him about a flood, and he built an ark (Hebrews 11:7). Abraham had faith: God told him to leave his home country, and he packed his bags and left (Hebrews 11:8-9). In each of these examples, we can see how God gave people a foundation for faith and, based upon that foundation, they made an informed decision to trust God and follow him. Before they responded in faith, God spoke to them, giving them a foundation from which faith could spring forth. It has helped me a great deal to learn that faith, according to the Bible, is an informed and reasonable trust in God. Faith is based on evidence, yet it goes a step beyond evidence. Most Christians have looked into their hearts and believed in Jesus based upon subjective and intuitive evidence (spiritual promptings) which makes them think that Christianity must be true.46 They also look at the teachings of Christ and the lives of those who truly follow him and reason that this way of life is right and must be true. Many have also researched the historical, philosophical, and scientific evidence for Christianity and found that good objective evidence supports faith. This evidence does not prove that faith is right in some kind of mathematical formula, but it supports and affirms it. We might say that faith stands between knowledge and opinion.47 Faith is based upon good evidence, but the evidence is incomplete; it leaves room for doubt. If there were no room for doubt, there would be no room for faith. 46 At this basic level, believing is like being in love. One falls in love because of subjective and intuitive factors. But these are often valid factors. 47 Arlie Hoover, Fallacies of Unbelief (Abilene: Biblical Research Press, 1975), 9. 65

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES In our first chapter, I (Bobby) mentioned my gospel “elevator speech” in which I can summarize my faith in Jesus. I include it here again. If you haven’t yet placed your faith in Jesus, then this is me making my elevator speech to you. God sent Jesus Christ into this world to show us the way to live by his life and teachings. He died on the cross to take away your sins, he rose from the dead, launched his eternal kingdom, and he is now enthroned as humanity’s Saving King at God’s right hand. Only King Jesus can save us from sin, Satan and eternal peril and give us kingdom life and his Spirit, here and now. He is coming back for the resurrection of the dead and final judgment. Make the decision to place your faith in him and enter his invisible kingdom, and he will give you the best way to live, both in this world and in the world to come. The fact that Christ died for our sins and is exalted to the right hand of God as King of kings does not save people in and of itself, but it provides the ground or basis upon which God, in full harmony with his holiness, offers to save those who have sinned against him. This salvation is “by grace,” which means that it is offered as a free gift. But it is a conditional gift. It is only granted to those who have faith in Jesus. Ephesians 2:8-10 gives the formula that summarizes the entire teaching on salvation in the Bible:48 “For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith—and this not from yourselves, it is the gift of God—not by works, so that no one can boast. For we are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance for us to do.” A careful reading of this passage shows how salvation works. The only thing of merit in God’s eyes is Jesus Christ and his atoning sacrifice. We respond and receive the merit of Christ as our own through faith. The merit of Christ is why we do not work for a right standing with God and why we cannot boast about it. All we can do is embrace Jesus and embrace a relationship with God, through Jesus by faith. 48 For more information on this theme in Ephesians, see Markus Barth, Ephesians, AB (Garden City: Doubleday, 1974). 66

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES This gracious provision on the cross is the focus of our faith. We believe that when Jesus died and rose from the dead, he paid the entire penalty for our sins, gave us access to his kingdom, gives us new life, both here and now (in this world) and then and there (in the next world). When we truly receive the gift of salvation and God’s grace by faith, we receive a new direction in life. As the end of Ephesians 2:8-10 teaches, those who have been saved by faith are sent forward “to do good works.” Nothing better summarizes the Christian life than this formula: we are saved “by grace through faith” and then “by faith” we are commissioned to do good works and serve God’s purposes. The Meaning of Faith “Faith,” “belief,” and “trust” are all similar, overlapping words in the Bible. The Bible says the entire Christian life is lived by faith. Romans 1:17 in the New Living Translation states it well: “This Good News tells us how God makes us right in his sight. This is accomplished from start to finish by faith. As the Scriptures say, ‘It is through faith that a righteous person has life.” Biblical faith is holistic.49 It starts as a simple trust in the heart, which says “yes” to Jesus and his sacrifice. Once planted, it grows into a living, dynamic power. Over time, it will transform a human life. Faith is the decision to treat the truths about God, Christ, and eternity as though they are as real as anything that can be touched, heard, smelled, tasted, or observed. As Hebrews 11:6 says, “Without faith it is impossible to please God, because anyone who comes to him must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who earnestly seek him.” The most succinct biblical definition of faith can be pictured by the words “allegiance,” “loyalty,” and “faithfulness.” Each of these words get at the heart of a relationship of trust and 49 For a thorough discussion of the biblical nature of faith, in addition to the work by John MacArthur, Jr., in The Gospel According to Jesus (Grand Rapids: Zondervan Publishing House, 1988) and The Gospel According to the Apostles (Nashville: Word Publishing , 2000), see Joseph Fitzmyer, Paul and His Theology: A Brief Sketch (Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey: Prentice Hall, 1987), p. 85ff and especially Everett Ferguson, The Church of Christ (Grand Rapids: Wm. B. Eerdmans, 1996), p. 165ff. 67

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES commitment. We sometimes say faith is to both trust and follow God through Jesus. Faith transforms the entire person—heart, mind, and will. In fact, all three elements must be involved. Jim Peterson offers us a very good analogy of this truth. “For example, a young man meets a young woman. They are immediately attracted to one another. They both say to themselves, ‘Now there is someone I’d like to marry.’ At that point, if the emotions had their way, there would be a wedding. But the intellect intervenes, questioning the impulsive emotional response. Would we be compatible? What is she really like? Can I afford to support her? Both conclude it would be better to take some more time and answer a few questions before they proceed. So the two begin spending more time with each other. He eventually concludes that she is as beautiful on the inside as she is on the outside. Now his intellect has sided with the emotions on the idea of marriage. But the final and heaviest vote remains to be cast—that of the will. It stops the march toward the altar with the questions, ‘Am I willing to give up this lifestyle for another? What about my freedom—is it worth the trade? Am I willing to assume the added responsibility?’ The marriage will occur only when the will finally agrees with the emotions and the intellect.”50 What happens in conversion and in the Christian life is very similar to this description of a marriage. True faith will involve the whole person. 1. Faith is a rational, factual, and mental assent. We must believe that Jesus Christ came to the earth to show us the way. We must believe that he reveals God’s way to us in his teaching and by his sacrifice on the cross (2 Peter 1:16-20). The Bible tells us that a Christian must take his or her stand on the historical facts of Jesus Christ and his death, burial, and resurrection. You must factually believe in these things. Even more than that, you must believe them enough to base your eternal destiny upon them (1 Corinthians 15:1-8). 2. Faith is a subjective, personal reliance. We also must personally rely and trust—in our subjective selves—that when Jesus died, was buried, and rose from the dead, God gave us the means to be forgiven (John 3:16-18; 36). Faith 50 Jim Peterson, Living Proof (Colorado Springs, Colorado: NavPress, 1989), p. 170. 68

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES is more than just a matter of the mind; we believe in our hearts. The apostle Peter describes the emotional elements of the faith. “Though you have not seen him, you love him; and even though you do not see him now, you believe in him and are filled with an inexpressible and glorious joy, for you are receiving the goal of your faith, the salvation of your souls.” (1 Peter 1:8-9) 3. Faith is a surrender of the will, an active commitment. We must surrender ourselves to God through Christ, trusting God to save us and enable us to follow him. Our pattern of obedience will ultimately reveal whether or not our will has been surrendered. If we claim to have faith but show a lack of obedience and don’t follow through on Christ’s teachings, something is deeply wrong. Consider these words from the book of James: “What good is it, my brothers, if a man claims to have faith but has no deeds? Can such a faith save him? Suppose a brother or a sister is without clothes and daily food. If one of you says to him, ‘Go, I wish you well; keep warm and well fed,’ but does nothing about his physical needs, what good is it? In the same way, faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action is dead. . . . As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without deeds is dead.” (James 2:14–26) This is why the Bible doesn’t recognize faith unless it leads to obedience. Good works do not earn salvation, but good works reveal the presence of genuine faith and a true “by grace through faith” relationship with God. John MacArthur has articulated the biblical balance properly with these fitting words: “Faith obeys. Unbelief rebels. The fruit of one’s life reveals whether that person is a believer or an unbeliever.”51 The Bible describes it this way: “We know that we have come to know him if we obey his commands. Whoever says, ‘I know him,’ but does not do what he commands is a liar, and the truth is not in that person” (1 John 2: 3-4). 51 John MacArthur, Jr., The Gospel According to Jesus (Grand Rapids: Zondervan Publishing House, 1988), p. 178. 69

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES William Booth, the founder of the Salvation Army, described it this way: “Faith and works should travel side by side, step answering to step, like the legs of men walking. First faith, and then works; and then faith again, and then works again—until they can scarcely distinguish which is the one and which is the other.”52 In short, faith is a “sub-missive trust,” where we depend on Jesus Christ and submit ourselves to God through him. Faith and Discipleship The Bible teaches us that when a person wants to get right with God, he is called to place his faith in Jesus and become Jesus’ disciple. A disciple is simply “a follower,” “a student” or, better yet, “an apprentice.”53 A Christian is an “apprentice” of Jesus Christ who, by faith, trusts and follows him. This was the original mandate that Jesus gave to his apostles. “Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, to the very end of the age.” (Matthew 28:19-20) According to this passage, disciples are those who are baptized in Jesus’ name and who commit to the process of obeying his commands, trusting that he is with us always, to the end of the age. Jesus’ call was both an invitation to salvation and a summons to discipleship.54 A Christian is an apprentice of Jesus Christ who is learning from him how to develop a deep and meaningful relationship with God through faith. The importance of being a disciple is highlighted by the fact that the word for disciple (or disciples) is used over 260 times in the Bible, while the word for Christian (or Christians) is used only three times. Disciples are Christians, but importantly, all Christians are to be disciples. A person simply cannot be a true Christian without being a disciple.55 It would be like trying to be a human without breathing. This truth is a major, fundamental, and underlying theme of the entire New Testament.56 God has saved us through faith in Jesus Christ (Romans 3:22-25), 52 William Booth, “The Founder’s Messages to Soldiers,” Christianity Today, October 5, 1992, p. 48. 53 Dallas Willard, “How To Be A Disciple,” Christian Century (April 22-29, 1998): 430-431. See also Dallas Willard, The Divine Conspiracy (San Francisco: Harper and Row, 1997). 54 Michael Wilkins, Following The Master: A Biblical Theology of Discipleship (Grand Rapids: Zondervan Publishing, 1992), p. 186. 55 See this point explained in the definitive biblical study on discipleship in Michael Wilkins, Following the Master: A Biblical Theology of Discipleship (Grand Rapids: Zondervan Publishing, 1992). 56 See Richard Longenecker (editor), Patterns of Discipleship in the New Testament (Grand Rapids: Wm. B. Eerdmans, 1996). 70

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES and now God is transforming us into the image of Jesus Christ as we follow him and live as his disciples (2 Corinthians 3:16-17). If you are to truly live as a faithful disciple, you need training and encouragement. To reiterate how important discipleship is (as an essential expression of faith), consider the following words spoken by Jesus in the Gospel of Mark. “Then he called the crowd to him along with his disciples and said: ‘If anyone would come after me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for me and for the gospel will save it.’” (Mark 8:34-35) This is a high calling! Which one among us can read this and not feel a little uncertain? “Wow,” we say, “can I really do that? I know my weaknesses and I am sure to stumble and fall.” We may conclude, “I want to live this way, but I do not have the ability.” And it’s true that we do not have the ability, but God will give it to us by his power and his Spirit. God is our helper, and he will enable us to truly follow Jesus. We will not do it perfectly and we will often stumble and fall, but by God’s grace working in us, we will make it.57 Our responsive faith (expressed in our efforts to follow Jesus) and the empowering work of God’s Spirit combine to produce the character of Jesus in our lives. The change in character is often called “spiritual formation.” Dallas Willard describes it this way: “Spiritual formation for the Christian basically refers to the Spirit-driven process of forming the inner world of the human self in such a way that it becomes like the inner being of Christ himself.”58 We like to use the framework of Matthew 4:19 to define a disciple. Jesus said, “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men” (ESV). So, a disciple 1) follows Jesus (“follow me”), 2) is changed by Jesus (“I will make you”) and 3) joins the mission of Jesus (“fishers of men”). When our inner world has been formed in such a way, then our outer actions will be more and more like those of Christ. 57 Joseph Fitzmyer does a good job in explaining biblical faith; see Paul and His Theology: A Brief Sketch (Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey: Prentice Hall, 1987), p. 85. 58 Dallas Willard, Renovation of the Heart (Colorado Springs: NavPress, 2002), p. 22. 71

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES Repentance, Confession, and Baptism The path of salvation and discipleship begins when faith is expressed in conversion. The commitment to place faith in Christ can be understood in three component parts: confession, repentance, and baptism. By his grace, God has provided this complete response so people can concretely express saving faith and experience a holistic conversion experience. 1. Repentance Repentance is an integral part of faith. The Greek word used in the New Testament for repentance (metanoia) literally means, “to have another mind” or “a change of mind.”59 To truly place our faith in Christ, we must make the commitment to turn away from sinful living. In this way, repentance is a necessary part of faith and a requirement God makes for those who wish to receive His salvation. The apostle Paul put it this way: “In the past God overlooked such ignorance, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent. For he has set a day when he will judge the world with justice by the man he has appointed. He has given proof of this to all men by raising him from the dead.” (Acts 17: 30-31) Repentance is a turning from sin to God. It is to turn away from what God says is sinful and turn to Jesus Christ. Genuine repentance is recognized by a sense of sorrow about how we have lived and the commitment that, with God’s help, we will change our ways. As the apostle Paul said, “Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation” (2 Corinthians 7:l0). Repentance is trusting what God says about sin, turning away from sin, and, with God’s help, living apart from the control of sinful lifestyles.60 59 For more information, see Walter Bauer, A Greek-English Lexicon of the New Testament and Other Early Christian Literature. 2nd. ed., revised by William Arndt and F. Wilbur Gingrich (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1979). 60 K. C. Moser, The Way of Salvation (Delight, Arkansas: Gospel Light Publishing Company, 1933), pp. 63-64. 72

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES 2. Confession In its irreducible essence, faith is quite simple. Faith is the pledge in one’s heart to trust and follow Jesus. The following passage shows the fundamental core of the conversion experience. “That if you confess with your mouth, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For it is with your heart that you believe and are justified, and it is with your mouth that you profess your faith and are saved. As Scripture says, ‘Anyone who believes in him will never be put to shame.’” (Romans 10:9-11) This is the essence of Christianity. It is a simple faith, expressed in a brief confession. In the Bible, this confession typically took place just prior to baptism.61 As Jack Cottrell says, “To confess Jesus to be our Lord is thus to confess that He is our owner and we are His slaves. It is the external expression of an internal spirit of complete submission to every aspect of His Word and will.”62 3. Baptism Covenants are a big deal in the Bible. A covenant is a special relationship where two parties formally commit themselves to each other. A covenant is an agreement where God freely binds and commits himself to human beings and human beings respond, in turn, and commit themselves to God. The Israelites had a special covenant relationship with God, where he made them into a nation and gave them a special place in history. God now commits himself to everyone who submissively trusts in Jesus Christ. He promises them the forgiveness of all sins, his personal presence in their lives through the Holy Spirit, and eternal life in heaven. The various parts of the human response of faith (repentance, confession, submission) are concretely embodied in baptism. 61 See C.B. Cranfied, Romans: A Shorter Commentary (Grand Rapids: Wm. B. Eerdmans Publishing, 1985), p. 257. In regard to Romans 10:9-10, he states, “It seems clear that ‘Jesus is Lord’ was already an established confession formula. It is probable that it was used in connection with baptism.” 62 Jack Cottrell, Romans: Volume 2, The College Press NIV Commentary (Joplin, Missouri: College Press, 1998), p. 175. 73

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES Water baptism was the normal means in Scripture by which a person made the formal commitment of faith.63 Faith in Jesus as saving King is the essential response, and baptism is the means of formal expression. Stated differently, baptism is the “new covenant” expression given to those who place their faith in Jesus. The apostle Peter gave an invitation to be baptized to a group of thousands of Jewish people gathered in Jerusalem to hear about Jesus. It was the first public declaration of what it meant to become a Christian after Jesus had ascended into heaven. Notice the emphasis on how baptism is a faith commitment “in Jesus’ name”: “Peter replied, ‘Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins. And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. The promise is for you and your children and for all who are far off — for all whom the Lord our God will call.’” (Acts 2:38-39) Baptism brings the forgiveness of sins and the gift of the indwelling Spirit because it is done in “Jesus’ name.” Placing our faith in Jesus in baptism has many similarities to a marriage ceremony. The Bible uses marriage as a central metaphor for God’s relationship with us. Baptism is a relational commitment to God just as a wedding ceremony is a relational commitment to one’s spouse. I have performed many wedding ceremonies. According to tradition, I always ask the man if he will take the woman to be his wife, promising before God, his family, and friends that he will be a faithful, loving and devoted husband, that he will stay with her in sickness and in health, in prosperity and in adversity, and that he will forsake all others and cling to her alone, so long as they both shall live. Then I turn and ask the woman the same thing. In this pledge, the marriage ceremony is a covenant, an agreement between two parties, where they pledge themselves to each other in the most “sacred of all human relationships.” 63 The position on the meaning of baptism which is sketched out here is the earliest Christian understanding of baptism, reflected in the writing of Christians in the first centuries. See the Nicene Creed of A.D. 381 in The Creeds of Christendom, 3 Volumes, edited by Philip Schaff (Baker Book House: Grand Rapids, 1996). A practical resource for everyday spiritual seekers and Christians is Baptism: What the Bible Teaches, by Tony Twist, Bobby Harrington, and David Young (Renew.org, 2018). It is available as a free download on Renew.org or to purchase on Amazon.com. For the best scholarly and technical resource (by consensus), see Everett Ferguson, Baptism in the Early Church: History, Theology, and Liturgy in the First Five Centuries (Grand Rapids: Wm. B. Eerdmans Publishing Co., 2009). 74

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES Again, baptism is like a wedding ceremony. It includes both verbal commitments (our confession of faith and the words of the one baptizing us) and a sacred ritual (going under water). This ceremony commits us to a covenant relationship with God. The ceremony expresses faith and is grounded in the “by grace through faith” way we are saved (see Ephesians 2:8-10). The Indwelling of the Holy Spirit When we enter into this special relationship, God comes to live within us through the Holy Spirit. The Bible describes it this way: “And now you also have heard the truth, the Good News that God saves you. And when you believed in Christ, he identified you as his own by giving you the Holy Spirit, whom he promised long ago (Ephesians 1:13, NLT). The Holy Spirit is the seed of God’s life in our hearts (1 John 3:9). This biblical doctrine has important practical ramifications. I can remember making the decision to become a Christian and being aware that I had to surrender to Jesus as “Lord.” Yet I had to think through the ramifications of my sinful habits because I knew that to truly surrender to him as “Lord,” I had to make some changes. I was willing to give up my habits, but I was not sure how I was going to do it. Yet, like a child, I knew that I would stumble and fall, but I believed that God could and would work it all out. And, over time, he did. The invisible power of the Holy Spirit is an important reality upon which we must rely. This is the answer for those of us who are afraid to commit ourselves to Christ because we doubt ourselves. We wonder if we can truly follow his teachings and obey his commands, but we must trust God to help us do what we could not do on our own. A few years later, I came across an analogy that has really helped me to understand how God helps us. It goes like this. Imagine being told you will write a play of the quality of Shakespeare’s plays. John Stott described what it would be like if someone told him that he had to do that. “It is no good giving me a play like Hamlet and King Lear, and telling me to write a play like that. Shakespeare could do it; I can’t. And it is no good showing me a life like the life of Jesus and telling me to live a life like that. Jesus could do it; I can’t. But if the genius of 75

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES Shakespeare could come and live in me, then I could write plays like that. And if the Spirit of Jesus could come and live in me, then I could live a life like that.”64 This is the secret of the Christian life: God working in us, giving us the desire and strength to obey him (Philippians 2:13). The important point about living the Christian life is your decision to ask God to give you his heart. If you truly trust God with your decision, he will help you develop a passion to follow him. A young woman once married a tyrannical and oppressive man. He demanded that his wife conform to his rigid standards in all things. He actually made lists of the things she was to do for him each day as a wife, mother, and homemaker. Although she tried hard to please him, she came to hate his rigidity, inflexibility, and lack of grace. Then he suddenly died—a merciful thing in the eyes of many, for she had never learned to truly love him. After a few years, this same woman fell in love with another man, and they got married. But this man was very different. He was full of love and grace. He was personally devoted to her, and she, in turn, was devoted to him. He filled her heart with his love. Then one day, she came across one of the lists of dos and don’ts that her first husband had written. To her amazement, she found that she was willingly doing for her second husband all the things that her first husband had demanded. But she wasn’t even aware of it. The whole Christian concept of having a personal relationship with God is based upon this same point. God gives us his love and grace, as he dwells inside us and walks with us. His Spirit leads us and shows us the way, by softening and leading our hearts into the right path (Romans 8:5-9). By the means of the indwelling Spirit, God comes within us and helps us to want to follow in his ways. The Local Church In New Testament times, those who became Christians always joined a group of fellow believers and became a part of the local church. Throughout the Bible, we see that faith and life 64 John Stott, Basic Christianity (London: InterVarsity Press, 1958), p. 102. 76

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES as a disciple of Jesus is to be expressed and nurtured by involvement in the local church.65 To the amazement of many, there are certain passages in the Bible that can only be obeyed if we are a part of a local church. It is essential to genuine faith. My favorite explanation of the importance of church involvement is an analogy taken from the 1800s before houses were heated by electricity or natural gas. A Christian man stopped attending church. A friend of his was one of the leaders in the local church and grew very concerned. One day the church leader decided to try to help his friend understand the importance of his involvement in the church. He showed up at the door in the middle of winter. The man invited the Christian leader into his home, but the leader said nothing to him. He simply walked into the house, took off his coat and hat and placed it on the coat tree. He then walked over to the fireplace and pulled up a chair. He looked down at the roaring fire for a few minutes. Then he grabbed a coal shovel and moved several of the red-hot coals out and onto the hearth and began to stare at them. Slowly they cooled and became darker and darker. When it appeared that the fire had gone out within the coals, he moved them back into the center of the fire and watched them get red-hot again. Then he stood up, went to the door and put on his coat and hat. He never said a word to his friend the whole time. Finally, as the Christian leader was about to leave, his friend stopped him and said, “I get the point. I will see you at church this coming Sunday.” It was hard for him to argue with such a poignant illustration. Here are some reasons we all need to regularly connect with each other as part of a local church. 1. We need to give and receive encouragement. Church is essential, the Bible tells us, because Christians need to give and receive encouragement. Hebrews 10:23-25 describes the right attitude that we want to develop in regard to church involvement: 65 For a thorough biblical theology of church involvement, see Bobby Harrington, “What is Church? And How Important is It,” https://renew.org/product/what-is-church-and-how-important-is-it/, Stanley Hauerwas and William H. Willimon, Resident Aliens (Nashville: Abingdon Press, 1989), and Robert Banks, Paul’s Idea of Community (Peabody, Massachusetts: Hendrickson Publishers, Revised Edition, 1994). 77

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES “And let us consider how we may spur one another on toward love and good deeds. Let us not give up meeting together, as some are in the habit of doing, but let us encourage one another—and all the more as you see the Day approaching.” It is too hard to live the faithful Christian life without help from others. 2. We need teaching and accountability from other believers. We not only need to give and receive encouragement, but we also need the teaching and guidance of other Christians. The world, which is full of unbelief and the denial of God, can be an extremely difficult place in which to live. Few, if any, can withstand the pressures of living a life consecrated to God without the teaching, support, and, at times, even the loving exhortation and accountability provided by Christian leaders. We need teachers, pastors, and everyday Christians to help show us God’s way (2 Timothy 3:14-4:4; Galatians 6:1-2). 3. We need to serve and help make other disciples. The church is the body of Christ, the physical presence of God in the world. The outside world sees Jesus Christ through his church body. Each of us, as human beings, has a body. Our bodies are comprised of various parts: hands, feet, eyes, lips, etc. Each of these parts of our bodies is critically important. Each Christian in the local church serves as an important part of the church body. Some people, continuing the analogy, serve as eyes, some as ears, some as feet, etc. Each Christian is an integral part, with an indispensable role. If a Christian should choose to withdraw from the body of Christ, then the body is hurt or crippled. The Bible teaches us that each person must assume his or her responsibilities in the church, “the body of Christ” (Romans 12:3-8; 1 Peter 4:10-11). Discipleship and the Christian life require a communal faith. We are to follow Christ with others. We need to be discipled and to make disciples. Christianity is personal, but not private. It is meant to be communal. God designed it this way. 78

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES It Is a Decision By faith, we enter into a relationship with God based on his grace revealed in Jesus Christ. God continues to provide us with his grace as we trust him in such a way that it transforms our lives. At this point in the eBook, you might be thinking about making a personal decision to trust and follow Jesus. Only you can make it. No one can do it for you. Momentous and life-changing decisions can be gut-wrenching. Perhaps another story will help. During the terrible days of Germany’s bombardment of London in World War II, a father, holding his small son by the hand, ran from a building that had been struck by a bomb. There was a big hole in the front yard of their house, from a bomb that had fallen on another occasion. The hole provided shelter from the falling debris and so the father jumped in it as quickly as possible. Down below, outside the vision of his son, he held up his arms for his son to follow. Terrified, yet hearing his father’s voice telling him to jump, the boy replied, “I can’t see you!” The father looked up from the hole and could see the shades and colors of wildly burning buildings. He saw the shadow of his son and called to him, “I know you can’t see me, but I can see you. Jump!” The boy hesitated but then jumped. The boy jumped because he knew enough about his father to trust him, even when he could not see him. That is the way of faith. We don’t know everything, but we know enough. We know enough to know that Jesus is worth trusting and following—and that even if we don’t see everything with perfect clarity, God sees us, he loves us, and he will catch us. And then we jump. We make the decision to trust and follow Jesus, expressing our faith in Jesus in repentance and baptism. We are born again, we enter Jesus’ kingdom, and we start living the most meaningful life possible—a life that doesn’t end in death, but which simply moves from life to life. What is holding you back from making that decision now? 79

pages.title: [CHAPTER] WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES
pages.content: WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT END TIMES INTRODUCTION A recent study by Pew Research found that about four in ten U.S. adults believe humanity is “living in the end times.”1 Their research found that Christians in America “are divided on this question, with 47% saying we are living in the end times, including majorities in the historically Black (76%) and evangelical (63%) Protestant traditions.”2 Those percentages tell us that a lot of Americans, especially Black and evangelical Christians, not only believe in the reality of end times, but that we are living in those times. How about you? What do you believe? And do you believe the Bible gives us accessible answers to these questions? This topic can be a difficult one. There are so many different beliefs and perspectives. This preacher says one thing; another preacher says something different. Some churches teach one perspective; the next church down the street teaches a different one. And then there are popular podcasts and books that teach still different perspectives. Then comes the hardest observation of all: the Bible itself seems hard to understand or even contradictory on these questions. How can an everyday person make sense out of this complicated topic? We want to help you. To show you what the Bible teaches, we are going to focus in on the basics.
