pages.content: Page intentionally left blank FOREWORD From an early age, I’ve told my kids that the truth is your friend. Truth can be hard to hear. Truth can be hard to accept. Truth can be even harder to center your life on. Today, we find a new struggle when it comes to truth: it is becoming ever harder to find. While truth is a friend, decep- tion is our neighbor. An ever-increasing avalanche of false information has caused a generation to live in constant suspicion and doubt. Let’s be honest. Generally speaking, it’s harder being a young person in this culture than it was for adults growing up. I know I wouldn’t want to trade places. I don’t envy the barrages they face daily. Surrounded by technological community, they feel isolated. With more information than at any other point in history, they don’t feel they can trust what they see and hear. While every gener- ation has faced an assault on truth, this generation receives fallacy as fact every minute of every day. They don’t feel they can trust the news. They no longer trust political power. They doubt adults in their life because they don’t know where the adults get their information. They look with skepticism at nearly everything, including the church. This book is an important tool to help young people set a firm foundation built on biblical truth that will serve them for a lifetime. Andrew and Daniel set out to invite students to search, speak, and build a theology of truth. A theology of truth that they will build, so when things get hard, they know not just what they believe but also why they believe. Andrew and Daniel offer deep biblical principles and allow students space to dive into Scripture. This book will help create healthy disci- pleship to build a faith that can stand in the storm. The church needs this book. We’ve longed for biblical teaching we can trust and tools that actu- ally help students solidify their story. Young people need this foundation. They will continue to be barraged with technology, and their trust in nearly all systems of power will continue to erode. So let’s give this next generation a rock to build on and not sand. I’m incredibly excited for this next generation. They question everything, which can be a won- derful thing for the church. In light of our current culture, we want them to question; we need 11

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook them to question. This book provides a framework for healthy conversations that will lead them to a truth they can trust. The doors for the gospel conversations are wide open for this generation. While they look with suspicion and are slow to trust, the good news is that when they receive truth, they will share it. They are one of the more evangelistic generations we’ve ever seen. What a beautiful collision! Truth seekers who will also be truth speakers! Let’s empower them with a foundation they trust and tools to help them on the journey. We have an incredible opportunity to raise up a generation of kingdom workers unlike anything we have seen in our lifetime. Don’t believe the lies you hear about this generation. I see over fifty thousand young people every year at our Christ In Youth conferences, and I can tell you firsthand, they are an incredible generation. Leaders, lean into this book. Let’s equip our young people for acts of service. Parents, walk with your young people through this book, and may they in turn walk with Jesus all the days of their lives. Students, you are God’s workmanship, his handiwork, and you were created to do good work. Dive into this book to prepare yourself for the hard work ahead. We are counting on you to lead the church. — Jayson French, President, Christ In Youth 12 BEFORE YOU GET STARTED . . . Thanks so much for picking up this book! We assume that you hope to grow and that’s why you picked up this book. And we wrote this handbook to help guide you into a very important type of growth: the kind that comes from believ- ing and living the truth. This book is an interactive summary of the twelve-book Real Life Theology series. We call this family of books “real life theology” because • We want to help you cultivate true beliefs about God (“theology”). • We want these beliefs to influence how you live (“real life”). So you’re going to find material in this book that challenges you to grow. You’ll read about import- ant beliefs that need to become core convictions—and you’ll get space to think about how these convictions can be lived out in real life. But be forewarned: this kind of spiritual and inner growth doesn’t happen automatically, such as when kids grow taller. Even with inner growth in the right direction, you’ll find that stagnation occurs pretty easily. Then how do we grow? What kind of “soil” helps us grow? • Goodness? Some people think convictions and character grow in the soil of personal goodness. As in, I’m going to be able to grow because I’m a good person. But that’s not how this works. We’ve all got some significant weaknesses (especially what the Bible calls “sin”) that make us unable to grow ourselves just by being “good people.” • Guilt? Some people think if they just feel guilty enough and get down on themselves enough, then they’ll grow. But that’s not how this works either. If focusing on our goodness and feeling guilt don’t help us grow, then what soil does? • Grace. If you really want to grow (and we certainly hope this handbook helps you grow), it’s going to happen in the soil of grace. Grace is God’s favor and forgiveness that he freely gives 13

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook us. Everyone needs God’s grace every day, and you’ll certainly need to receive God’s grace along the way if you’re going to let these chapters help you grow. Thankfully, God’s grace is stronger and more stubborn than all our weaknesses put together. He just keeps giving it and giving it. As John 1:16 puts it, “Out of his fullness we have all received grace in place of grace already given.” Thank God for grace. Just a quick note about the structure of the chapters. The thirteen chapters follow this pattern: • Self-Assessments: A straightforward look at your options and space to get honest about where you are. • Study: Helpful tools for digging into crucial questions, such as: How did we get the Bible? Should suffering weaken or strengthen our faith? • Scripture: Space for wrestling with the meaning of important Bible verses and how we can embrace their significance in our lives. • Snapshot: A story of an everyday disciple of Jesus who applied these truths to their life. • Summary: A three-point summary of the main truths of the chapter. • Self-Reflection and Discussion: A list of questions about the chapter’s main ideas for individual reflection or group discussion. • Study More: A list of recommended resources for further study. Throughout the book, there will be opportunities to look up Scriptures and journal your thoughts. So you might have a Bible and pen/pencil ready. This book is written in such a way that you can go through it by yourself, OR you can work through it together as a group. If You Walk Through This Book as a Group . . . • The chapters are written so you could either do one chapter per week (thirteen weeks total) or one chapter over two weeks (twenty-six weeks total). • If your group spends two weeks on each chapter, we recommend doing the Self-Assessments, Study, and Scripture the first week, and then the Snapshot, Summary, and Self-Reflection and Discussion the second week. • Watch for the “Let’s Talk About This” icon throughout each chapter. These indicate sections that are ideal for group discussion. 14 Before You Get Started . . . Let’s start with a prayer: Our Father in heaven, we thank you so much for your patience with us and your grace for us. Left to ourselves, we fall far short of what you created us to be. But it’s not our performance that gives us our identity; rather, it’s your grace that makes us who we are. “But by the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15:10). By your grace, we are your beloved children, and we are so thankful to be part of your family, growing day by day into the likeness of your Son. We pray that you will use this handbook to help people grow into what you created them to be. Thank you. Grateful, — Daniel and Andrew 15

pages.content: Page intentionally left blank 11 HOW DO I RESPOND TO TRUTH? We’ve all been there. Sometimes you hear truth that isn’t fun to hear. Maybe you do something wrong, and someone confronts you. Maybe you believe something untrue, and someone cor- rects you. And you know they’re right, and it doesn’t feel great. When you hear truth—especially truth you don’t really want to hear—how do you respond? There are basically three ways to respond. Take a couple minutes and ask yourself which of these three sounds most like how you respond to truth. Answer honestly. Option 1: I run from truth. One of the earliest Christians was a guy named Stephen. When it came to convincing people to trust and follow Jesus, he was pretty persuasive. The leaders in charge didn’t like his growing influence, so they arrested him and put him on trial. This was the same court that had put Jesus on trial—and the trial didn’t end well for Jesus. If Stephen was afraid, he didn’t show it. In front of the court, he used the opportunity he could have taken to defend himself to give a sermon about Jesus instead. The leaders became so angry upon hearing Stephen’s words that they “covered their ears and, yelling at the top of their voices, they all rushed at him, dragged him out of the city and began to stone him” (Acts 7:57–58). Covering your ears, yelling, and trying to silence the truth-teller is a picture of running from the truth. Maybe for you, this looks like avoidance: you stay away from people who tell you truth you don’t want to hear. Or maybe it looks like arguing as you shut down what you don’t want to hear by raising the volume. Option 2: I create truth. The German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) was a preacher’s kid who became an atheist. He believed that God didn’t exist and that Christianity was bad for society because it taught that everybody is equally important in God’s eyes. For Nietzsche, society needed to let strong peo- ple rule over lesser people as they saw fit. In fact, since God wasn’t around to tell us what’s true and false, the strong ones should create truth in their own image. 17

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook “Metamorphosis” is a word that means a core change, like what happens when a caterpillar becomes a butterfly. Nietzsche thought that humans need to undergo three metamorphoses. First, because of all the burdens of life, the human spirit becomes a weighed-down camel. Next, the cam- el transforms into a lion. As a lion, the human spirit can tear down all the commands (all the “thou shalt” commands” and “thou shalt not” commands) that are hard to follow. Finally, now that the lion is free, it transforms into a child. Why a child? Well, a child is inventive and playful. Children play games and create their own realities.1 According to Nietzsche, without the existence of God, like children, we’re able to define our own reality and create our own truth. Instead of discovering truth, we can create truth. So instead of calling it the truth, maybe you talk about “my truth” and “your truth.” And if someone questions you, then you can ask, “Who are you to challenge my truth?” Option 3: I seek truth. Plato is probably the most famous philosopher who ever lived. He once told a parable about a group of captives chained up in a cave from birth. They were bound so they could face only one direction their entire lives, which happened to be the back wall of the cave. One of the captives broke free and felt his way through the cave until he saw a faint glow, which grew brighter until he finally arrived at the mouth of the cave. Then outside the cave’s entrance were glorious sights he had never seen before: grass, trees, the sky, the sun! Transfixed by the beauty of this reality, he made his way back through the cave to awaken the rest of the captives and tell them about the true world they were missing out on. Annoyed, they killed him. This parable was personal to Plato because it described what had happened to his mentor Soc- rates, who had pursued truth until the authorities put him on trial and eventually had him killed. This parable is also a picture of seeking truth. Seeking truth means that you see truth as light in the darkness—and you follow it at whatever cost. This means having curiosity and wanting to learn and grow. This means doing what James 1:19 says: when someone says something that’s true but tough to hear, you are “quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to become angry.” It means being grateful to receive truth even if it isn’t fun to hear. SELF-ASSESSMENT My three main options when it comes to truth are: 1. I run from truth. 2. I create truth. 3. I seek truth. 18 How Do I Respond to Truth? When it comes to responding to truth, here’s how I would describe where I am: When it comes to responding to truth, here’s where I want to be and why I want to be there: If you choose to be a seeker of truth, then you’ll find freedom. You’ll find freedom from destructive choices. You’ll find freedom to be who God created you to be. Here’s what Jesus said about people who seek the truth: “If you hold to my teaching, you are really my disciples. Then you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John 8:31–32). Definition: Truth Definition: General Revelation Conformity with reality. A statement What God has revealed that has been made available is true when it corresponds with what to all people, not just to his chosen people (e.g., what actually is (i.e., with reality). God has revealed about himself through nature). Definition: Opinion Definition: Special Revelation What a person believes to be true, What God has revealed to specific people in specific which may be true or false. times and circumstances (e.g., prophecies and mira- cles that God accomplished in ancient Israel’s history). STUDY How should you respond to truth? Here are some thoughts to help you as you wrestle with this question. Can We Know Truth About God? It’s clear that we can know truth when it comes to the world around us. We can know things like the speed of light and the temperature at which water boils. But what about when it comes to God? Can we know truth about God? 19

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook Some people say no. Why not? Well, God isn’t physical, so how can we know truth about him? A British philosopher named David Hume reasoned that the only things that count as true are: 1. Statements that are already true by definition (such as 1+1=2) 2. Statements about the physical world around us Hume put it this way: “Does it contain any abstract reasoning concerning quantity or number? No. Does it contain any experimental reasoning concerning matter of fact and existence? No. Com- mit it then to the flames: for it can contain nothing but sophistry and illusion.”2 But if Hume was right, then what about his own statement? Is his statement about truth some- thing that is true by definition, such as a mathematical statement? No. Is his statement about truth something that we can discover by exploring the physical world? Nope. Then by his very logic, his own statement should be “committed to the flames.” The truth is if God created us and the world around us, we can know quite a bit of truth about him just from looking at creation: we can know God is powerful, creative, and intelligent. “General revelation” is a term for how God reveals himself to everybody at all times through creation. WE CAN And God also revealed himself throughout history in various ways (e.g., KNOW GOD IS speaking through messengers and doing miracles). “Special revelation” is a term POWERFUL, for how God reveals himself throughout history in particular ways to people. So, CREATIVE, AND for example, God revealed himself to Abram, promising that his descendants INTELLIGENT. would be a great nation whom God would use to bless all nations. God revealed himself to Moses, telling him that he would be God’s instrument for deliver- ing his people from slavery. God also inspired people to write these and other stories down, so that we have a book, called the Bible, filled with accounts of God revealing himself in particular ways throughout history. So, yes, we can know truth when it comes to God. How? Because he revealed himself to people. Don’t Fall for This Contradiction Believing a lie is easy when you haven’t heard the whole story. But have you ever wondered how peo- ple can believe things that are clearly not true? We’d like to tell you a statement that is about as clearly false as any statement could ever be. Yet a lot of people believe it. Let’s look at the statement, and then we’ll talk about why a lot of people can still believe it’s true. Here’s the statement: all religions are basically true. 20 How Do I Respond to Truth? Here’s why the statement is clearly false: Inside this statement are literally thousands of contra- dictions. For example, pick any two religions. Let’s say Islam and Christianity. If you say they are both true, then you are saying that Jesus is both the Son of God (Christianity) and definitely not the Son of God (Islam). You are saying that God is both a triune (three-in-one) God (Christianity) and most certainly not a triune God (Islam). You are saying that the New Testament is both God’s authoritative message (Christianity) and is not God’s authoritative message but a corrupted version of Jesus’ true teachings (Islam). That’s just scratching the surface of the many deep differences between Islam and Christiani- ty. And those are just two religions. Islam and Christianity are a lot closer to each other than, say, Islam and Buddhism. To say, “All religions are basically true” is to say that thousands of fundamen- tal beliefs that cancel each other out are all somehow true at the same time. Saying all religions are basically true with a straight face should be impossible. But it’s not. Lots of people believe it very sincerely. In fact, some believe it so passionately that when they meet some- one who believes Christianity is the only religion that accurately tells us the way of salvation, they get angry. Now why do intelligent people believe that all religions are true when that involves believing thousands of contradictions? Here’s why: They have come to assume that the point of religion is to help you get through this life. Want to be a better student or a kinder person, to have inspiration for your mundane moments, to have a better marriage, or to ensure safety for the upcoming trip or good weather for the upcoming holiday? Religion can help. Most days, people just look to make it through life because it can be stress- ful, confusing, lonely, and dark. We all need help making it through. And you can probably find parts of any religion that can help you cope in various CHRISTIANITY ways. You’ll find ethical principles and stress-reducing techniques all over the TEACHES MORE religious map. THAN JUST Without question, Christianity helps people get through life. It certainly HOW TO GET helps us get through tough times, and we’re thankful it does. But that’s not all THROUGH LIFE. that Christianity is meant to do. Christianity also teaches about who God is, IT PREPARES US what lies beyond this life, and how to receive salvation. In other words, Christi- FOR THE NEXT. anity teaches more than just how to get through life. It prepares us for the next. 21

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook SCRIPTURE What does each passage teach me about what it means to be a seeker of the truth? Jesus said, “Everyone on the side of truth listens to me.” (John 18:37b) “Each of you must put off falsehood and speak truthfully to your neighbor.” (Ephesians 4:25a) “They exchanged the truth about God for a lie, and worshiped and served created things rather than the Creator—who is forever praised. Amen. Because of this, God gave them over to shameful lusts.” (Romans 1:25–26a) “If one of you should wander from the truth and someone should bring that person back, remember this: Whoever turns a sinner from the error of their way will save them from death and cover over a multitude of sins.” (James 5:19–20) Jesus answered, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.” (John 14:6) SNAPSHOT . . . FROM NEPAL I was born into a small family in rural South Nepal. My family are from a low caste, the Dalit. Thus, I was never allowed to enter any temple or even have any association or interaction with any 22 How Do I Respond to Truth? high caste people because of the rules and regulations within Nepal’s caste system. Being from the Dalit, I learned at a young age always to obey all the rules but was never told why. My parents used to tell me, “This is the way it is.” I was not able to understand why these rules existed and why no one could explain their history to me. I was born into it and had to live isolated from most of society, which led to a lot of frustra- tion and humiliation. In school, I was never permitted to sit on the same bench or at the same desk with higher caste members, and I grew up very lonely. I had a lot of questions in my mind but no answers. One day I heard about a man named Jesus who loves everyone equally—without any discrimination—and provides salvation not only from social injustice but also from all sins. And through him, we can have eternal life. The day I heard that news was the happiest day of my life, and that day I accepted Christ in my life. The decision to accept Jesus came at a price, however, as others in my village constantly beat me because I had become a Christian. The unanswered questions I had while being a Hindu caused me to dive deep into my newfound faith. For the first time in my life, I found freedom. I found truth. I found that Christianity didn’t have questions that couldn’t be answered, but rather it offered answers to all my questions. I knew I couldn’t keep Jesus to myself, and I wanted to share him with every- one around me, including my family. I met a spiritual mentor who encouraged me I KNEW I to enroll in a discipleship course. I took the class and through it decided to become a COULDN’T full-time pastor. My mentor helped train me to become a pastor. KEEP JESUS I know the risks of being a pastor and the cost of being a disciple in my village, TO MYSELF. but I continue to share Jesus today. I continue to preach and teach God’s Word wher- ever and however I can. I have a deep love for God’s Word and love offering my neigh- bors and friends answers to the questions they have. I deeply treasure God’s Word because all God’s answers are found in it. I know the power of God’s Word and that “all Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16–17). — Siddhilal, Nepal SUMMARY 1. So many voices in our lives claim to be the truth. But we get to determine which voice speaks loudest in our lives. 2. Telling people the truth is loving. 3. We must pick wisely what will be our main source of truth. 23

What did you like about this passage? 25

pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook 2. What was hard to understand? 3. What does this passage teach about God? 4. What does this passage teach us about the enemy (Satan)? 5. What does this passage teach us about humans? 6. What is one truth I will live out from this passage? 7. What truth from this passage will I share with someone? 26 22 WHAT STORY AM I IN? In 1968, football fans were glued to their television sets watching an intense game between the Oakland Raiders and the New York Jets. The game had a remarkable finish, with the Raiders scor- ing two touchdowns in the final minute to win the game. The problem is the game went too long. So before the final minute, the television station switched to its next program, a sweet movie about a Swiss orphan living in the Alps. The football fans missed the final minute because their game was cut short. Often, when I (Daniel) am putting my young son to bed, I’ll tell him a story. But since I often run out of ideas, sometimes I’ll buy myself time by getting halfway through the story and then just say, “The end.” My son will facepalm and say, “That’s not the end!” But I’ll say, “You’re right. Then Tom tells Billy, ‘Let’s follow the treasure map . . .’” and the story keeps going. Even though he’s young, my son understands that stories aren’t meant to get cut short. Yet if you think about it, stories get cut short all the time. The friend who overdosed. The family whose car was hit head-on when the other car crossed the center line. The unexpected cancer diag- nosis. That’s what death does: it cuts stories short. We all die. However, do all stories end there? Thankfully, it makes sense that there’s a bigger story than just my lifetime and your lifetime. We’re going to look at three big-picture stories people have believed throughout history. These are stories that can help you make sense of your life. Which of the following three stories do you think best describes your life and where it fits in? They can’t all be true, so you’ll need to pick one: Option 1: My life is a merry-go-round until I get off. Many centuries ago in India, a prince named Gautama lived in luxury. But one day, he took a char- iot drive through the city and saw sights that unsettled him: sickness, old age, death. He realized that even though he lived a privileged life at the moment, he too would grow old, get sick, and die. He made up his mind to figure out how to keep himself from coming to such a futile ending. 27

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook So Gautama left his wife and child to seek answers. Through meditation, he discovered that life is a series of rebirth after rebirth, each going well or poorly based on your behavior in the previous life. And whether you come back as a gnat or a god, each life ends in futility because you merely start the process over again in a never-ending merry-go-round. The people you love die. The stuff you collect rots. Everything is futility and suffering. To get off this merry-go-round of rebirths, Gautama realized he needed to stop connecting his heart to people and possessions. Instead of desiring this or that, he would extinguish his desires and live a peaceful life unattached to worldly comforts and strong relational connections. As he accomplished this unattached state of mind, he became enlightened. Then he became known as the enlightened one, or the “Buddha.” As an enlightened person, when he died, he would not be reborn into another life. Rather, he would enter a reality known as nirvana, which is described as being extinguished, like a blown-out candle. Whether you’re a Buddhist or not, you can still look at your life as something that’s basically miserable until you “get off.” Option 2: My life is an accident I’ve got to make the most of. Another story your life could fit into is seeing life as basically an accident. As in, humans came about not through the creativity of a Creator but as a byproduct of nature. According to this view, the physical world we emerged from is also an accident—but an admittedly cool one. It’s a dance of moons circling planets and planets circling stars. Each pixel of the universe is a trillion syncopated clocks of electrons orbiting their nuclei. It’s an endless flow of energy waves through space, water through roots, and blood through veins. But the same world that welcomed us as surprise visitors will just as quickly see us out the door and into extinction. We will one day be a blip on the universe’s timeline. And the universe itself, alive with motion and animated with energy today, will one day be a blip when set against the even- tual coldness of heat death. This will happen when all the universe’s usable energy runs out and everything reaches absolute zero. Lights out. So if this is your story, you’d better make the most of it. Live as long and fully as you can. Per- petuate the species, so that at least your genetics, and humanity in general, live beyond you. Don’t blow your nanosecond of the blip. Option 3: My life is a paragraph in the story God is writing. Like the previous two, this third option feels a bit like death too. But it’s not the end of rebirths or the death of a species. Instead, it’s the death of my ability to write my own story. If this is God’s world and I’m his creation, then he’s the author, and I’m one of the characters he thought up. 28 What Story Am I In? Now, it’s true that God made humans with the ability to make their own decisions. Will I follow what God says? Will I ignore God? Will I hate him? These are my choices. However, regardless of what I choose, God will write my tiny story into his grand story. Maybe I’ll follow him and help others do the same. Or maybe I’ll reject him, and my life will be a warning to others. Either way, my life will be used for his purposes. SELF-ASSESSMENT My three main options when it comes to the big-picture story are: 1. My life is a merry-go-around until I get off. 2. My life is an accident I’ve got to make the most of. 3. My life is a paragraph in the story God is writing. When it comes to what story I see myself in, here’s how I describe where I am: When it comes to what story I see myself in, here’s where I want to be and why I want to be there: If you choose to see your life as a paragraph in the story God is writing, it means a couple of R words for your life: 1. Resignation: I must give up my right to call my own shots and create my own identity. I’m not God; he’s God. I must resign my role of trying to play God. 2. Restoration: As I humble myself as a character in his story, God restores me to the good purpose he had in mind when he created me. In this way, my story becomes one of restoration. Are you willing to live in the story God is writing for your life? Why or why not? 29

Definition: Apologetics The practice of defending your faith with good reasons. STUDY What story are you in? Here are some thoughts to help you as you wrestle with this question. What Story Is God Writing? Here’s the short answer: God’s story, as found in the Bible, is a story of restoration. It tells us the story of lost things being found, of broken things being rebuilt and restored. This “story of stories” has a symmetrical pattern, with the first half ending in loss, but with the second half being a resto- ration of what was lost in the first half. 30 What Story Am I In? Tree of Life – God creates humans in his image (the imago dei), places them in a garden, and gives them access to the Tree of Life, so they can live forever. Serpent – A tempter taking the form of a serpent convinces the humans they can’t trust God. They reject God and chaos follows. This event is called the fall. Call – God picks a man named Abram and tells him to go from his land to a promised land and that he will make Abram into a great nation. Lamb – Abram’s descendants are slaves until God rescues them. The way he rescues them is through a sacrificed lamb in an event called the Passover. Community – God gives them commands through his servant Moses and builds them into his chosen nation. Kingdom – God appoints kings over the nation and promises to send a future messianic king to rule over them. Temple – King Solomon builds a temple for God, a place for the nations to meet God. Broken Covenant – The nation splits into two (north and south), rejects God, and gets conquered (the north by Assyria, the south by Babylon). This is the low point of the story. Temple – Under the Persian Empire, the nation returns and rebuilds their homeland, along with a second temple. Kingdom – After centuries of waiting for the Messiah, the nation of Israel receives a visit from a man named Jesus who announces the kingdom of God has come. Community – Jesus gathers disciples together who become a new community of God. He teaches them how to love each other and show compassion when people are hurting. Lamb – Jesus is put on trial for claiming to be God. The religious leaders hand him over to the Romans to be crucified. He dies for the sins of the world, sacrificed as the Lamb of God. Through his sacrifice, he “buys them back” out of their slavery to sin (buying back is called “redemption”). Call – Jesus rises from the dead on the third day. He later calls his disciples to go make disciples of all nations. A few weeks later in Jerusalem, the church begins with thousands baptized. Serpent – The church’s mission to make disciples is violently opposed. Now pictured as a dragon (in the book of Revelation), the tempter opposes God and persecutes God’s people. Tree of Life – At the end of history, God creates a new heavens and earth for his people, a place with no dying or mourn- ing, complete with a Tree of Life.3 Five Clues That This Story Is True For this grand story the Bible tells us to be true, some important facts also need to be true. There needs to be a God in the first place. This needs to be the kind of God who can make decisions and intervene in history. He also needs to be a God who cares about what humans do—that is, he is 31

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook good and wants us to do good things and not evil things. Below are five clues that tell us this story is totally possible and actually very likely to be true. The technical word for showing that Christi- anity is true is called “apologetics.” In our opinion, clues to the truth of Christianity are everywhere you look. Listed below are five big ones, and we put them in the form of oxymorons, which is a phrase in which two truths appear to cancel each other out. For example, here are some common oxymorons you might have heard: “plastic glasses;” “pretty ugly;” “tight slacks;” and “Micro- CLUES TO THE soft Works.” Here are five oxymoronic clues that this story is true: TRUTH OF CHRISTIANITY 1. Friendly Explosion ARE EVERYWHERE Scientists tell us the universe didn’t used to exist. Then an explosion happened YOU LOOK. (commonly called the “big bang”) and formed a universe. The universe that resulted from the explosion had certain conditions just right—to where, if those conditions hadn’t been just right, life couldn’t arise. It’s like dials in the shower. A little to the left, and it’s too hot. A little to the right, and it’s too cold. But this universe came into being with just the right conditions for life to be able to arise. One philosopher of science puts it like this: One could think of the initial conditions of the universe and the fundamental parameters of physics as a dart board that fills the whole galaxy, and the conditions necessary for life to exist as a small one-foot-wide target: unless the dart hits the target, life would be impossible. The fact that the dials are perfectly set, or the dart has hit the target, strongly suggests that someone set the dials or aimed the dart, for it seems enormously improbably that such a coincidence could have happened by chance.4 2. Simple Life This doesn’t sound like too much of an oxymoron. Surely, simple life exists, right? The simplest form of life would be a single cell, and the cell is something we’ve learned about since we were kids. But there’s a twist when it comes to the cell: they used to think the cell was simple life. As scientists dis- covered more and more about the cell, it became clear nothing is simple about it at all. As just one example, the genetic information of a cell is contained in DNA. DNA contains a shockingly complex system of letters providing specified instruction for what a cell does and how it replicates itself. Richard Knopp, author of Truth About God: What Can We Know and How Can We Know It?, writes, “One gram of DNA can hold 215 petabytes of information. With that capacity, DNA could physically store all the information ever recorded by humans in one room!”5 32 What Story Am I In? Here’s another example: two scientists, Chandra Wickramasinghe and Fred Hoyle, took a hard look at the cell and at how complex even a single cell was. And the scientists determined that for a cell to have come about through purely natural processes (without any help from a designer) would be the equivalent of 1 chance in 1040,000 (10 with 40,000 zeroes after it).6 As Hoyle, an astronomer, put it, even an astronomer has trouble envisioning that number. (After all, it’s estimated that only between 1078 and 1082 atoms are in the observable universe.7) 3. Unbreakable Piñata Let’s say a marine jumps on a live grenade to save his buddies. If the point of life is merely for peo- ple to survive and pass their genes on to the next generation (“survival of the fittest”), then that guy was an idiot. Yet we know the marine who jumped on a grenade to save his buddies was the opposite of an idiot. We know he was a hero. He didn’t do the wrong thing; instead, he did the right thing. A deep-seated sense of right and wrong is within us that goes way beyond, Did I survive the lon- gest and get my genetics into the next generation? We know that to do what’s right sometimes means self-sacrifice, not self-survival. But how do we know that? The apostle Paul called this the moral law being “written on our hearts” (Romans 2:14–15). Hav- ing this sense of right and wrong written on our hearts is the reason we know that even if Adolf Hit- ler had won and had brainwashed the entire planet to believe that it was a good thing to kill millions of Jews, it would still be evil. This is why we know that when Martin Luther King, Jr. said, “I have a dream,” his dream was right. And even if no one else had listened, his fight for equality between white and black people would have still been right. So why are we calling this an “unbreakable piñata”? Because even when people try to break this moral law within (and we’ve all tried to break it from time to time), it’s still there. It remains true from generation to generation that certain things are valuable and good (e.g., honesty, kindness, and courage) even if we don’t put them into practice. And other things remain evil (e.g., murder, theft, lying, envy) even if we do put THIS MORAL LAW them into practice. This moral law “written on our hearts” is a clue that this “WRITTEN ON OUR story of a good God who created us is true. HEARTS” IS A CLUE THAT THIS STORY 4. Deserted Grave OF A GOOD GOD Somehow after Jesus was crucified and placed in the tomb, his tomb turned WHO CREATED up empty within days. The grave was somehow deserted. How do we know? US IS TRUE. Well, because as soon as Jesus’ disciples started saying, “He is risen!” what was the quickest way to shut them up? Get the body and show everybody that Jesus was very much dead. But they didn’t get the body. They couldn’t get the body—because the tomb was empty. 33

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook After Jesus’ crucifixion, there’s no good reason his tomb should have turned up empty, yet it did (Matthew 28:11–14). There’s no good reason why so many people should have said they saw Jesus alive after he died, yet they did (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). There’s no good reason why even skep- tics, such as Paul and James, should have become Christians, yet they did (Acts 9:1–5; John 7:5; Galatians 2:9). There’s no good reason why the church should have begun with thousands of people just weeks after the crucifixion in the very city where Jesus had been publicly crucified, yet it did (Acts 2:1, 5, 38, 41). There’s no good reason why Jesus’ disciples should have been willing to suffer and eventually die for their faith in Jesus, yet they were (Acts 5:18, 29). No good reason except for one. There is one reason that can explain 1) the empty tomb, 2) the post-death appearances of Jesus, 3) the conversion of skeptics such as Paul and James, 4) the huge beginning of the church in Jerusalem just weeks later, and 5) the willingness of the apostles to die for their faith in Jesus. The reason? Hear it from the apostles themselves: Peter and the other apostles replied: “We must obey God rather than human beings! The God of our ancestors raised Jesus from the dead—whom you killed by hanging him on a cross. God exalted him to his own right hand as Prince and Savior that he might bring Israel to repentance and forgive their sins. We are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.” (Acts 5:29–32) 5. Cross Necklace You don’t turn execution tools into jewelry. You don’t see people wearing electric chair earrings or nooses for bracelets. Yet we have cross necklaces. Why? These people had just seen their leader get crucified. That was the Roman Empire’s way of say- ing, “Game over. You lost.” Yet within days, with smiles on their faces, these same people were tell- ing everybody how their leader had won. They saw him die, but then told everybody how he had beaten death. And the church started in the very city where Jesus had been publicly executed—just a few weeks after it happened. The church never should have gotten off the ground. The cross should have been the end. Yet the cross wasn’t the end. And the church continues to spread today all over the globe, even multiplying in places where governments try hard to shut it down. The persistence of faith in a crucified Messiah is a strange twist that hints that the crucifixion was just one chapter in a story that God was writing. 34 What Story Am I In? SCRIPTURE What does each verse teach about why God created you? Then God said, “Let us make mankind in our image, in our likeness, so that they may rule over the fish in the sea and the birds in the sky, over the livestock and all the wild animals, and over all the creatures that move along the ground.” So God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them. (Genesis 1:26–27) “From one man he [God] made all the nations, that they should inhabit the whole earth; and he marked out their appointed times in history and the boundaries of their lands. God did this so that they would seek him and perhaps reach out for him and find him.” (Acts 17:26–27a) “For in him all things were created: things in heav- en and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or powers or rulers or authorities; all things have been created through him and for him. He is before all things, and in him all things hold togeth- er.” (Colossians 1:16–17) “For we are God’s handiwork, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance for us to do.” (Ephesians 2:10) SNAPSHOT . . . FROM EL SALVADOR I was serving as a youth pastor in Pennsylvania, we had just had our third kid, and life was good. Then we felt God call us to move to El Salvador, live there, and tell the Salvadorans about Jesus. As 35

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook if that weren’t disruption to our lives enough, the next five years of stumbling toward this goal were chaotic: we moved six times, lived in three states, had four more kids, and I had four job changes! Still this call to El Salvador would not go away. We began raising support, asking people to give us money so we could do God’s work, and . . . it did not go so well. In those five years, we felt no closer to going to El Salvador than when we had first started. Also, people began asking if it was really God’s will. You have seven kids; your first responsibility is to them, right? You could always go once they are out of the house. Or maybe you are supposed to help others go to the mission field. You must have misunderstood the call you thought you heard from the Lord. Still, I continued pitching the vision to potential donors as to why we should be missionaries in El Salvador and why their church should support us. Looking back, I realize my presentation was all about need and how their money could help us live over there and fix people’s problems. Amid this entered a farmer named Phil into my life. He was also the elder over missions at the church we had just started attending. I gave Phil the pitch as to why their church should support us. Instead of saying no, Phil invited me to ride along in his combine and get to know one another. I found these ride-alongs so refreshing. Sometimes we talked about farming, sometimes about El Salvador, sometimes about my family or his. This went on for almost three months, and then one day Phil asked if I would be willing to go to a training to learn how to raise support. His church would pay for it, so I agreed. One night, as I read one of the books for training in missions, I heard an audible voice. It said, “Will you continue to build your own kingdom, or will you start building mine?” I remembered all those times I had tried to raise support for El Salvador but had failed. I was soon crying at my desk and asking God for wisdom and strength to make the right decisions. My wife and I began making a list of roughly thirty churches to contact each day. Still, at the end of six months we had raised only 15 percent of our monthly support. Something was broken. At this point, some very critical things happened in our story. We were broken. We did not know what to do, whom to ask, or where we were going. Everything was wrong. Isn’t it supposed to work out for missionaries? Aren’t God’s people supposed to win in the end? Why would no one support us? At this point, my friend Jim, who was an ex-missionary helping to fund ministry to refugees, gave me some advice. He had been listening in on my thirty rejections every day for the past six months, and he gave me this advice informed by Matthew 6:33 (“Seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well”): raise prayer partners first, and then invite people to participate in kingdom work. After this conversation with Jim, my wife and I decided to stop raising support and concentrate on raising prayer partners. As God had said, it wasn’t about building our kingdom but his. This was 36 What Story Am I In? his story, not ours. Over the next five months, we sent out letters and focused on surrounding our- selves with people praying to God for his mission to be done. Before long, we were able to map a direct correlation between prayer partners and financial support. When we were at one hundred prayer partners, we were IT WASN’T also at 35 percent raised. At two hundred prayer partners, it was 70 percent raised. ABOUT And when we reached three hundred prayer partners, we had 100 percent raised! BUILDING OUR I’m not suggesting this is a formula for raising support; rather, it’s a heart posi- KINGDOM tion. We had spent all those hours and years trying to get to El Salvador, under BUT HIS. our own power and wisdom. We had been writing our own story. But when we positioned our hearts and lives to be directed by God, as characters in his story, he made the impossible possible. — Ryan, El Salvador SUMMARY 1. Each one of us is made in God’s image, as a male or female, to join his story of restoration. 2. God created us on purpose for a purpose. 3. God is continually writing his story into our lives. What truth from this passage will I share with someone? 40 33 WHAT’S MY MAIN SOURCE OF TRUTH? Where do you go when you have a question? Well, it probably depends on what kind of ques- tion. What’s the weather going to be like tomorrow? Check the weather app. What year did World War I start? Google it. How do you make things right with the friend you hurt? Talk it over with a friend or family member and get advice. And then there are the really big questions. Why does the universe exist? What’s my purpose in life? Why is there so much sadness and suffering? Who decides what is good and evil? What hap- pens after I die? Whom can I trust with my ultimate destiny? For these massive questions about reality, there are four ways people find their answers. Take a few minutes and ask yourself which of these ways is your typical way of trying to answer these big questions. Option 1: Trust my gut. Sometimes you can trust your gut. When you stop and pay attention, sometimes you can arrive at the truth about a question you have. You have five senses (sight, sound, feel, etc.) that tell you a lot about the world around you. You also have the ability to think logically. For example, let’s say I tell you, “Anybody who picks up a book like this is a wise person.” That should feel nice to hear. Why? Well, it’s because you can think logically. You basically did a “syllo- gism” in your mind in less than a second. It went like this: Anybody who picks up a book like this is a wise person. I picked up a book like this. Therefore, I’m a wise person. 41

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook Not only can you use your senses and think logically, but you also have a moral compass that instinctively lets you know that some actions are good and others are evil. So trusting your gut can lead you to some truth. At the same time, can you know how to answer the biggest questions (e.g., Why does the universe exist? What happens after I die?) just by going with your gut? Option 2: Ask my friends. It’s such a gift to have good friends. Friends are a source of fun times and lasting memories. And—if they’re good friends—they can be an amazing source of helpful advice. Being able to lean on trust- ed friends in confusing times is a blessing. Even still, do your friends know the answers to the big- gest questions in life—just because they’re kind to you and fun to hang out with? Without some outside help, would they automatically know the purpose of life or whom we can trust with our eternal destiny? Option 3: Ask the experts. We consult experts all the time. And it’s a good thing we do. Here are some examples: • When an electrical outlet stops working, you consult an electrician. • When you’re curious what events led to the French Revolution, you consult a historian. • When you’ve got abnormal things going on in your body, you consult a medical doctor. • When a light on your dryer blinks red, you consult the user’s manual, written by the people who created it. Historians can be very helpful, but what historian can tell me how the universe came into exis- tence? A physicist can explain to me how gravity works, but can a physicist tell me why gravity exists? Or why there are scientific laws in the first place? Or why there’s a universe in the first place? A med- ical doctor might be able to cure my body, but can a medical doctor restore my soul after I’ve doing something I’m ashamed of? Is there a user’s manual to help us understand why we exist? Experts are impressive in their lane of expertise. Yet some things we will never know the answers to just by studying hard and getting smarter. There are God-sized questions we won’t be able to figure out the answer to unless God shows us the answers. They’re above our abilities to figure out without help. Option 4: Seek God. My (Andrew) girls have loved the Chronicles of Narnia movies from a young age. We love movie nights together and watching Aslan defeat the White Witch! The movies are adaptations of books written by C. S. Lewis, a former Oxford University professor, who wrote not only children’s fic- tion but also theology books. He was once an atheist (someone who doesn’t believe in the existence 42 What’s My Main Source of Truth? of God) but realized that his atheism didn’t provide good enough answers to the big questions he had. He found that Christianity provided grown-up answers to his tough questions, so he became a Christian. In his spiritual autobiography Surprised by Joy, Lewis suggested that humans are somewhat like characters in a book.8 We live within the pages and plot laid out in the book. Our experiences are limited to life inside the book. Yet at the same time, there’s a whole world outside the book. An author wrote the book, and the author lives in an even bigger world that isn’t bound by the same limitations placed on the book (which is limited to what lies between its front and back covers). So how can the characters in the book learn about the author and his world? One way, Lewis explained, would be for the author to write himself as a character within the book. The author could then interact with the other characters and teach them what life is like outside the book. According to the Bible, that is precisely what God did. After creating us, he wrote himself into our story. He entered our history. Sometimes, he spoke messages. Other times, he did miraculous acts. Eventually, he wrote himself very literally into our story by coming as God in human flesh, in the person of Jesus (what Christians call the “incarnation”). AFTER And it’s a good thing he did! Because without his help, we would be in the CREATING US, dark about life’s biggest questions. We wouldn’t know why we exist or what comes HE WROTE next or how we can be made right again. But by seeking God—and by accepting HIMSELF INTO what he tells us about himself—we can find answers to life’s biggest questions. OUR STORY. “Seeking God” can sound a little confusing; how exactly do we do that? Well, it’s not a matter of just going up on a mountain and asking for an answer. It can involve quite a few things, such as reading the Bible, talking with trusted people, and praying. It can mean bringing decisions into the light of God’s presence and seeking the peace that comes from knowing you’re doing the right thing and not rushing to force your own will. SELF-ASSESSMENT My four main options when it comes to answering life’s biggest questions are: 1. Trust my gut. 2. Ask my friends. 3. Ask the experts. 4. Seek God. All these sources of truth can be helpful at different times. But what’s your main source of truth? Whom do you trust to give you answers to the big questions of reality? 43

pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook When it comes to my main source of truth, here’s how I would describe where I am: When it comes to my main source of truth, here’s where I want to be and why I want to be there: Definition: Revelation Definition: Canonization A revealing or disclosing of something. STUDY What should be your main source of truth? Here are some thoughts to help you as you wrestle with this question. How Did We Get the Bible? In the beginning, God did stuff. People saw it and wrote it down. Of course, the process is more nuanced than that (and we’ll get into some details in a minute), but that’s not a bad thumbnail over- view of how we got the Bible. Everybody agrees that people can see stuff happen and write it down. But not everyone believes that God does stuff, or even that a God exists who can do the kind of stuff like we read about in the 44 What’s My Main Source of Truth? Bible. I mean, what kind of stuff are we talking about? Splitting the sea so people can walk through? A kid being born of a virgin? Raising a corpse to life? These sorts of fantastic events go against how life typically works for most of us. And don’t events like these also go against a scientific view of the world in which we take medicine for sickness and flip on lights and scroll through smartphones? I know that we’re looking at the question “How did we get our Bible?” but an even bigger ques- tion (before we can get to how we got the Bible) is this: How did we get the universe? If God creat- ed the universe (and there are some compelling scientific reasons to believe that he did), then he is completely able to act within his universe IF GOD CREATED THE to do the kinds of fantastic events we read about in the Bible. If he can UNIVERSE, THEN HE make a universe out of nothing, then any other miracle that follows takes IS COMPLETELY ABLE as much energy from him as an Olympic runner jogging a lap for fun. TO ACT WITHIN HIS The first step of understanding how we got our Bible is to acknowl- UNIVERSE TO DO THE edge that God did stuff. As the Creator of the universe, he’s totally able to KINDS OF FANTASTIC act within his universe. So here are some of the things he did: God picked EVENTS WE READ Abram’s family as the group through whom he would save the world. He ABOUT IN THE BIBLE. chose Moses to lead the Israelites out of slavery. He rescued people from disaster, gave laws, spoke to (and through) prophets. He did stuff. And each time God did something that ended up being written down, it was meant to tell us something. It was his way of “revealing” more of himself and his will to his people. Step 1. Revelation If you’ve ever been to a live play, you’ve probably seen a curtain drawn back at the beginning of the play to show what’s on stage. This drawing back of the curtain is a bit like God revealing himself and his will more and more each time he does stuff. By creating the universe, he draws back the curtain a bit, showing us that he is powerful and intelligent. By picking Abram’s family to eventual- ly rescue the world, he reveals that he cares about bringing people back into relationship with him. By powerfully rescuing his people from slavery through plagues on Egypt, he shows that he takes injustice seriously. This drawing back of the curtain, revealing himself and his will over time, is called “revela- tion.” How did we get our Bible? It all starts with God’s revelation of himself and his will by doing stuff (doing miracles, speaking messages, making predictions, etc.). Here are some Scriptures that describe God’s revelation: 45

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook • “When there is a prophet among you, I, the Lord, reveal myself to them in visions, I speak to them in dreams.” (Numbers 12:6b) • “The secret things belong to the Lord our God, but the things revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may follow all the words of this law.” (Deuteronomy 29:29) • “There he revealed himself to Samuel through his word.” (1 Samuel 3:21b) • “In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia, a revelation was given to Daniel.” (Daniel 10:1a) • “I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it; rather, I received it by revelation from Jesus Christ.” (Galatians 1:12) Step 2. Inspiration But God didn’t just stop with revealing himself and his will. He also inspired people to write down what they saw or heard. Here are a couple ways this process is described in the Bible: • “Prophets, though human, spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.” (2 Peter 1:21b) • “All Scripture is God-breathed.” (2 Timothy 3:16a) So here’s a quick summary so far of how we got our Bible: God revealed himself and his will (“revelation”). The Holy Spirit then inspired people to write down what they saw or heard (“inspi- ration”). Finally, the individual books were gathered into one book, which we know as the Bible. This is a process known as canonization. GOD REVEALED HIMSELF AND Step 3. Canonization HIS WILL. THE When it came to gathering the books together, not just any book made the HOLY SPIRIT THEN cut. There were certain standards. For example, the people who put the New INSPIRED PEOPLE Testament library together met together and asked important questions. TO WRITE DOWN Since the apostles’ teachings were authoritative for the church, they asked, WHAT THEY SAW “Was this book written by an apostle of Jesus or by a close friend of an apos- OR HEARD. tle?” They also asked, “Has this book been used by the churches from the beginning?” and, “Is it unified with other biblical teachings?” In this way, they gathered the books together into what we now call the Bible. These were the standards by which they measured these books. Since the word “canon” originally meant “measuring stick,” this process of recognizing which books were Scripture was called “canonization.” So how did we get our Bible? To summarize, there were three main steps in the process: 46 What’s My Main Source of Truth? 1. Revelation: God revealed himself. 2. Inspiration: The Holy Spirit inspired people to write it down. 3. Canonization: The people of God recognized which books were Scripture. Is the New Testament Reliable? It’s one thing to have a Bible. It’s another thing to trust that what we have today is the Bible that was written back then. It’s still another thing to trust that it’s telling us the truth. Here, we’re going to focus on the New Testament and look at eleven numbers that strongly suggest the New Testa- ment we have today is the same as what was written back then and that we can trust what it says: 1. 5600+ Manuscripts We have over 5,600 handwritten copies (manuscripts) of parts of the New Testament in its original language (Greek). The number jumps to 24,000+ manuscripts if you count other languages. This helps explain the next number: 99. 2. 99% of the Original We don’t have the original copies of the New Testament. But we do have thousands of manuscripts that allow scholars to piece together the original. With that many manuscripts, scholars have recon- structed the original, with 99 percent of the text being certain and 1 percent of the text still in dis- pute. When it comes to the 1 percent, there are two or more different ways of reading a passage of Scripture, so we’re not sure which reading goes back to the original. With 99 percent of the text sol- idly reconstructed, we can be confident we know the New Testament’s original message. 3. (AD) 95, the Date of the Last Book The books of the New Testament were written between the 40s and 90s in the first century. The final books were written by Jesus’ apostle John in his old age, sometime between AD 90 and 95. This puts the writings of the New Testament in the first century and within the lifetime of eyewit- nesses who would have seen what happened. 4. 66 Books The sixty-six books of the Bible provide a grand narrative woven throughout the centuries and even- tually create a tapestry forming the likeness of Jesus. In Jesus, we see that so many Old Testament themes (e.g., the sacrifice of the beloved son, the Passover lamb, the sacrificial system, the temple veil, the suffering servant, redemption, kingdom, covenant, etc.) provided pictures of Jesus and his min- istry to come. Jesus was conscious of this connection and quoted Old Testament prophets to show how they pointed ahead to him (e.g., Matthew 12:40; Mark 14:62; Luke 4:16–21; 24:27). 47

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook 5. (AD) 62, the Probable Date of Acts This date seems significant because of what came before it. Let us explain: Acts narrates the ear- ly church. In doing so, it tells numerous stories, including the story of the first Christian martyr (Stephen) and the first apostle to be martyred THE SIXTY-SIX (James the apostle). It primarily focuses on the ministries of Peter and BOOKS OF THE BIBLE Paul as the gospel spreads all the way from Jerusalem to Rome. Acts ends PROVIDE A GRAND with Paul in Rome, awaiting trial around AD 62. It doesn’t mention the NARRATIVE WOVEN death of Jesus’ brother James (AD 62), the deaths of Paul or Peter (late THROUGHOUT 60s), or the destruction of Jerusalem (AD 70). This makes it likely that THE CENTURIES Acts was written in the early 60s (although a case can be made for mid- AND EVENTUALLY 60s).9 In his two-part work, Luke wrote the Gospel of Luke before Acts CREATE A TAPESTRY (Luke’s Gospel was Part 1, and Acts was Part 2). Luke likely used the FORMING THE Gospel of Mark as a source in writing the Gospel of Luke. So this puts LIKENESS OF JESUS. two Gospels (Mark and Luke) prior to AD 62, placing them within thir- ty or so years of the events themselves. Prior to being written down, these stories would have circulated as the apostles’ teaching (Acts 2:42) by a population that was used to memorizing and passing along what they learned. 6. 12 Post-Resurrection Appearances After Jesus died, numerous people claimed to see Jesus alive. His apostles saw him multiple times as they talked and ate with Jesus. At one time, over five hundred saw him alive at one time, and Paul challenged the readers to check it out because, at the time of his writing, most of the five hundred were still alive and could verify what they saw (1 Corinthians 15:6). At least two separate sightings were by skeptics of Jesus, but seeing Jesus alive marked their turning point. Altogether, we are told of twelve separate appearances by the risen Jesus after his death, and there could have been more. 7. 10+ Non-Christians Writing About Jesus Within 150 years of his life, at least 10 non-Christians wrote about Jesus, showing they believed him to be a historical figure. This includes Roman historians Tacitus and Suetonius as well as Jewish sources Josephus and the Talmud. Although these writers did not believe in Jesus, we gather some important facts about his life from their writings, such as that he was crucified under Pontius Pilate, he performed supernatural acts, and his followers worshiped him as God. 8. 10 Apostles Martyred According to church tradition, of Jesus’ original twelve apostles, ten were killed for their faith in him (except for Judas the traitor and John who likely died a natural death). It’s true that some of 48 What’s My Main Source of Truth? these stories were written down earlier than others (and therefore more likely to be historical), while other stories were written quite a bit later and there seem to have been legendary add-ons to some of the stories. So we can’t know for sure that all ten of these stories are authentic. However, with the persecutions against Christians that rose in these early decades, their martyrdoms fit the era. What makes the martyrdoms of the apostles significant is that it shows they were completely convinced that the resurrection story they’d been telling people was legitimate. They, of all people, would have known whether it was true or false. And if they weren’t sure of it, it is hard to see why they would have willingly gone to their deaths (some being quite brutal forms of death) trying to persuade peo- ple that Jesus had risen. 9. 5 Years Between the Resurrection and 1 Corinthians 15:3–7 No one quite knew what to do with the news. Paul, a religious leader notorious for putting Chris- tians in prison, had himself become a believer in Jesus. Then, between two to five years after Jesus’ death and resurrection, Paul traveled back to Jerusalem to meet with the leaders of the church there. There, he received their summary of the gospel (which he quoted in 1 Corinthians 15:3–7): Jesus had died, was buried, and rose from the dead, all to fulfill the Scriptures. Then he appeared to numerous people, proving he was alive. This means the story of Jesus dying and rising from the dead didn’t originate on a different continent hundreds of years after Jesus lived. Rather, Paul went to Jerusalem (the city where Jesus had died) and received this information within two to five years of the events themselves. 10. 3 Denials The New Testament contains some embarrassing details about its own authors. For example, hours after assuring Jesus that he would never disown Jesus—even if he had to die for it—Peter got scared during Jesus’ trial and THE APOSTLES denied three times even knowing Jesus. Similarly, Paul never whitewashed WHO TOLD THE his violent past (1 Corinthians 15:9) or even his sinful present tendencies GOSPEL STORIES (Romans 7:14–20). The apostles who told the gospel stories in the first place IN THE FIRST painted themselves as doing brainless things: falling asleep when Jesus asked PLACE PAINTED them to stay awake and pray for him, constantly fighting amongst themselves THEMSELVES AS as to which of them was the greatest, being repeatedly corrected by Jesus DOING BRAINLESS for not understanding what he was trying to say, and refusing to believe the THINGS. women who told them Jesus had risen from the dead. These authors were far from perfect, and their honesty about themselves makes them seem like trust- worthy guides to the events. People usually tell lies for one of two reasons: to get out of trouble or to make themselves look good. The apostles got neither out of telling the gospel stories. 49

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook 11. 1 This number applies to the New Testament in more than one way. When it comes to the number of ancient manuscripts, the New Testament comes in first place, having more handwritten copies than any other ancient writing. It also comes in first in how close the earliest manuscript is to the original document. (For example, we have an ancient fragment of the Gospel of John written some thirty years after John wrote his Gospel.) The Bible, in general, is the world’s number one bestsell- ing book. Perhaps most importantly, the New Testament is about history’s number one influential person: Jesus. SCRIPTURE What does each verse teach me about the importance of God’s Word? “Blessed is the one . . . whose delight is in the law of the Lord, and who meditates on his law day and night. That person is like a tree planted by streams of water, which yields its fruit in season and whose leaf does not wither.” (Psalm 1:1–3a) “How sweet are your words to my taste, sweet- er than honey to my mouth! I gain understanding from your precepts; therefore I hate every wrong path. Your word is a lamp for my feet, a light on my path.” (Psalm 119:103–105) “From infancy you have known the Holy Scrip- tures, which are able to make you wise for salva- tion through faith in Christ Jesus. All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness, so that the servant of God may be thoroughly equipped for every good work.” (2 Timothy 3:15–17) 50 What’s My Main Source of Truth? “We also have the prophetic message as some- thing completely reliable, and you will do well to pay attention to it, as to a light shining in a dark place. . . . For prophecy never had its origin in the human will, but prophets, though human, spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.” (2 Peter 1:19, 21) SNAPSHOT . . . FROM AFRICA We would describe ourselves as a very typical American family—probably very similar, we imagine, to most of the other families who attend our church. Not too long ago, we would have said we were on the right track. We would have said we were accomplishing our career goals. We never set out to become missionaries. In fact, ministry work was nowhere on our radar. But about two years ago, we started to feel that God was calling us to the global mission field. At first, we resisted, because this was a big change. We didn’t know what it meant to become missionaries. So we began to really pray and listen, and we spent intentional, focused time in God’s Word, seeking his plan for our lives. We both admit that for years, we took our faith for granted. We both grew up in church. We both knew that our eternal salvation rests securely in acceptance of Jesus Christ. But we never really gave a lot of thought to the people around the world who have never heard the name of Jesus even once. We sort of knew there were people like this in other countries, WE STARTED but we didn’t really think about it, or we didn’t really listen. At this point in our LISTENING lives, we started listening and taking his Word seriously. AND TAKING At first, we assumed that to become missionaries we needed to hear an audible HIS WORD voice telling us a specific place and time to go. We thought we needed Bible college SERIOUSLY. degrees. But what we’ve learned is that we have his Word, and we must be obedient to what God asks us to do. We are all capable of being obedient. Nothing is partic- ularly special about us, or any others who have gone before us, or any others who will come after us. You must listen and obey. God orchestrates everything. He strategically places people in your path, and these people give you what you need to move forward, one step at a time. God also gives you a burden on your heart for those in need, which is like the burden he has for all his people. Paul says in Romans 10:14–15, “How, then, can they call on the one they have not believed in? And how can they believe in the 51

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook one of whom they have not heard? And how can they hear without someone preaching to them? And how can anyone preach unless they are sent?” God’s Word tells us that we must go so others can call on the name of the Lord and be saved. We have had many questions along the way about whether we can do this, or whether we even should. Sometimes we try to do things on our own accord and on our own time. But we are learn- ing that we must relinquish that desire for control. Nothing is achieved through our means; only through God can eternally significant things be done. We’ve learned that each time we give up a little bit of control of our lives to God, he gives us exactly what we need to move forward. — The L’s, Africa SUMMARY 1. God has communicated to us through his Word, which we have in the Bible. 2. God’s Word is trustworthy. 3. As the ultimate source of truth, the Bible should guide our character and convictions.
