pages.content: Page intentionally left blank 44 HOW DO I READ THE BIBLE? People throughout history have done all sorts of things with Bibles. Some have bought them and left them on shelves. Others have burned them in book burnings. Bibles have been manipulated like sock puppets in the hands of people who want to make the Bible say what they want it to say. So what is the best way to use the Bible? Here are six options for how you might read the Bible. Why don’t you take a few minutes and ask yourself which of these six best describe how you read the Bible? Option 1: I don’t. Just owning a Bible doesn’t mean you read it. (And if we’re being honest, just reading it doesn’t mean you understand it.) The truth is the Bible is a massive book that was written a long time ago, and it can be intimidating to open. Especially since it’s been known to change the lives of people who take it seriously. So one option is simply not to read it. Here’s another reason people, even Christians, might not feel like reading their Bibles: They feel like they already basically know what it says. But do they? A lot of people who grew up in the church basically learned a seven-year-old’s version of the Bible. They learned some stories, they learned some moral lessons (we should be a good person, not a bad person), and they learned that Jesus died and rose from the dead. And that’s about all they learned. The truth is the seven-year-old’s version is like a swimming pool, whereas the Bible is like an ocean. You could spend your life studying just a few of the Bible’s books and still have more to learn by the end. Option 2: I proofread it to find problems. Some people read the Bible looking for reasons not to like it. Slavery was a part of everyday life in the ancient world, so people might read the Bible to say, “See! There’s slavery in the Bible!” Wom- en were often treated as second-class citizens in the ancient world, so people might read the Bible, get to tragic moments where men treated their wives and daughters cruelly, and say, “See! The Bible is anti-women!” 57

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook Now, it’s important to recognize that the Bible often describes things that God didn’t approve of. Even still, God did approve of some things in the Bible (like pouring out his wrath on groups of people who did evil things), which can make us feel uncomfortable. Some people take these uncom- fortable parts of the Bible as reason not to take it seriously. Option 3: I manipulate the Bible to make it say what I want. Did you know you can make the Bible say whatever you want it to say? Here are the main steps: 1. Figure out ahead of time what you want the Bible to say. 2. Focus on a verse or two that can be made to say what you want them to say, and ignore the context (the verses that come before and after). 3. Formulate a new meaning, saying, “Actually, this is what the Bible teaches!” Here’s an example: Let’s take a very straightforward Bible verse. In John 14:6, Jesus said to his disciples, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.” Then along comes Eckart Tolle. Tolle is a well-known spiritual advisor for the Oprah Winfrey Net- work. In his book A New Earth, Tolle sadly takes Christian passages, jerks them out of context, and drags them kicking and screaming into a pantheistic mold. Pantheism is the belief that everything is made up of God (especially us). Listen to how Tolle uses John 14:6, the verse we just read. Tolle writes, “The Truth is inseparable from who you are. Yes, you are the Truth. If you look for it elsewhere, you will be deceived every time. The very Being that you are is Truth.” And then lis- ten to what Tolle writes next: “Jesus tried to convey that when he said, ‘I am the way and the truth and the life.’”10 Did you catch what Tolle did? He took the verse where Jesus says he’s the only way to God, and he used that verse to say, if you want to know the truth, don’t look up there (to God) but look in here (in your own heart). We are the truth. That’s manipulating the Bible to say what we want it to say. Option 4: I read it to find inspiration (and ignore the rest). Many Bible verses and stories can be very inspiring. The ending especially is very inspiring, as it describes heaven and how evil is finally defeated. So if we go to the Bible looking for inspiration, we’ll find some. Here’s an example of a verse that has inspired a lot of people to believe they can do anything if they put their mind to it: “I can do all things through Him who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13, NASB). People have used this verse to inspire themselves to run faster, throw harder, and lift more pounds than they thought possible. Yet is that what this verse truly says? Does it say, “Christ gives me the strength to accomplish anything I want to accomplish”? 58 How Do I Read the Bible? Actually, if we zoom out to the context, we’ll see that the verse refers to going through hard times. The author Paul says, “I know what it is to be in need, and I know what it is to have plen- ty. I have learned the secret of being content in any and every situation, whether well fed or hun- gry, whether living in plenty or in want. I can do all this through him who gives me strength” (Philippians 4:12–13). In other words, whatever life throws at me, Jesus can give me the strength to handle it. That’s much different from, “I am able to do whatever great things I want to accomplish.” Yes, a lot in the Bible is inspiring. But we can find inspiring stuff in concerts, movies, and sport- ing events too. The Bible isn’t meant to be a succession of fortune-cookie declarations about the success we’ll have in life. The Bible is first and foremost about God, and it tells us truth, not just inspirational sayings that make us feel good. Option 5: I study it so I can be smart. The Bible contains truth, and truth does make us smarter. But learning something to get smarter can be good or bad. On the negative side, learning can be a means of pridefully puffing yourself up. (1 Corinthians 8:1 says, “Knowledge puffs up while love builds up.”) People who think they’ve arrived because they know the Bible are tragically fooling themselves. The point was never just knowing with your head but believing in your heart and putting it into practice with your hands and feet. On the positive side, learning can be a means of growing in wisdom to make sensible deci- sions (see Proverbs 1:1–6). If you like the idea of growing in wisdom, the book of Proverbs makes it clear that it starts with fearing the Lord: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge” (Proverbs 1:7). But, again, the point of reading the Bible is never meant to be only about getting smarter. In fact, it will teach you to do things that a lot of people will see as not that smart. It’ll teach you to care about people nobody else cares about. It’ll teach you to forgive people who seem unforgiveable. It’ll teach you to share the gospel even if people don’t understand why you care so much about it. There’s a much better reason to read the Bible. Option 6: I see it as the authority over my convictions and character. Over and over, throughout the Bible, the authors claim to be writing messages they’ve received from God. If that’s true and the Bible is from God, then the only logical response would be to let the Bible be your authority. What do we mean by “authority”? This means letting the Bible be the main voice you listen to when it comes to what you believe (your convictions) and how you live (your charac- ter). If you really believe that the Bible is the Word of God, then you’ll go with what it teaches even if the people around you believe something else. 59

pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook SELF-ASSESSMENT My six main options when it comes to how I read the Bible are: 1. I don’t. 2. I proofread it to find problems. 3. I manipulate it to make it say what I want. 4. I read it to find inspiration (and ignore the rest). 5. I study it so I can be smart. 6. I see it as the authority over my convictions and character. If the Bible is the Word of God as it claims to be, you should ask yourself which option makes the most sense. When it comes to how I read the Bible, here’s how I would describe where I am: When it comes to how I read the Bible, here’s where I want to be and why I want to be there: Definition: Old Testament Definition: Messiah Thirty-nine books containing God’s promises, Hebrew for “anointed one”; the anointed covenant laws, and guidance for ancient Israel prophet, priest, and king who was proph- through its history. STUDY How should you read the Bible? Here are some thoughts to help you as you wrestle with this question. What Is the Old Testament? Have you ever watched a movie trilogy? If so, think back to the second movie. The ending of the second movie probably felt unfinished, didn’t it? For example, the second movie in the original Star Wars trilogy, The Empire Strikes Back, culminates in a lightsaber battle in which the evil Darth Vad- er beats the good guy Luke Skywalker—and then the movie ends. Not a great way to end a movie, is it? But that’s okay because a third and final movie is still to come. Are you curious what the Old Testament is? If you want a really simple answer, here goes: if you’ve ever flipped through a Bible, the Old Testament is basically the first two thirds of it. That’s not super helpful, but it’s a start. Let’s go a little deeper. The Old Testament isn’t so much a book as it is a library of thirty-nine books. (And it’s the best kind of library: no late fees for the book that gets knocked behind the pia- no and doesn’t turn up until you move ten years later.) This library of thirty-nine books was written by Jewish people over roughly a THE OLD thousand years (e.g., from the fifteenth century to the fifth century BC), mainly TESTAMENT in the Hebrew language. Some books are filled with laws for the nation to fol- ISN’T SO MUCH low (e.g., Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy). Others are history books (e.g., Josh- A BOOK AS IT IS ua, Judges, 1 and 2 Samuel). Still others are collections of Hebrew poetry (e.g., A LIBRARY OF Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes). Then at the end of the Old Testament are sev- THIRTY-NINE enteen books filled with messages spoken by God (“prophecy”) through Jewish BOOKS. prophets (e.g., Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel). Altogether, this series of books tells one grand story of how God picked a group of people, the Jews, to be his chosen people. He rescued this group of people from slavery, made them into a kingdom, and taught them the way to live. He also made promises to them, for 61

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook example, that someday from this nation he would bring about salvation—not just for them, but for the whole world. Sounds great, huh? But it doesn’t end well. (Remember The Empire Strikes Back?) The Old Testament feels a lot like watching only the first two movies in a trilogy. By the end of the Old Testament, it doesn’t really feel like it has much of an ending. Before we get to the ending, let’s zoom back out and look at the basic story of the Old Testa- ment: God created a beautiful world and then crafted a special type of creation in his own image— humans—to rule over the rest of what God had made. God created humans to reflect his glory on earth (kind of like how the moon reflects the light of the sun). But the first humans rebelled against God and decided to call their own shots and be their own gods. Things got ugly quick. In just the first chapters of the first book of the Old Testament (Genesis), we see murder, drunkenness, kidnap- ping, war, and other awful things (suffice it to say, a movie version of Genesis would get an R rating). Out of this chaos, God chose a man who had faith in him (Abram) and promised to make Abram’s descendants into a powerful nation. Through the centuries, he built Abram’s descendants into a kingdom and gave them commandments that guided them on how to live. However, they eventually refused to follow his commandments and decided to reject God and worship idols (manmade gods). Although he was mostly patient with them for centuries, God finally punished them in a huge way by allowing foreign empires to conquer them, destroy their capital city and temple, and carry them off into exile. (For example, if you live in the United States, this would be like a foreign country burning down Washington, DC, and carrying you off to live as servants in the foreign country. Not fun!) Still, God loved the nation he had created and promised to someday send a Messiah (meaning “anointed one”) to rescue them from their enemies. When would it happen, though? So they waited for the Messiah to show up. And waited. And waited. Eventually, the Jews were allowed to return home and rebuild their homeland, which they did, but the nation wasn’t nearly as glorious as it had once been. And still no Messiah. And that’s how the Old Testament ends. The Messiah still hadn’t come, and the Old Testament ends without a real ending. Thus, the Old Testament is basically a bloody-yet-beautiful sto- THE OLD TESTAMENT ry without an ending. Along the way, the nation of Israel saw God IS BASICALLY A do beautiful and powerful acts for her. He delivered her from slavery BLOODY-YET-BEAUTIFUL through the Exodus. He rescued her from foreign oppressors through STORY WITHOUT “judges” (such as Gideon and Samson). He guided her through AN ENDING. 62 How Do I Read the Bible? righteous kings (such as David and Josiah). Yet through persistent unbelief and disobedience, the Old Testament Israelites eventually rejected God and paid the price. The Old Testament ends with no Messiah. But it’s okay: the Old Testament was just the first two thirds of the Bible. The “third movie” was still in production. What Is the New Testament? Do you remember how the Old Testament ends? Well, it kind of doesn’t. God promised to send a Messiah to save them from their enemies, but then the Old Testament ends with the Jews still under the rule of a foreign empire (the Persians)—and no Messiah. Just promises. And then after the final Old Testament prophet wrote his book (a prophet named Malachi), the Old Testament closes out and—silence. And it’s not an “Ah, that’s nice” kind of silence; it’s more the uncomfortable silence like when you tell a joke, deliver the punchline, and everyone just stares. The silence went on for approximately four hundred years. That’s a long time. Some people may had given up hope along the way. But others never stopped believing that God would make good on his promises. And you know what? Faith in God paid off in the end (it always does) because, as it turned out, the Old Testament was not the full story. It was never meant to be. Rather, it was only like the first two movies in a trilogy. Speaking of trilogies, do you know the two most famous movie trilogies of all time? They are Lord of the Rings and the original Star Wars (as already mentioned). And both have something fas- cinating in common: In both trilogies, the third movie has a title that starts with the words “Return of the.” For Star Wars, it’s Return of the Jedi. For Lord of the Rings, it’s The Return of the King. Similarly, when it comes to the Bible’s “third movie,” it might as well be called Return of Hope (otherwise known as the “New Testament”). This is because—after four hundred years of silence from heaven—hope finally made its comeback. As it turned out, God really was there all along, and he hadn’t forgotten what he’d promised. What a relief! GOD REALLY What’s funny is how God decided to break his silence. The Old Testament WAS THERE ALL prophets had predicted the Messiah would be a glorious king who would also ALONG, AND be divine (e.g., Isaiah 9:1–7; Daniel 7:13–14). That means the Messiah would HE HADN’T come into the world with trumpets and parades, right? Not exactly. That FORGOTTEN WHAT means his nation would welcome him and worship him as their long-awaited HE’D PROMISED. Messiah, right? Nope. When the Messiah finally came, his entrance was actually unimpressive. He was a baby born to peasant parents who had nothing fancier to cradle him in than a feeding trough (a “manger”). This was the Messiah? Yep, that’s exactly who he was. He checked all the box- es: He was born in the town of Bethlehem, as Micah 5:2 had predicted. He was both human and 63

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook divine, as Isaiah 9:6 had predicted. He came during the Roman Empire, as Daniel 7:7–14 had pre- dicted. But still . . . the Messiah in . . . a manger? Yes, which was God’s way of saying the Messiah was here for everybody. And when Jesus the Messiah grew up and started telling people who he was and why he had come, he didn’t start by having dinner with governors or high priests. Instead, he hung out with blue-collar fishermen. His disciples (another word for “students”) were extremely regular people. In fact, most of the time, they acted like C-minus students. Sure, Jesus was cool (he did miracles, he taught amazing stuff), but couldn’t he have picked smarter, godlier dudes for his disciples? Confusing. But nothing was more confusing than how Jesus ended his ministry. He kept talking about how he needed to go to Jerusalem (the capital city). Why did he have to go there so badly? Well, when he first got to the city, it was like your favorite football team running onto the field at the beginning of a game: the crowd cheered wildly. Was that why Jesus was so determined to go to Jerusalem? No. He had to go to Jerusalem for this: Five days after arriving in the city, Jesus was nailed to a cross, the Roman way of telling criminals “Game over.” Six hours after being nailed to the cross, he was dead. That’s why he felt compelled to go to Jerusalem. Why did they kill him? The accusation was that he was guilty of calling himself God (Mark 14:61–63). This is typically a bad thing to say about yourself—unless you are God, which is exactly who Jesus was. This was God’s grand plan?! To have the Messiah be born in order to die? Yes, that was the plan all along (see Isaiah 53:4–10). But then came the great plot twist—the definitive return of hope: Jesus didn’t stay dead. On the Sunday after the Friday he was crucified, Jesus rose from the dead, which is how all four biographies of Jesus (“Gospels”) end. Because of Jesus’ resurrection, people who trust and follow Jesus have a living hope that doesn’t die. So what is the New Testament? Like the Old Testament, the New Testament is a library: a library of twenty-seven books that record the teachings of Jesus and his apostles (his handpicked closest followers). The New Testament contains the four Gospels, which tell about the life of Jesus; the book of Acts, which describes the early church and how the message of Jesus spread all over the Mediterranean world; letters to churches written by Jesus’ apostles, such as Paul, Peter, and John; and the book of Revelation, a vision of Jesus’ final victory over evil to encourage the church to stay faithful to Jesus even through persecution. Types of Literature in the Bible • Historical Narrative. A lot of the Bible is the people of God telling stories of what God did throughout their history. Because the Bible has so many stories, it’s basically a story of stories. 64 How Do I Read the Bible? • Law. These are the commands God gave to his people (the Israelites) after rescuing them from slavery in Egypt, both dos and don’ts. Some commands described what’s good and evil for all time, and they aren’t bound to one time or place; others were limited to describing how to run the ancient nation of Israel many centuries ago. The first five books of the Old Testament are referred to as the “law of Moses,” the “Pentateuch” (“penta” means “five”), and the “Torah” (“to instruct”). • Poetry. This is a way of writing in verse, often using figurative language and evoking strong feeling. Hebrew poetry used a lot of parallelism (parallel lines of poetry), often where the second line restates or reinforces the first line in some way. Poetry is sprinkled throughout the Bible, with some books being entirely poetic. Around a third AROUND A of the Bible is written in poetry. THIRD OF • Wisdom Literature. These are collections of wise sayings and theological THE BIBLE reflection given by Jewish sages. These range from short statements that IS WRITTEN give practical advice for particular situations (Proverbs) to deep explorations IN POETRY. of difficult questions, such as why good people suffer (Job) and why life seems futile sometimes (Ecclesiastes). Much wisdom literature is written in poetic form. • Prophecy. These are messages from God’s messengers to God’s people, sometimes given when the people were unwilling to listen. Typically, these were messages meant for the prophet’s own generation, but sometimes they were interspersed with predictions of the future (e.g., events such as the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC and the coming of the Messiah). It’s been said that God gave these messages to comfort the afflicted—and afflict the comfortable. • Gospels. These are biographies of Jesus, with the name “gospel” meaning “good news.” They narrate Jesus’ ministry, including his teachings and miracles. Each spends a good percentage of its space narrating the events of the final week of Jesus’ life, climaxing in Jesus’ death and resurrection. • Parables. These are fictional stories told using the stuff of everyday life (e.g., a fisherman separating good and bad fish, a farmer sowing seed, a guy getting robbed) to point to spiritual realities. The word literally means “to throw alongside” (“para” = alongside; “bole” = to throw). These stories were “thrown alongside” the truth being taught. Jesus taught numerous parables. • Letters. These are letters written by early church leaders such as Paul, Peter, and John to early Christians to help them navigate questions they had and issues their churches faced. Many were written to churches in particular cities, such as Romans (written to the Christians in Rome) and Ephesians (written to the Christians in Ephesus). These are also referred to as “epistles.” Many were written by Paul, and thus are called “Pauline Epistles.” The letters that 65

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook other people wrote to a more generic audience (not a particular church in a particular city) are called “General Epistles.” • Apocalypse. This genre describes cataclysmic events using rich symbolism. The word means an “uncovering” or “revelation.” Bible books that use the apocalyptic genre are Daniel in the Old Testament and Revelation in the New Testament. A Crash Course in Biblical Interpretation The Bible was written a long time ago in very different cultures than most of us are used to. The process of trying to understand and interpret what the Bible means is called “hermeneutics.” Why do we need hermeneutics? (Can’t we just read the Bible and understand it?) Sort of. It’s true that the Bible is written in a way that we can get the general message just by reading it. And it’s especially important that we come to the Bible with humility, wanting to seek God’s will for our lives—otherwise we’ll miss the point. But even someone who reads the Bible and tries to put its wisdom into practice will find it dif- ficult to understand in parts. Why? Well, if you live in the twenty-first century and in a different region of the world, quite a bit of distance exists between you and the world of the Bible. Here are some of the types of distance between us and the world of the Bible: • Time: We live in a different time from the world of the Bible. • Language: We speak different languages from the languages of the Bible (Hebrew, Greek, and some Aramaic). • Geography: Many of us live in a different part of the world from the geographical world of the Bible. • Cultural: We live in a different culture from the cultures of the Bible. Because we live with these distances between us and the world of the Bible, we must approach the Bible with humility, not assuming we already know the answers. And we must try to “close the distance” as much as possible so we can understand what a particular passage meant to its original audience. In other words, when you are unfamiliar with a biblical expression or a biblical custom you read about, it’s good to research what it’s talking about. There are helpful tools for this, such as Bible commentaries, Bible dictionaries, Bible software, and study Bibles. It’s also helpful to keep in mind what genre you’re reading, because we don’t read all genres the same way (e.g., we read a his- torical account differently from how we read a poem). When it comes to trying to understand a passage of Scripture, there are basically three main steps. They are observation, interpretation, and application. 66 How Do I Read the Bible? 1. Observation This means looking closely at something. Why don’t you take a minute and really observe this Bible verse that Jesus told his disciples before ascending back to heaven: “But you will receive pow- er when the Holy Spirit comes on you; and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8). What are some aspects that stood out to you as you read the verse? 2. Interpretation This is where you go beyond just looking at a verse to figuring out what it means. One of the most helpful tools for figuring out what something in the Bible means is by looking at its context (what comes before and after it). ONE OF THE MOST For example, Jesus once said, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). What HELPFUL TOOLS was he talking about? Well, let’s zoom out and look at the context. Here’s a FOR FIGURING summary of the first half of John 6 before verse 35: Jesus miraculously fed a OUT WHAT crowd of thousands of people. They were so excited they were ready to make SOMETHING IN him their king by force. Jesus withdrew, knowing they weren’t really wanting THE BIBLE MEANS him, but just what he could do for them. The people found him and asked for IS BY LOOKING more miracles. Now here’s a summary of the second half of John 6 after verse AT ITS CONTEXT. 35: Jesus explained that he was what they needed. He was the source of life. They would find what they were spiritually hungry for in him. Can you tell from the context what Jesus meant by saying, “I am the bread of life”? That’s the step known as interpretation. 3. Application This is taking what the Bible says to do and figuring out how to live it out in the world today. James 1:22 says, “Do not merely listen to the word, and so deceive yourselves. Do what it says.” Just reading the Bible and not doing what it says is a way of lying to ourselves. Acting in faith and doing what God says is the best way to truly understand his will. So when we read a passage just to observe it and interpret it (but don’t act on it), we miss the point. Seven Questions to Ask When You Read the Bible Have you ever read a passage of Scripture and then wondered, What did I just read? or, Okay, now what? To help you understand what the Bible says and apply it, we recommend asking yourself seven questions. Here are seven Discovery questions you can ask each time you get done working through 67

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook a passage of Scripture. (They’ll look familiar; we are walking through each of these questions at the end of each chapter): 1. What did you like about this passage? 2. What was hard to understand? 3. What does this passage teach us about God? 4. What does this passage teach us about the enemy (Satan)? 5. What does this passage teach us about humans? 6. What is one truth I will live out from this passage? 7. What truth from this passage will I share with someone? SCRIPTURE What does each verse teach me about the importance of reading the Bible? “And we also thank God continually because, when you received the word of God, which you heard from us, you accepted it not as a human word, but as it actually is, the word of God, which is indeed at work in you who believe.” (1 Thessalonians 2:13) “Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who does not need to be ashamed and who correctly handles the word of truth. . . . Opponents must be gently instruct- ed, in the hope that God will grant them repen- tance leading them to a knowledge of the truth.” (2 Timothy 2:15, 25) “Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to become angry. . . . FROM THE UNITED STATES As a senior in high school, I face so many of the typical challenges that come with being a disciple of Jesus at this age. I struggle with how I am going to showcase God through all that I am. I struggle with identifying who in my life has the qualities of God that I aspire to have. And ultimately how I can spread the light that God has given me. Most of my life has been used by God to mold who I am in his love. He has built up the parts of me that showcase his love, and with each day he continuously chips away at the parts of me that cling to worldly desires. God continues to bring convictions on held beliefs that don’t align with his heart, and he truly shifts my understanding on so many AS A FOLLOWER controversial topics to align with his Word. He helps me to hold his truth up to OF JESUS, I everything that the world speaks. As a follower of Jesus, I have received the tools HAVE RECEIVED for faithfulness in his Word. THE TOOLS FOR Being the child of a father in the army, I was constantly moving. My envi- FAITHFULNESS ronments were constantly changing until eighth grade. I changed schools, IN HIS WORD. houses, and friends nearly every school year. I grew skills in being adaptable, overcoming obstacles, and meeting new people. Although these skills are all helpful, I still struggle to accept change. But with my faith in God, I have learned to trust that he will be constant no matter the magnitude of change that I experience. He tells me through his Word that he is always right beside me (Philippians 4:5). He has been there in every state and at every school. I couldn’t even begin to list every moment he has been there for me, and I especially can’t list all the amazing ways he has refueled and used the light that he has given me. It has been a true blessing getting to be the capsule of God’s love for so many people during a time that they feel defeated. Although those situations hold a lot of responsibilities, God has always pulled through. One of the greatest lessons he has taught me is that if we don’t look to him and 69

But when we look to him and listen to him, he directs our lives to help a lot of people. Although I haven’t been through much of life, I know that if you put your trust in God, he will provide no matter what. Also, make sure you surround yourself with a good community, a commu- nity that can build you up and be there for you during the rough times. pages.content: Page intentionally left blank 55 WHAT ARE MY CORE BELIEFS? What does “core” mean? The core of the earth is its centermost layer, some 9,000 degrees Fahr- enheit. The core of an apple is its hard center, the location of seeds and a stem. If you exercise to work out your “core,” that means to strengthen your central muscles, primarily in your abdomen and back. Without a core, things crumble. They don’t last. You also have core beliefs. These are the beliefs you believe so strongly that they explain why you make the most important choices you make. Just because somebody reads the Bible or even “believes” the Bible doesn’t mean the teachings of the Bible form their core beliefs. Here are three possibilities when it comes to how seriously people take the Bible. Take a couple of minutes and ask yourself which of these options best describes where you are: Option 1: I don’t really believe what the Bible teaches. A lot of people don’t believe what the Bible teaches. Maybe they follow a different religion. Maybe they are skeptical about the Bible’s claims (for example, when it talks about miracles). Or maybe, when the Bible says one thing, but the people around them say another, they feel they should go with whatever the people around them say. For whatever reason, many people don’t believe what the Bible teaches. Option 2: I believe what the Bible teaches, but it doesn’t form my core beliefs. Many people believe what the Bible teaches, but it doesn’t make a big difference in how they live. Maybe they go to church each week, sing the songs, and listen to the sermon, but by the next day, they don’t think much about God. They don’t spend much time listening to him by reading the Bible or talking to him by praying. For them, it’s more of a weekly thing to do, like a weekly to-do item to check off the list and be done with. Option 3: I believe what the Bible teaches, and it forms my core beliefs. The Bible makes claims that, if true, are world changing. If God truly exists, then he’s the one who decides what’s true and false, right and wrong. If Jesus truly is the Savior of the world and the ris- en king, then we’ve got the solution for the deepest problems we could ever face. If death truly isn’t 75

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook the end and “we will all stand before God’s judgment seat” (Romans 14:10), then nothing is more important to get right in our lives than getting right with God. What this means is that Option 1 and Option 3 both make more sense than Option 2. If the teachings of the Bible are not true, then don’t believe it (Option 1). But if they are true? Nothing could be more important. If you want to be a consistent, logical person, then believing these teach- ings will mean allowing them to form the innermost core of who you are and how you live. Atheist-turned-Christian C. S. Lewis explained that when it comes to Jesus, there are three main ways to view him.11 If Jesus really said the kinds of things we read about in the Gospels—claiming to be God in human flesh—then we’re basically down to these three options: 1. Either he was a madman. 2. Or he was a liar. 3. Or he was God in human flesh. Those are your three options. Trying to have a fuzzy view somewhere in the middle (e.g., saying, “I think Jesus was a great moral teacher, but I don’t believe he was the Son of God”) isn’t really a logical option. If he claimed to be God in flesh and the Savior of the world, and that was the center of his teaching, you either reject that or you accept it. And if you accept him as those things, then that should rock you to the core. SELF-ASSESSMENT My three main options when it comes to how the Bible relates to my core beliefs are: 1. I don’t really believe what the Bible teaches. 2. I believe what the Bible teaches, but it doesn’t form my core beliefs. 3. I believe what the Bible teaches, and it forms my core beliefs. When it comes to how the Bible relates to my core beliefs, here’s how I would describe where I am: 76 What Are My Core Beliefs? When it comes to how the Bible relates to my core beliefs, here’s where I want to be and why I want to be there: Definition: Essential Elements Definition: Personal Elements Elements of the faith that are necessary for salva- Elements of the faith that are not essential or im- tion. The essential truths are that God exists, Jesus portant. These are based on convictions or pref- is Lord, Jesus is the risen Savior, and salvation erences that are minor or not biblically clear. is by grace and not by human effort. The essen- tial markers of our salvation are the indwelling of the Holy Spirit and a faith that perseveres. Definition: Important Elements Definition: Progressive Christianity Secondary elements to the faith that we A rewriting of essential and important elements of seek and pursue out of faithfulness to God, biblical Christianity to fit Western secular values. even as we acknowledge that our salvation is not dependent on getting them right. STUDY What should your core beliefs be? Here are some thoughts to help you as you wrestle with this question. What Are the Core Beliefs of Christianity? Not everything we read about in the Bible was meant to become a core conviction. After all, in the Bible we have everything from “Do not cook a young goat in its mother’s milk” (Exodus 23:19) to “For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16). So how do we figure out which teachings of the Bible are meant to form our core, innermost convictions—and which teachings are meant to stay more on the outer edges? If you’re curious which teachings of the Bible are meant to form our innermost convictions, it will be helpful to understand three types of “elements” in our faith, set out in Chad Ragsdale’s Real Life Theology book Christian Convictions: Discerning the Essential, Important, and Personal Elements. These are essential elements (these are necessary for salvation), important elements (these are important 77

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook in order to follow Jesus faithfully), and personal elements (these are based on marginal convictions or preferences). If you drew a target, personal elements would be the outermost ring, followed by important elements, and essential elements would form the bullseye. We’re going to use 1 Corinthians, a letter that the apostle Paul wrote to the church in Corinth as a way of unpacking these three categories. Personal Elements. In 1 Corinthians, Paul brought up an issue that is in the category of per- sonal elements: the issue of food sacrificed to idols. In that culture, idol worship was common, and much of the meat sold in markets came from animals that had been sacrificed in idolatrous ritu- als. So if a Christian were to buy that meat, would that be participating in idolatry? Paul tackled a question on the minds of the Corinthian Christians: Is it okay to eat food sacrificed to idols or not? Paul explained that it’s a matter of personal preference, so we need to give people freedom and encourage them to be gentle with those who disagree: Some people are still so accustomed to idols that when they eat sacrificial food they think of it as having been sacrificed to a god, and since their conscience is weak, it is defiled. But food does not bring us near to God; we are no worse if we do not eat, and no better if we do. Be careful, however, that the exercise of your rights does not become a stumbling block to the weak. (1 Corinthians 8:7–9) When it comes to personal elements, there’s not a clear right or wrong, so there’s freedom to do what you think is wisest. One thing you must remember is not to misuse your freedom in such a 78 What Are My Core Beliefs? way that, by your decisions, you make another person stumble. Just because you’re free to do some- thing doesn’t mean you have God’s permission to do what will lead another person down a bad path. It’s important when someone disagrees with you to respond with a lov- ing attitude. Sometimes the disagreement centers on a “personal” element, JUST BECAUSE and when it does, trying to persuade someone else to see things from your YOU’RE FREE TO point of view is not important. When it comes to “important” and “essen- DO SOMETHING tial” elements, it is important to try to persuade people of the truth—but DOESN’T MEAN even then, you want to do so with a loving attitude. Gentleness is far more YOU HAVE GOD’S powerful (and Christlike!) than getting angry and impatient with people PERMISSION TO DO who disagree with you. WHAT WILL LEAD Important Elements. Then there’s the middle ring, the important ele- ANOTHER PERSON ments. Clearly, the Corinthians to whom Paul wrote were already saved (see DOWN A BAD PATH. 1 Corinthians 1:2–6). Yet they clearly had some major issues in the church that Paul needed to help them with. They were saved but needed help living out their faith in Jesus faithfully. Here are some samples from this letter: • They had divisions and different factions in the church (1 Corinthians 1:10). • They were caught up in worldly jealousy and quarreling (1 Corinthians 3:3). • They were not bringing proper church discipline on a man who was sleeping with his father’s wife (1 Corinthians 5:1–6). • They were suing each other and taking each other to court (1 Corinthians 6:1–6). • They were getting rowdy and drunk during the Lord’s Supper (1 Corinthians 11:17ff). • They were not acting right regarding spiritual gifts (1 Corinthians 12:1–13:13). So were these issues in the church important or unimportant? Definitely important. That’s why there’s a middle category called “important elements,” which we need to pay attention to since these are part of your ongoing faithfulness to God and for living as God intended. Essential Elements. In 1 Corinthians 15:1–3, Paul outlined some of the essential elements of the Christian faith: Now, brothers and sisters, I want to remind you of the gospel I preached to you, which you received and on which you have taken your stand. By this gospel you are saved, if you hold firmly to the word I preached to you. Otherwise, you have believed in vain. For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures. 79

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook What are the essential elements in this passage? Paul reminded the church about the importance of the gospel (the “good news” about Jesus). He spent his life teaching, preaching, and sharing the gospel. He has already declared the truth of the gospel to the Corinthian church, and he wanted them to continue to take their stand on it. His life was gospel-centered, and he told the church to remember the gospel that saved them. Paul then explained more fully what the gospel is, and he considered this “of first importance.” This is fascinating: the apostle Paul who wrote so much of the New Testament is saying that there’s something that should be at the top of your list of what matters most. If any- thing deserves to be a core belief that you build your life on, this is it. If any IF THERE IS truth should define our lives, this is it. ANYTHING WE And what is this core essential to which Paul points the Corinthian Chris- SHOULD BE tians? It’s that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was PASSIONATE buried, and that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures. ABOUT, IT’S THE For Paul, this is the main thing. This is what his life was focused on. If there GOSPEL OF THE is anything we should be passionate about, it’s the gospel of the risen, saving RISEN, SAVING King Jesus. KING JESUS. There has been a trend in the Western world among some Christians to try to change some of the essential and important elements of Christianity to fit what the secular culture teaches. For example, they might try to change what the Bible says about sexuality to fit the Western world’s “sexual revolution,” which makes actions such as premarital sex, homosexual sex, and adultery seem fine. Or they might try to change what the Bible says about Jesus being the only way to God, saying there are actually many paths to God through the major world religions. This trend to rewrite essential and important elements of Christianity is often called “progres- sive Christianity.” Going progressive can seem like it would be a way to get more people to become interested in Christianity. However, as David Young shows in his book A Grand Illusion,12 progres- sive Christianity might look like an on-ramp to Christianity, but it always ends up turning into an off-ramp as people lose interest in this watered-down faith that is grounded in a changing culture instead of the Bible. Six Essential Elements What are the essentials of the faith? We’ve already talked about how the gospel is core to our faith, but is there anything else? In Christian Convictions, Chad Ragsdale describes six essential elements of our faith that are necessary for our salvation. There are four essential truths we must believe and two essential markers of our salvation. They all connect at some level with the gospel. 80 What Are My Core Beliefs? We must believe these essential truths: • God exists. • Jesus is Lord. • Jesus is the risen Savior. • Salvation is by grace and not by human effort. These are the essential markers of saved people: • The indwelling of the Holy Spirit • A faith that perseveres You probably noticed three persons listed in the six essential elements above: God, Jesus, and the Holy Spirit. Who are they, and how do they relate to each other? First, who is God? God is, by definition, the greatest possible being. God is the ultimate in good- ness, power, and wisdom. He is the only being who is “self-existent,” which means his existence isn’t dependent on anything else (he just exists). God’s uniqueness and self-existence explain why God refers to himself in Exodus 3:14 as “I am who I am.” Many other religions also teach that there is a God, but Christianity’s view of God comes with a unique twist. The Bible refers to three persons when it refers to God: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. There’s God the Father who sent Jesus to rescue us. There’s God the Son (Jesus) who added humanity (what we call the “incarnation”), died to take the CHRISTIANITY’S punishment for our sins, rose from the dead, and is now enthroned as king. Then VIEW OF GOD there’s God the Spirit (the Holy Spirit) whom the Father and Son sent to dwell COMES WITH A within believers and draw people to Jesus. UNIQUE TWIST. Why do Christians believe in one God in three persons (what Christians call the “Trinity”)? Because when we put together what the Bible teaches, this is what emerges: • There’s one God (e.g., Deuteronomy 6:4; Isaiah 44:6; 45:18; 1 Corinthians 8:4). • There are three persons (each with a mind, will, and emotions) who are each called God (e.g., Father: Romans 15:6; Son: John 20:28; Spirit: Acts 5:3–4). 81

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook Another way of putting it is: • First, the people of God experienced God above (God the Father). • Second, the people of God experienced God beside (God the Son). • Last, the people of God experienced God within (God the Spirit). The more we trust and follow Jesus, the more central God becomes to our core convictions and life choices. As Acts 17:28 puts it, “In him we live and move and have our being.” SCRIPTURE What does each verse teach me about how people respond when they truly believe God’s Word? “Jonah began by going a day’s journey into the city, proclaiming, ‘Forty more days and Nineveh will be overthrown.’ The Ninevites believed God. A fast was proclaimed, and all of them, from the greatest to the least, put on sackcloth. When Jonah’s warning reached the king of Nineveh, he rose from his throne, took off his roy- al robes, covered himself with sackcloth and sat down in the dust.” (Jonah 3:4–6) “Then the king called together all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem. . . . He read in their hearing all the words of the Book of the Covenant, which had been found in the temple of the Lord. . . . Then all the people pledged themselves to the covenant.” (2 Kings 23:1–3) “Many of those who believed now came and openly confessed what they had done. A number who had practiced sorcery brought their scrolls together and burned them publicly. When they calculated the value of the scrolls, the total came to fifty thousand drachmas. In this way the word of the Lord spread widely and grew in power.” (Acts 19:18–20) 82 What Are My Core Beliefs? “The seed on good soil stands for those with a noble and good heart, who hear the word, retain it, and by persevering produce a crop.” (Jesus in Luke 8:15) SNAPSHOT . . . FROM THE UNITED STATES I was in the eleventh grade and a few months into a new small group that our missions pastor had created. One day, the missions pastor handed each of us our next book. At the time, I still wasn’t sure why I was there. Missions always seemed boring to me, and I had no desire to ever move to another country. Little did I know this book would serve as the match to be dropped upon barrels full of dried-out Scripture that I had read many times over, but never “got.” As with many called to the mission field, it started with Matthew 28:19–20, the Great Com- mission. Just as Adam had been given a task in the garden, which he failed, so Jesus, our second Adam, was given a task. Yet at the end of his work, he could cry, “It is finished!” as he accomplished our redemption. And shortly after his ascension, Jesus sent the Holy Spirit to apply redemption to his people. Yet what Paul brings out in Romans 10:14–17 is that the Holy Spir- it’s chosen instrument is the word of the gospel from the mouths of his people. FOR ME, Hence, we have the Great Commission. Every believer is tasked with proclaim- THE GREAT ing this message of the gospel to the world with the prayer that the Spirit will COMMISSION open eyes and give life. WENT FROM A For me, the Great Commission went from a sort-of belief to a core conviction. SORT-OF BELIEF When these truths clicked together, it became clear that I had a task, some- TO A CORE thing to do. The light of Scripture further revealed my task. Romans 1 and 3 CONVICTION. showed me the guilt of all people—even those who had never heard the gos- pel. These weren’t merely innocent people who would be judged guilty only on account of their ignorance. No, these were people living in darkness and rebellion against their Cre- ator. And Romans 9–10 taught me that God had designed to save people such as these. Before the book of Romans concludes, Paul tells of his own desire to “preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named, lest I build on someone else’s foundation” (Romans 15:20, ESV). Passages like these, along with a common-sense calculation that one light has the largest impact in the darkest place, drove me to pray for an opportunity to proclaim the gospel and plant churches in unreached people groups. 83

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook Soon after, God laid on my heart one specific people group in a highly restricted country with rampant persecution of Christians. In my youthful zeal (along with quite a bit of pride, I might add), I figured I would go there soon after high school. God had much more to teach me, however. Over the next five years, I had plenty of opportunities to explore this call further. I went on mission trips, both short-term and long-term. I went to a Christian college and got a missions degree. And I start- ed evangelizing amongst the rapidly growing Muslim community near me. None of these steps was taken without mistakes. But they were steps taken in faith. For how could I ever expect God to use me on the mission field if I wasn’t faithfully praying now? How could I plant churches in a strange culture if I couldn’t communicate the gospel in my own? About seven years after being awakened to the Great Commission, I crossed the border into the country for which I had prayed for so long. We only got to stay four days. Mountains of work need- ed to be done in the country, but none of it was legal. So we prayed for those four days to be fruit- ful. And one night, my friend and I sat across the table from one of the local men who could speak English. And we explained the gospel to him. A year later, I tried to organize a team to go back. In God’s wisdom, that door was shut. To this day, it is still shut. Thus, I have committed myself to doing the “boring” things. Praying. Studying God’s Word. Being a faithful member of my local church. Evangelizing. And I do all these things in faith because I know that God blesses faithful- ness, not shortcuts. The gospel is worth it. — Sam, US SUMMARY 1. Our core beliefs shape how we live our lives and the decisions we make. 2. Some elements of the Christian faith are essential to salvation, some elements are important, and some are personal. 3. At the core of the Christian faith is the gospel, the good news of the risen, saving King Jesus. SELF-REFLECTION AND DISCUSSION 1. If someone asked you what are the “essential” elements of Christianity you need to believe to be saved, how would you answer? 84 What Are My Core Beliefs? 2. What are some of the reasons it can be tempting to change essential or important elements of Christianity, as we see in progressive Christianity? Do we have the right to do this? 3. What role does the Bible play in shaping, leading, and guiding how you live your life? 4. If someone asked you to define God, Jesus, and the Holy Spirit, how would you answer? 5. What is one step you can take so the essential elements of the Christian faith become your core convictions? pages.content: Page intentionally left blank 66 WHAT’S THE BEST NEWS? We’ve all heard good news. Our favorite sports team finally won the national championship. Our semester grades got calculated and—we passed! Our family is finally going on the vaca- tion we’ve always wanted to take. What’s the best news you could ever hear? This is the kind of question that, if you answer hon- estly, says a lot about yourself. The Bible word for “good news” is gospel. When Jesus came on the scene, he came preaching the gospel. As we can see from the following verse, in Jesus’ mind, the best news possible was the king- dom he was bringing to earth: Jesus went into Galilee, proclaiming the good news of God. “The time has come,” he said. “The kingdom of God has come near. Repent and believe the good news!” (Mark 1:14–15) But not everyone felt that Jesus’ kingdom was the best news possible. For them, there were bet- ter gospels. It’s the same in our day: a lot of people take a look at Jesus’ kingdom and say, “That’s nice,” but they have better gospels they believe in. Below are some options for what people think is the best news possible. Take a couple of minutes and ask yourself which of these options you feel would be the best news: Option 1: Good news for good people Jesus could have spent most of his time with the really good people in society: the Pharisees. They were professional holy men. They knew the Hebrew Scriptures (the Old Testament). They could quote Scripture and pray fancy prayers in public. They fasted and tithed. The problem is they didn’t believe in Jesus’ good news. Instead, they had their own good news: good news for good people. That was their gospel: God loved the people who had it together morally and spiritually. 89

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook Option 2: Good news for rich, powerful people Jesus could have spent most of his time with the really powerful people in society. For example, the rich, politically savvy Sadducees who oversaw the temple. They had an inside relationship with the government. And they were financially loaded. The problem is they didn’t believe in Jesus’ good news. For them, the best news was when everything works out well for the rich and powerful. Option 3: Good news for oppressed people Without fail, every culture seemingly has a group or groups of people whose needs get ignored. Sometimes they are mistreated by people in power. This is what we mean by “oppressed people.” But isn’t this the gospel that Jesus preached—good news for oppressed people? Sort of. When he described his ministry, Jesus quoted from the book of Isaiah: The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim freedom for the prisoners and recovery of sight for the blind, to set the oppressed free. (Luke 4:18) And all throughout his ministry, Jesus lifted up marginalized people through compassionate deeds. On the other hand, Jesus didn’t side with the Zealots, the people who wanted to drive out the Roman oppressors. Instead, he hung out with Zealots and tax collectors (who got rich off oppressing their countrymen) alike, embracing them all as people whom God loves. He advocated paying tax- es to Rome and even extended miracles of compassion to Roman soldiers. His version of good news included helping oppressed people—but went beyond it. Ultimately, he aimed to defeat the things that oppress everybody: sin, death, and Satan. Option 4: Good news for everybody Jesus disappointed a lot of people by loving their enemies. The professional holy people couldn’t believe Jesus hung out with notorious sinners. The rich people couldn’t believe Jesus hung out with people who were dirty and poor. Revolutionaries couldn’t believe Jesus hung out with the oppres- sors as well as the oppressed. But Jesus knew something most of them had forgotten: “For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). He recognized our deepest enemy isn’t each other; it’s our own wrong decisions, as we choose to trust ourselves over God and love ourselves and neglect others. For those of us who see ourselves clearly, Jesus came with the best news we could imagine: we can be forgiven of our sins and welcomed as citizens into his kingdom of love and holiness. In his kingdom, we join as brothers and sisters of people we once called enemies. 90 What’s the Best News? SELF-ASSESSMENT Here are my four main options when it comes to the best news imaginable: 1. Good news for good people 2. Good news for rich, powerful people 3. Good news for the oppressed 4. Definition: Justification The process of gaining right standing before God so we are no longer under the penalty of sin. We are justified by his grace through our faith. Justification is a priceless benefit made possible to us because of the gospel. STUDY What should you see as the best news? Here are some thoughts to help you as you wrestle with this question. Why Do We Need the Gospel Anyway? The gospel includes a lot of big words: “preexistence,” “incarnation,” “resurrection,” “justification.” And behind each of these big words are massive, mountain-moving acts of God: the Son of God being born in history. The Son of God absorbing all of history’s sins while being crucified. The Son of God rising from the dead and being enthroned as our saving king. The return of the king to rule and reign over a renewed creation. Awesome story. But it can be confusing, making us want to pause, zoom out, and ask a big-pic- ture question: Why? Why did God feel that he needed to go to all this trouble? What could have been so messed up with us that God needed to go through all of this to rescue us? Let’s zoom out. Why do we need the gospel? We’ll be able to understand why we need the gos- pel as we answer three basic questions: 1. Why did God create us? 2. What happened to us? 3. What happens to us if we don’t have the gospel? 92 What’s the Best News? Why Did God Create Us? God made humans for a surprisingly important purpose. Here are a couple Scriptures that tell us what this purpose is: Then God said, “Let us make mankind in our image, in our likeness, so that they may rule over the fish in the sea and the birds in the sky, over the livestock and all the wild animals, and over all the creatures that move along the ground.” So God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them. God blessed them and said to them, “Be fruitful and increase in number; fill the earth and subdue it. Rule over the fish in the sea and the birds in the sky and over every living creature that moves on the ground.” (Genesis 1:26–28) What is mankind that you are mindful of them, human beings that you care for them? You have made them a little lower than the angels and crowned them with glory and honor. You made them rulers over the works of your hands; you put everything under their feet. (Psalm 8:5–6) Why did God create us? He made us in his image to rule wisely over the earth and spread his image and glory all over the planet. What Happened to Us? Have you ever made something really cool, like a piece of art, that someone else ruined? Perhaps it was a picture you drew that your younger brother or sister scribbled over. If so, then you know what it was like for God when his image bearers mangled his likeness in them through sin. A tempter (we now know him as Satan) took the form of a serpent and convinced the first humans they couldn’t trust God. He implied that God had something grand he was keeping from them and that freedom meant taking control and being their own gods. They needed to do their own thing and rule themselves. When the first humans followed Satan into sin, chaos followed. Shame, blame, pain. That’s in Genesis 3, and, within a few chapters of Genesis, we see brother killing brother, a warrior boasting to his wives of the people he has killed, and humanity as a whole turning violent and devoted to doing evil things. What happened? Humans sepa- HUMANS SEPARATED rated themselves from God and ruled themselves as they saw fit. THEMSELVES FROM What Happens to Us If We Don’t Have the Gospel? GOD AND RULED If we don’t have the gospel, then when we die, that separation from God THEMSELVES AS continues for all eternity. THEY SAW FIT. 93

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook The Bible talks about a final judgment at the end of time followed by a glorious restoration of creation as it was meant to be (the “new heaven and new earth”). At this final judgment, God, the righteous Judge, will separate humanity into two groups: those who have given God permission through faith to restore them back into their original image, and those who continue to reject God’s rule and mar his image in them by their sin. In other words, there are those who obey the gospel and those who reject the gospel. Through the gospel, God removes the following types of destruction caused by sin: • Personal effects of sin (the shame and self-hatred we feel) • Social effects of sin (the hostility we have toward each other) • Cosmic effects of sin (the death and decay in our fallen world) So long as we reject the gospel, we continue to keep God away and cut ourselves off from his work to restore us into his image. If we reject God’s gospel, then at the final judgment, he will give us our wish: we will be separated from him eternally. In other words, if we have kept IF WE HAVE KEPT God out of our lives, then he, in the end, will keep us out of his life. GOD OUT OF OUR This is why we desperately need the gospel. LIVES, THEN HE, IN THE END, WILL The Gospel in the Old Testament: Predictions of a Saving King KEEP US OUT If “good news for everybody” sounds like the best option, then you need to OF HIS LIFE. know how it happens. This gospel comes about through only one way: Jesus is king. In the Old Testament are dozens of prophecies of the coming king. It is as if throughout the Old Testament, we can paint a target with increasingly focused circles as time goes on. The picture that emerges is a king bringing his reign to earth by rescuing us from our sins: • Genesis 3:15: A human will defeat the serpent even as the serpent strikes him. • Genesis 12:1–3: Hope for all nations will come from the Jewish people. This is affirmed for Abraham (Genesis 18:18; 22:18), his son Isaac (Genesis 26:4), and his son Jacob (Genesis 28:14), whose name God changed to “Israel.” • 2 Samuel 7:12–16: An everlasting kingdom will be established through the lineage of David. • Isaiah 9:1–7: A king will arise from the lineage of David, one who will also be divine. • Micah 5:2: A ruler will arise in Bethlehem who existed from ancient times. 94 What’s the Best News? • Daniel 2: Although four empires will come (Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome), the kingdom of God will then arise and become a mountain that covers the whole earth (see especially 2:44–45). • Isaiah 53:1–12: A servant of the Lord will be killed (v. 9) for the people’s sins (v. 5)—and then God will “prolong his days” (v. 10). A Ten-Scripture Tour Through Jesus’ Life on Earth 1. Jesus’ Birth: “But the angel said to her, ‘Do not be afraid, Mary; you have found favor with God. You will conceive and give birth to a son, and you are to call him Jesus. He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over Jacob’s descendants forever; his kingdom will never end’” (Luke 1:30–33). 2. Jesus’ Baptism: “At that time Jesus came from Nazareth in Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan. Just as Jesus was coming up out of the water, he saw heaven being torn open and the Spirit descending on him like a dove. And a voice came from heaven: ‘You are my Son, whom I love; with you I am well pleased’” (Mark 1:9–11). 3. Jesus’ Mission: “The scroll of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him. Unrolling it, he found the place where it is written: ‘The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to pro- claim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim freedom for the pris- oners and recovery of sight for the blind, to set the oppressed free, to proclaim “TODAY THIS the year of the Lord’s favor.’ Then he rolled up the scroll, gave it back to the SCRIPTURE IS attendant and sat down. The eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fastened FULFILLED IN on him. He began by saying to them, ‘Today this scripture is fulfilled in your YOUR HEARING.” hearing’” (Luke 4:17–21). 4. Jesus’ Teachings and Healings: “Jesus went throughout Galilee, teach- ing in their synagogues, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom, and healing every disease and sickness among the people” (Matthew 4:23). 5. Jesus’ Parables: “Jesus spoke all these things to the crowd in parables; he did not say any- thing to them without using a parable” (Matthew 13:34). 6. Jesus’ Claim: “When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralyzed man, ‘Son, your sins are forgiven.’ Now some teachers of the law were sitting there, thinking to themselves, ‘Why does this fellow talk like that? He’s blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?’” (Mark 2:5–7). 7. Jesus’ Enemies: “Every day he was teaching at the temple. But the chief priests, the teachers of the law and the leaders among the people were trying to kill him. Yet they could not find any way to do it, because all the people hung on his words” (Luke 19:47–48). 95

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook 8. Jesus’ Death: “And they crucified him. Dividing up his clothes, they cast lots to see what each would get” (Mark 15:24). 9. Jesus’ Resurrection: “Suddenly Jesus met them. ‘Greetings,’ he said. They came to him, clasped his feet and worshiped him” (Matthew 28:9). 10. Jesus’ Commission: “Then Jesus came to them and said, ‘All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything I have com- manded you. And surely I am with you always, to the very end of the age’” (Matthew 28:18–20). So What Is the Gospel? Matthew W. Bates, author of The Gospel Precisely: Surprisingly Good News About Jesus Christ the King, has done much studying to define the gospel. It’s not hard to know how we receive the gospel: we receive it by grace through faith (Ephesians 2:8–10). But what THE GOSPEL exactly is the gospel (literally, the “good news”)? In short, the gospel is that Jesus IS THAT is the saving king. JESUS IS THE In The Gospel Precisely, Bates lists ten events that are part of what the Bible SAVING KING. calls the gospel. He writes: The gospel is that Jesus the king: 1. preexisted as God the Son, 2. was sent by the Father, 3. took on human flesh in fulfillment of God’s promises to David, 4. died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, 5. was buried, 6. was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures, 7. appeared to many witnesses, 8. is enthroned at the right hand of God as the ruling Christ, 9. has sent the Holy Spirit to his people to effect his rule, and 10. will come again as final judge to rule.13 That’s a lot to remember. (Although it’s worth memorizing at some point!) But something we can all memorize right now is the short answer. What is the gospel? Jesus is the saving king. 96 What’s the Best News? What Makes Jesus’ Resurrection So Important? Have you ever wondered what was so great about Jesus rising from the dead? For his disciples in the first century, it was such amazing news that they were willing to be persecuted and even killed for preaching it. They knew that any hostility that came their way was worth it because Jesus had ris- en from the dead. But what about us? What makes Jesus’ resurrection worth celebrating for us, living so many cen- turies later? Here are six reasons his resurrection is so important for us today. To help us remember these reasons, they’ll spell the word “EASTER.” E – Jesus’ Execution wasn’t the End. Jesus’ resurrection is important because it means that history’s greatest injustice, the crucifixion of God’s Son, didn’t end in tragedy. We can be hopeful because his execution wasn’t the final chapter in his story. A – There’s an Afterlife. When Jesus rose from the dead, it showed us that death doesn’t have the final say. There’s an afterlife. And Jesus didn’t rise from death and then become a disembodied soul. He was raised to a physical body (Luke 24:41–43) that would no longer wear out or die. In the same way, at the “final resurrec- tion” at the end of time, God promises to raise us up to physical bodies fit for the new heaven and new earth (1 Corinthians 15:42). S – Jesus was Successful in forgiving our Sins. Jesus’ resurrection is important because it means the crucifixion wasn’t just an unfortunate event. Jesus’ resurrection means the crucifixion was effective in doing what Jesus meant it to accomplish: to save us from our sins. Because Jesus rose, we can have confidence that, because of the cross, God really did forgive us of our sins. T – Jesus Told the Truth. BY RAISING If the cross had been the end of the story, we couldn’t have confidence that HIM FROM THE Jesus had been telling the truth about his Father, the right way to live, and his DEAD, GOD WAS heavenly identity. But since the cross wasn’t the end, it shows that what Jesus CONFIRMING had said was true. By raising him from the dead, God was confirming that THAT JESUS Jesus came from him and was telling the truth. And we can entrust our life— CAME FROM HIM and afterlife—to him. AND WAS TELLING THE TRUTH. 97

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook E – Jesus Ended the reign of our Enemies. “Enemies” refers to our greatest enemies: death, sin, and the devil. Jesus’ resurrection defanged and defeated death, proved our sins were forgiven, and sealed the fate of the devil. Even though the cross was the Roman Empire’s way of saying, “Game over,” the resurrection was God’s way of saying, “Jesus wins.” R – Jesus has begun Restoring all Reality. Throughout Jesus’ ministry, he gave us a preview of how creation was meant to be: he healed the hurting, welcomed outsiders, lifted up the forgotten, restored the broken. His ministry was basical- ly a movie preview of what heaven would eventually be like. As Jesus put it, in him “the kingdom of heaven has come near” (Matthew 3:2). In his kingdom, things were being made new, the way they were meant to be. He was restoring reality. After he died, it looked as though this beautiful kingdom was just another disappointment— but then he rose from the dead. His kingdom continues to grow, as his disciples today wait for him to return to earth. When he returns, we will experience the kingdom in its undiminished goodness and glory: And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, “Look! God’s dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the old order of things has passed away.” He who was seated on the throne said, “I am making everything new!” (Revelation 21:3–5a) Now that we have looked at what makes Jesus’ resurrection so important, try memorizing this acronym (EASTER) to help you remember these reasons. SCRIPTURE What does each verse teach me about the gospel? “Jesus went throughout Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, proclaiming the good news [gospel] of the kingdom, and healing every disease and sickness among the people.” (Matthew 4:23) 98 What’s the Best News? “Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle and set apart for the gospel of God— the gospel he promised beforehand through his prophets in the Holy Scriptures regarding his Son, who as to his earthly life was a descendant of David, and who through the Spirit of holiness was appointed the Son of God in power by his res- urrection from the dead: Jesus Christ our Lord.” (Romans 1:1–4) “For I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God that brings salvation to every- one who believes: first to the Jew, then to the Gentile. For in the gospel the righteousness of God is revealed—a righteousness that is by faith from first to last, just as it is written: ‘The righ- teous will live by faith.’” (Romans 1:16–17) “I am astonished that you are so quickly desert- ing the one who called you to live in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel— which is really no gospel at all. Evidently some people are throwing you into confusion and are trying to pervert the gospel of Christ. But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gos- pel other than the one we preached to you, let them be under God’s curse!” (Galatians 1:6–8) SNAPSHOT . . . FROM SOMALIA I was born sometime between 1979–1982 in a rural area. In my culture, time is not important at all, so I have no birth certificate, and I am just guessing my real age. I am the son of a Muslim reli- gious leader (a sheik). My family is highly religious and respects all religious people if they follow Islam. Having been born into an Islamic family, that was all I had ever known. In my country, it is illegal to convert to Christianity, and there is no room for Christianity in society. I am from one of the most persecuted countries in the world. My city has more than 3500 mosques and not one church building. 99

pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook I was first introduced to Jesus when I was about twenty years old by a visiting doctor. He was there helping people who had suffered injuries from the civil war going on in my country and try- ing to help the community to recover. When my friends and I first met him, he started talking with us about God and heaven. As he witnessed to us and shared the gospel of God’s love for each of us, his message seemed too good to be true. When we realized he was a Christian, we decided we should take him to the mosque to try to convert him. When we asked him to come with us to the mosque, he replied, “Do you know that Jesus is coming, not Mohammed? And I am waiting for Jesus, and Jesus is coming very soon.” Then he said, “Let me give you a Bible, and then you will read it for yourself.” He predicted that if we read it even once we wouldn’t remain in Islam. He gave us the Bible written in our language (Somali), and I remember feeling very scared to receive it. We had been taught in Islam not to read about Christianity because we could lose our faith. But when THE STORIES we started reading the Bible in our language, it felt like a new language because MADE US WANT what we were reading was all new. We started reading at the genealogy of Jesus TO READ MORE Christ and kept going; the stories made us want to read more and more. We hon- AND MORE. estly had taken the Bible to read it just to find the weak points of Christianity and tell the doctor that he was completely wrong and should repent. As I continued to read it all, I found such amazing love and peace. At this time, I began the deci- sion to follow Jesus. As soon as I converted, I was baptized alongside one of my brothers in Christ who is another Somali believer. I became a missionary very soon after. This is because one of the biggest struggles I had with the Quran was that it could never give me assurance of heaven. I had no assurances of heaven even though I was constantly told to work hard to earn my way to heav- en. I love that Jesus came and brought heaven to earth. His Word is full of love and truth, which is the best news ever. I must it share with those around me despite the cost of being persecuted and losing my family. — Ahmed, Somalia SUMMARY 1. Jesus is the long-awaited saving king. 2. The gospel reveals that through Jesus, God made a way for us to be restored in relationship with God in this life and in the life to come. 100 What’s the Best News? 3. The gospel shows the way to God the Father through God the Son (Jesus) by the power of God the Spirit. SELF-REFLECTION AND DISCUSSION 1. Why should you believe the gospel? 2. The apostle Paul said, “For I am not ashamed of the gospel.” Does that describe your life? How does being unashamed of the gospel play out in your life? 3. What is so significant about Jesus’ resurrection? 4. Why should we follow Jesus’ mission of making disciples? 5. How are you sharing the best news (the gospel) with those in your life? 101
