pages.content: Page intentionally left blank 77 AM I COMMITTED TO THIS? The Bible talks a lot about faith. But what is faith? You’ll find that people define “faith” in dif- ferent ways. For example: • A lot of skeptics think faith means believing in something when you don’t have any evidence. • A lot of kids’ stories make it sound like faith means believing in something so your dreams will come true. • A cartoon version of Christianity says faith is believing the right beliefs so you can go to heaven. But what is faith according to the Bible? Everybody places their ultimate faith in somebody or something, and the Bible invites us to put our faith in Jesus. Having faith in Jesus means: • You believe what Jesus says: “They believed the scripture and the words that Jesus had spoken” (John 2:22b). • You trust in Jesus to save you: “To those who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12). • You remain faithful/loyal to Jesus: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7). That means you’ve got some options to choose from. Are you going to have real faith in Jesus (believ- ing, trusting, and staying faithful to him)? Or are you just going to follow him for a little while and then move on to something else? In Matthew 13:1–9, Jesus told a story that lays out four options. According to Jesus’ story, a farmer scatters seeds in a field, hoping for a crop. But not all the seeds fall on good soil. 1. Some seeds fall on the footpath and get eaten up by birds. 2. Some seeds fall on rocky soil, and although a plant grows, the plant doesn’t last because its roots aren’t deep. 105

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook 3. Some seeds fall on thorny soil, and although a plant grows, it doesn’t bear fruit because the thorns choke it out. 4. Some seeds fall on good soil and yield a successful crop. This story has direct relevance to a huge choice you’ll make in your life. Here are your four options, based on Jesus’ story. Ask yourself which of these four best describes you: Option 1: I don’t really get it. This means that you hear God’s Word, but you don’t ever take the time to understand what it’s talking about. You hear about Jesus, but you don’t take time to figure out who he is or why you should follow him. Just as the birds ate up the seeds that fell on the footpath, the enemy of your soul, Satan, will snatch up the Word before you allow it to take root in your mind and heart. Option 2: I won’t really last. This means that you hear the Word of God and, at first, you get excited about it. Maybe you grow up in church, hear about Jesus, and get excited about following him. But you don’t take the time to let God grow your faith very deep. The “roots” stay shallow. So when tough times come, you end up giving up on Jesus. When it gets hard to follow Jesus, you drop out. This is like the seed planted on rocky soil; when the sun comes up, the plant withers because the roots never grew deep enough for the plant to last. Option 3: I don’t really care. This means that you believe in Jesus, and you decide you’ll follow him—but you stay so busy that you barely take any time to have an actual relationship with Jesus. You’ve got so much going on and so many other interests that your faith in Jesus never really goes anywhere. Your faith doesn’t “bear any fruit.” This is like the seed planted on thorny soil, a “faith” that basically responds to Jesus by saying, “Yeah, I believe and everything . . . but I’ve got more important stuff going on.” Option 4: I am committed to this, and I’m not giving up. This is the type of soil that takes the time to understand Jesus (unlike the path), stays faithful to him (unlike the rocky soil), and makes him a priority in your life (unlike the thorny soil). This is the type of faith described in the Bible. It’s a faith that “bears fruit.” 106 Am I Committed to This? SELF-ASSESSMENT Here are my four main options when it comes to how committed I am to Jesus: 1. I don’t really get it. 2. I won’t really last. 3. I don’t really care. 4. I am committed to this, and I’m not giving up. When it comes to how committed I am to Jesus, here’s how I would describe where I am: When it comes to how committed I am to Jesus, here’s where I want to be and why I want to be there: Definition: Faith Definition: Fruit Having faith in Jesus means to believe what Jesus A metaphor for the results that come from particu- says, trust in Jesus to save you, and remain faith- lar actions or decisions; the fruit could be good or ful/loyal to him as your Savior, Lord, and king. bad. We are known by the “fruit” our lives produce. The Holy Spirit bears the “fruit of the Spirit” in our lives: love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, good- ness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Definition: Works Good deeds that should be seen as the outworking Definition: Apostasy of our salvation, never its foundation. We are saved The desertion of the faith through engag- to do good works, and faith without works is dead. ing in ongoing lifestyles of rebellion toward God, rejecting essential Christian beliefs, or falling away because of hardship. 107

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook STUDY How committed should you be to Jesus? Here are some thoughts to help you as you wrestle with this question. Fickle vs. Faithful A seismic shift has taken place in America’s earliest universities, and this shift can provide a picture of our own lives if we’re not careful. • New England Puritans began Harvard University in 1636. Each student had to study the Bible twice a day and to “consider the main end of his life and studies to know God and Jesus Christ which is eternal life.” • In 1693, Anglicans started the College of William and Mary in hopes that Virginia might be equipped “with a seminary of ministers of the gospel,” so that “the Christian religion may be propagated amongst the Western Indians, to the glory of Almighty God.” • In 1701, Congregationalists started Yale College, partly out of a burden to “propagate in this wilderness the blessed reformed Protestant religion in the purity of its order and worship.” • Princeton University emerged out of “this great and general awakening” of the 1730s and 1740s, with its Presbyterian founders eventually calling on the Great Awakening’s preeminent theologian Jonathan Edwards to be its president. • Anglicans began King’s College, later Columbia University, in 1754 with morning and evening services conducted every day according to the Anglican liturgy. • In 1755, the Dutch Reformed established Queen’s College, later called Rutgers, to train students to “enter upon the sacred ministerial office in the church of God.”14 Needless to say, something shifted between then and now. All that remains of these schools’ clear Christian commitment is usually a chapel building here or a forgotten motto there, what one article calls “a fossilized artifact of the college’s Christian past.”15 Historian George Marsden narrates the slope in stages: The American university system was built on a foundation of evangelical Protestant colleges. Most of the major universities evolved directly from such nineteenth-century colleges. As late as 1870 the vast majority of these were remarkably evangelical. Most of them had clergy- men presidents who taught courses defending Biblicist Christianity and who encouraged periodic campus revivals. Yet within half a century the universities that emerged from these evangelical colleges, while arguably carrying forward the spirit of their evangelical forbears, 108 Am I Committed to This? had become conspicuously inhospitable to the letter of such evangelicalism. By the 1920s the evangelical Protestantism of the old-time colleges had been effectively excluded from leading university classrooms.16 Here’s a crucial lesson these stories illustrate about our relationship with God: Starting well isn’t what counts. Having a relationship with God that starts out great but fizzles out over time isn’t what God wants for us. So what does actual faith look like? Biblical faith is serious-minded commitment. It’s lifelong. It’s allegiance to a STARTING king. It’s a faithful faith. It’s not the kind of thing you get excited about for a while WELL ISN’T only to get bored or tired and move onto something else. It’s a serious, lifelong WHAT COUNTS. commitment to follow Jesus faithfully. How do we cultivate this lifelong, faithful faith? Where does it come from? Psalm 86 shows us what makes for a faithful faith: it’s a commitment to being faithful to him (vv. 2–4) that is based on his faithfulness to us (vv. 11, 15). Again, we commit to being to being faithful to God . . . Guard my life, for I am faithful to you; save your servant who trusts in you. You are my God; have mercy on me, Lord, for I call to you all day long. Bring joy to your servant, Lord, for I put my trust in you. (Psalm 86:2–4) . . . because he is committed to being faithful to us. Teach me your way, Lord, that I may rely on your faithfulness; give me an undivided heart, that I may fear your name. . . . But you, Lord, are a compassionate and gracious God, slow to anger, abounding in love and faithfulness. (Psalm 86:11, 15) We’re able to commit to being faithful to God not because of our goodness or reliability but because of his faithfulness to us. Because of his faithfulness to us, we can place wholehearted trust and allegiance in him: BECAUSE OF HIS Therefore, brothers and sisters, since we have confidence to enter FAITHFULNESS TO the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way US, WE CAN PLACE opened for us through the curtain, that is, his body, and since we WHOLEHEARTED have a great priest over the house of God, let us draw near to God with TRUST AND a sincere heart and with the full assurance that faith brings, having our ALLEGIANCE IN HIM. hearts sprinkled to cleanse us from a guilty conscience and having 109

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook our bodies washed with pure water. Let us hold unswervingly to the hope we profess, for he who promised is faithful. (Hebrews 10:19–23) Faith and salvation don’t describe events alone; they describe a lifelong relationship of faithful- ness. It’s a relationship of staying faithful to God just as he has remained faithful to us. If Jesus didn’t give up on us but went all the way to execution on a cross to reconcile us with his Father, then surely we can resolve not to give up on him. After the Crowd Left Jesus Behind Jesus performed a miracle that was so astounding that it shows up in all four Gospels: Jesus fed a crowd of thousands of people with nothing more than one kid’s lunch. John 6 is unique in telling the rest of the story. After the miracle, the people were excited and decided it was time to make Jesus their king (John 6:15). Everybody—the disciples, the crowds—was excited except for one person: Jesus, who withdrew. When the crowd found him again the next day, still excited, Jesus preached a sermon. The sermon was so uncomfortable to listen to that the crowd left disappointed, saying, “This is a hard teaching. Who can accept it?” (John 6:60). What was so offensive about the sermon? He kept saying strange things about how he was the real Bread of Life and they needed to “eat his flesh” and “drink his blood” to have life (John 6:53). Gross. They were out of there. They’d gone from “This is our king” to “This is too hard.” When they left, Jesus turned to his disciples who remained, the twelve he had already chosen, and asked, “You do not want to leave too, do you?” “LORD, TO WHOM (John 6:67). SHALL WE GO? Simon Peter responded, “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words YOU HAVE THE of eternal life. We have come to believe and to know that you are the Holy WORDS OF One of God” (John 6:68). ETERNAL LIFE.” That’s a faithful faith. Five Ways You Relate to Faith Here are some ways you relate to faith. Faith is: 1. Something you have (e.g., “You have great faith,” in Matthew 15:28). 2. Something you do (e.g., “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved,” in Acts 16:31). 3. Something you can be full of (e.g., “Kindness, goodness, and faithfulness,” in Galatians 5:22). 110 Am I Committed to This? 4. Something you can grow in (e.g., “Your faith is growing more and more,” in 2 Thessalonians 1:3). 5. Something you hold fast to (e.g., the “faith that was once for all entrusted to God’s holy people,” in Jude 1:3). Should Suffering Weaken Our Faith—or Strengthen It? Suffering is never fun, but it can be a good thing for us, especially for those who love God and are willing to be conformed to Christlikeness (Romans 8:28–30). Far from being something that should slice away at our hold on God, suffering is something that ought to strengthen our grip and con- vince us that he is trustworthy, even when life scams us. Here are five reasons why suffering points us to God. 1. If we never suffered, we would never hate evil. Without suffering, people could do as much evil as they wanted, but would never suffer the conse- quences. No one would ever see the ugliness of evil, so no one would ever actually hate evil. 2. If we never suffered, we would never appreciate goodness. Without suffering, everything good that happened to us, we would just expect. We would never thank God for the blessings he gives us because we would figure that’s just the way it’s supposed to be. Gratitude, a fuel for so much virtue, would have trouble taking root within us. 3. If we never suffered, we would never need God. We would never feel the need to have God in our lives. We would never need to seek him, to get right with him. We would remain blissfully but hopelessly lost. 4. If we never suffered, we would never hope for heaven. We would never hope for the day that God would come and rescue us. Rather, we would naturally hope to stay on earth, content with an empty and self-absorbed “life.” 5. If we never suffered, we would never grow. HOW DO YOU How do you become a truly loving person? Not by being around people who BECOME A TRULY are always lovable. Similarly, you grow in courage only through having to face LOVING PERSON? fear. You grow in patience only through being in frustrating situations. You NOT BY BEING grow in joy by going through tough circumstances. You grow in self-control AROUND PEOPLE through being tempted. You grow in peace when you’ve had your world go WHO ARE ALWAYS crazy. You grow in grace through experiencing brokenness. LOVABLE. 111

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook Many people follow Jesus until they start to experience pain, and then they say, “This path must be the wrong one.” Faithful disciples of Jesus, however, have trained their minds to think past the pain. How will God use this suffering for my good and for his glory? SCRIPTURE What does each verse teach me about what it means to have faith? “Lord, if it’s you,” Peter replied, “tell me to come to you on the water.” “Come,” he said. Then Peter got down out of the boat, walked on the water and came toward Jesus. But when he saw the wind, he was afraid and, beginning to sink, cried out, “Lord, save me!” Immediately Jesus reached out his hand and caught him. “You of little faith,” he said, “why did you doubt?” (Matthew 14:28–31) “For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and all are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus. God pre- sented Christ as a sacrifice of atonement, through the shedding of his blood—to be received by faith.” (Romans 3:23–25a) “Now faith is confidence in what we hope for and assurance about what we do not see. This is what the ancients were commended for. By faith we understand that the universe was formed at God’s command, so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible.” (Hebrews 11:1–3) 112 Am I Committed to This? “What good is it, my brothers and sisters, if some- one claims to have faith but has no deeds? Can such faith save them? Suppose a brother or a sister is without clothes and daily food. If one of you says to them, ‘Go in peace; keep warm and well fed,’ but does nothing about their physical needs, what good is it? In the same way, faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead.” (James 2:14–17) SNAPSHOT . . . FROM NEPAL I was born in the beautiful city of Pokhara, Nepal, and into a high caste of Nepalese society. I was just three months old when my father passed away, so my mother moved our family to the southern part of Nepal, to be near her brother. My family members were Hindus, so I used to worship the Hindus gods and goddess. But I had some questions in my mind. For example, where would we go after death? This question always played a major role in creating fear in my mind. I never found any good answers from Hindu priests. One day a classmate of mine, the son of a British army officer, gave me a Bible to read. When I took it home, my older brother and some villagers started mocking me that I had brought the Bible home. They thought bringing the Bible inside my home was a crime. When my mother found out about this, she gave me two options: leave this so-called cow-eating religion (Christianity) or leave her home. Many times, I have heard a prayer of the Hindus priests that goes like this: “From untruth, lead me to truth. From darkness, lead me to light. From Death, lead me to immortality. Om, peace, peace, peace.” This is a cry for peace, a cry for God, a cry for rest from a restless world. I thought it over and decided to leave my restless home and find peace. I left my home because at that time I didn’t agree with my community’s rule that bringing the Bible inside my home was a social crime. Also, I was interested in finding what exactly was wrong with the Bible. I had won- dered why our people hated the Bible so much. So I started reading the Bible, but I didn’t find any- thing wrong in the Bible. When I read the verses that say, “I am the resurrection and life. He who believes in me will live, even though he dies. And whoever lives and believes in me will never die” (John 11:25–26), I accepted Jesus as my Savior and Lord, and I was baptized by water baptism in a local church. 113

Where will you live? What kind of legacy will you leave behind? These are serious questions. But none of them is life’s central choice. Throughout the Bible, we are confronted with two options that matter more than any other choice we’ll ever make. Here are some of the ways the Bible talks about this choice: Yes or No? “The true light that gives light to everyone was coming into the world. All of us also lived among them at one time, grat- ifying the cravings of our flesh and following its desires and thoughts. Like the rest, we were by nature deserving of wrath. But because of his great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in transgressions—it is by grace you have been saved.” (Ephesians 2:1–5) 119

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook STUDY What does it mean to be made new? Here are some thoughts to help you as you wrestle with this question. Jesus’ Death and Resurrection If a flood swept through your city and you were trapped on your roof, a rescue helicopter could low- er somebody down to where you’re waiting, secure a harness around you, and lift you into the heli- copter. That would be good news, right? But being rescued from our sin and inner brokenness is quite a bit more complicated. Some- times we kind of enjoy the things God wants to rescue us from. There can be habits and attitudes we’d rather God not touch. A lot of days, we would rather God leave us alone and not mess with the way we live. So when Jesus came to rescue us from our sins and inner brokenness, he didn’t just swoop by with a rescue helicopter and lift us away. He took the time to enter history and live among people. John 1:14 says, “The Word [Jesus] became flesh and made his dwelling among us.” In person, he showed people what it looks like to live the life God had in mind when he created humans. Jesus showed us what it looks like to show grace to people who have blown it. To show compassion on people who are going through a rough time. To shine light where there is confusion. To tell hard truth where there is arrogance. He showed us the real life we were missing out on. And he did it all as a human. Jesus, the Son of God, added a human nature to where he did the kinds of things you’d expect from God and the kinds of things you’d expect from humans. He miraculously fed hungry crowds—yet he got hungry. Like God, he showed himself more powerful than the scariest things we face: life-threatening storms, demon-pos- LIKE GOD, HE sessed people, contagious and lethal diseases. Yet like us, he got scared facing his RAISED THE own death, knowing he was going to die for everybody’s sins. Like God, he raised DEAD. LIKE the dead. Like us, he died. US, HE DIED. Thus, Jesus became like us by adding a human nature. But that’s not the only way he became like us. When he died, he took on himself the sins that humans have committed throughout history. That means your sins and my sins became his sins as God poured out his anger toward sin on Jesus while Jesus was on the cross. “God made him who had no sin be sin for us” (2 Corinthians 5:21a). If you’re ever wondering if God truly loves you (or if that’s just an inspiring statement people say to make themselves feel good), remember this: Jesus knows you very well. He knows your sins very intimately because he experienced the penalty for each one of them on the cross. And yet, even 122 Have I Been Made New? though he knows you to your darkest depths, he loves you enough to die for you. Don’t ever forget that you are very well loved. Jesus became like us so we can become like him. Our Death and Resurrection Jesus became like us, taking on our nature and then our sins, so we could become like him. Paul in 2 Corinthians 5:21 continues, “God made him who had no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.” The Son of God took on our sins and became treated as the sinner so we could take on his righteousness and be THE SON OF treated as children of God. GOD TOOK ON So how do we become like him? It goes back to what we talked about in OUR SINS AND the last chapter: we place our faith in him. This means we place our trust in BECAME TREATED him as our Savior and commit our loyalty and allegiance to him as our Lord AS THE SINNER and king. Here are some verses that explain the connection between faith and SO WE COULD salvation as we place our faith in Jesus to rescue us from our sins: TAKE ON HIS RIGHTEOUSNESS • “For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that AND BE TREATED whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16). AS CHILDREN • “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved” (Acts 16:31). OF GOD. • “For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith—and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8). In the New Testament, we see three expressions of faith that describe how people placed their faith in Jesus: • They repented of their old way of living (“repentance”). • They publicly declared that Jesus is their Savior, Lord, and king (“confession”). • They were baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (“baptism”). In baptism, we are buried in the water and brought out of the water. The Greek word for “baptism” is baptizo, which means “to dip, immerse, or plunge under.” It is a way of reenacting the death, burial, and resurrection of Jesus. As Romans 6:4 says, “We were therefore buried with him through baptism into death in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may live a new life.” In this way, we also undergo a death and resurrection—death of the old self and a resurrection to a new life. As we live this new life of faith in Jesus, God makes us more and more like Jesus. 123

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook RESURRECTED DIED JESUS BURIED RAISED TO A NEW LIFE DIED WITH CHRIST OLD LIFE BURIED WITH CHRIST Grace and Faith After describing our lostness without Jesus, Ephesians 2:8–10 says we are saved “by grace through faith.” Grace is what he gives us, and we respond with faith. But what is grace? For starters, the Greek word translated “grace” is charis. (It helps that the two words sound alike, doesn’t it?) Before Christians picked up charis and connected it to the gospel, the word was useful for describing the patron-client relationship (we’ll get to that in a second) as well as for an everyday greeting—which is why it wouldn’t have been strange to receive a letter from Paul starting with, “Grace and peace to you” (1 Corinthians 1:3).17 The patron-client relationship was “the basic building block of Greco-Roman society.”18 If you weren’t one of the few wealthy people, it was important to attach yourself to a wealthy “patron” to survive financially. In return for the material well-being that the patron provided, the “client” served his patron and showed him public honor whenever the opportunity arose. Charis refers to the favorable attitude that the patron showed the client as well as to the gifts and other provisions the patron gave. Charis could also refer to the gratitude the client gave the patron in return. Interestingly, another term for what the client owed the patron was pistis (the Bible word for “faith/faithfulness,” “trust,” or “loyalty/allegiance”). Let that sink in: the client received charis and responded with pistis. Clearly, charis had various meanings even before the New Testament picked up the term. 124 Have I Been Made New? This shouldn’t feel too strange, as it’s not uncommon for many of our English words to take on various meanings too. Whereas the word “bard” basically just means one thing (a singing poet), the word “board” can mean all sorts of interrelated but distinct things: a flat surface (later expanded to mean a table), a group of people in charge (who sit around a table), meals (e.g., room and board, such as you would eat around a table). In this way, charis functions more like “board” than “bard. In the New Testament, charis sometimes means something more concrete (like a gift given or a favor bestowed), and other times it describes more of a general reality (as in God’s favor or grace toward us). Even when charis clearly refers to God’s grace, nailing down a single definition can be difficult. It can be helpful to think of grace in terms IT CAN BE HELPFUL of both 1) favor that God shows, and 2) gifts that he gives. TO THINK OF There may be more, but here are eight ways God’s grace interacts with us: GRACE IN TERMS 1. To Us. Grace is a gift, and gifts are given to people. As Paul wrote, OF BOTH 1) FAVOR “Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” THAT GOD SHOWS, Grace is “given to each of us” (Romans 12:6). Because God gave his grace to AND 2) GIFTS us, we can respond in faith and be saved. (Interestingly, in the Greco-Roman THAT HE GIVES. world, when a gift of charis was given, the beneficiary would give a gift in return—otherwise it was a sign the beneficiary had rejected the gift. Chris- tians respond to God’s gift of grace with the gift in return of faith/allegiance.)19 2. Around Us. When we receive God’s grace through faith, we live in grace. It’s the new home we inhabit. Through Jesus “we have gained access by faith into this grace in which we now stand” (Romans 5:2). We who are saved “live in the grace of Christ” (Galatians 1:6). Now adopted into God’s family, we are surrounded by grace. 3. Above Us. Although we once lived in slavery to sin, we have a new master: grace. As such, “You are not under the law, but under grace” (Romans 6:14). Grace reigns over us: “Just as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign through righteousness to bring eternal life” (Romans 5:21). 4. Under Us. God’s grace is the sure foundation we count on. We place all our dependence on it. We rely “not on worldly wisdom but on God’s grace” (2 Corinthians 1:12). Praise God that his grace always proves sufficient (2 Corinthians 12:9). It won’t crumple under us as we stand fast in it (1 Peter 5:12). 5. Before Us. God’s grace is ever before us. Hebrews pictures God’s throne as a throne of grace that we can always approach in times of struggle. As we approach, we can have complete confidence that we will receive grace there: “Let us then approach God’s throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need” (Hebrews 4:16). 125

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook 6. With/within Us. God’s grace is with his people (Galatians 6:18). His grace strengthens us (Hebrews 3:9). It can fill us (Acts 6:8), and we can grow in it (2 Peter 3:18). God’s grace works with- in us in power to expand God’s kingdom (Acts 4:33). 7. From Us. God’s grace was never meant to flow into us and stay put as if we were stagnant pools with no outlet. God’s grace motivates us to pass grace onto others (Colossians 3:13). Grace calls us to live a holy life (2 Timothy 1:9). Grace mobilizes us for ministry (Romans 1:5; 12:6). As Paul put it, “His grace to me was not without effect” (1 Corinthians 15:10). 8. After Us. In some sense, grace comes after us like a relentless pursuer. Grace was after Paul even as he hated Jesus and persecuted the faith. He describes how grace transformed his identity: “For I am the least of the apostles and do not even deserve to be called an apostle, because I perse- cuted the church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15:9–10). Grace is always on the pursuit: Paul calls it “the grace that is reaching more and more people” (2 Corinthians 4:15). The incredible truth about grace is that as your faith deepens and grows WAVES AND WAVES in Jesus the more amazing God’s grace becomes. We may not be able to OF GRACE FROM define grace perfectly, but we’re grateful that God’s grace defines us. With EVERY DIRECTION. Paul, we can say, “By the grace of God I am what I am.” In addition to defin- AND SOMEHOW ing us, God’s grace also drenches us. As John 1:16 puts it, “Out of [Jesus’] THERE’S EVEN fullness we have all received grace in place of grace already given.” The ESV MORE ON ITS WAY. calls it “grace upon grace.” Waves and waves of grace from every direction. And somehow there’s even more on its way: And God raised us up with Christ and seated us with him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus, in order that in the coming ages he might show the incomparable riches of his grace, expressed in his kindness to us in Christ Jesus. (Ephesians 2:6–7) Our response to this grace? We respond by placing our faith in Jesus, which means believing what Jesus says, trusting in Jesus to save us, and remaining faithful/loyal to him as our Savior, Lord, and king. How do we place our faith in Jesus to be saved? As mentioned above, in the New Testament, we see three expressions of faith that describe how we place our faith in Jesus and are “born again”: • We repent of our old way of living (“repentance”). • We publicly declare that Jesus is our Savior, Lord, and king (“confession”). • We are baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (“baptism”). 126 Have I Been Made New? Being Born Again Is Kind of Like . . . An Adoption. The New Testament refers to being born again as an adoption. As in, it is the moment at which God adopts us as his children into his family. Since we are adopted into his family, we are heirs of all the blessings that come with it: In love he predestined us for adoption to sonship through Jesus Christ, in accordance with his pleasure and will—to the praise of his glorious grace, which he has freely given us in the One he loves. In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, in accordance with the riches of God’s grace that he lavished on us. (Ephesians 1:4–8a) A Wedding. Throughout the Bible, the people of God are pictured as God’s bride, with God as the groom. The book of Revelation specifically pictures the church as the bride, with Jesus as the groom. With this metaphor in mind, it might be helpful to see being born again as like getting married. When we place our faith in Jesus, we declare that we WE ENTER THIS enter this relationship for better or worse, richer or poorer, in sickness or health, RELATIONSHIP until death. In keeping with this metaphor, getting baptized can be compared FOR BETTER OR to the wedding ceremony. WORSE, RICHER A Homecoming. Being born again is a lot like going back home after run- OR POORER, ning away and bringing shame on the family name. Jesus told a parable of a son IN SICKNESS who seriously disrespected his father, asking for his inheritance early and leaving OR HEALTH, home. He got in some major financial trouble because of his poor decisions as UNTIL DEATH. well as a famine-fueled economic downturn. He found himself in poverty, miss- ing his father’s house. He decided to go home, apologize, and ask to be brought on as a hired hand. When the father saw his son coming from a distance, the father ran to meet him, embracing him. The son couldn’t even get out his apology before his dad interrupted him with, “This son of mine was dead and is alive again!” and, “Quick! Bring the best robe!” and, “Let’s have a feast and celebrate!” That’s what being born again is like. 127

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook SCRIPTURE What does each verse teach me about receiving Jesus’ salvation? “When the people heard this, they were cut to the heart and said to Peter and the other apostles, ‘Brothers, what shall we do?’ Peter replied, ‘Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the for- giveness of your sins. And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. The promise is for you and your children and for all who are far off—for all whom the Lord our God will call.’” (Acts 2:37–39) “He then brought them out and asked, ‘Sirs, what must I do to be saved?’ They replied, ‘Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.’ Then they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all the oth- ers in his house. At that hour of the night the jailer took them and washed their wounds; then immediately he and all his household were baptized.” (Acts 16:30–33) “Then Paul left the synagogue and went next door to the house of Titus Justus, a worshiper of God. Crispus, the synagogue leader, and his entire household believed in the Lord; and many of the Corinthians who heard Paul believed and were baptized.” (Acts 18:7–8) “If you declare with your mouth, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For it is with your heart that you believe and are justified, and it is with your mouth that you profess your faith and are saved.” (Romans 10:9–10) 128 Have I Been Made New? SNAPSHOT . . . FROM INDIA After I completed my master’s studies, I was very enthusiastic about doing something meaningful for the Lord. I returned to my homeland in India and started to teach Bible classes in the large liv- ing room of my rented house, as we had no other place at that time. A traveling evangelist used to come to our town, and he visited Christian families, prayed for them, and shared devotional messages. He used to come to our home also. Once during his visit, he shared that a Christian family was hungry for Christian fellowship in a village approximately fifty miles away. He said that it would be good if I could visit them sometime. So one Sunday, I asked a friend to travel with me to that village. We did not have any transport as the mission had just started and there were very limited funds. So we took a train and arrived about 2:30 p.m. after a four-hour trip. We introduced ourselves to the head of the Christian family and shared the purpose of our visit. He, along with his household, was overwhelmed that we had taken pains and traveled to be with them. Immediately, a meeting was arranged, inviting all those who wanted to attend. We were surprised to see that there were more Christians than we anticipat- ed. They were all related, being the descendants of an old man who had become a Christian and settled there a long time ago. We had good fellowship, and I was able to preach a gospel message. By the time everything was over, the ladies had prepared a delicious meal for us, which we thoroughly enjoyed. There was no hurry as the return train was at 7:30 p.m. They requested me to come again sometime and help them as they had no regular Sunday services and no spiritual leader. I returned home full of enthusiasm, and then shared everything with my wife. I slept very sat- isfied and peacefully that night. I returned to the village the following Sunday and enjoyed the fel- lowship and meal. This went on for a few more Sundays. Then one Sunday, after we had arrived at the village and started our meeting in the courtyard of one of the church members, in the middle of my message, a rough-looking man stood up and started accusing me of coming to his village and misleading the people. I asked, “What wrong have I done?” He said, “We don’t need any Christian teaching from you. We are living peacefully here, so don’t come here anymore.” With that, he left. I looked around to the group. No one said anything. Apologetically, the headman explained that the man was a notorious person in the area and had a criminal record. Everyone was afraid of him. I asked, “So what do we do?” He said, “Please don’t stop coming to us. We need you.” At that point I didn’t know what to do. I returned home feeling very disappointed. I hardly slept that night. 129

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook Even though I was very reluctant, I went back to the village the next week. The same thing happened again. In the middle of my message, the man came around, yelling and threatening me. This went on for a few Sundays. Then one Sunday, in the middle of our service, he came in looking annoyed, interrupted me, and said, “I have been warning you, but you don’t listen to me. Next time you come here, I am going to break your head open.” I was stunned, and the group was stunned too. Some of the members came to the railroad station to see us off. My disappointment was at its peak. However, I prayed a lot, gathered my strength, and returned to the village, with a friend who joined me reluctantly because of all that was going on. As we arrived, we saw this man with his friends. They had staffs and iron rods in their hands, and they were running toward us. We knew what was coming, so we turned around and bolted. We ran the five miles back to the railroad sta- tion. Every minute was difficult even when it seemed we had lost them, as we were afraid that they would appear from somewhere. We arrived at the railroad station that we had left a few hours before. We sat there for several hours, hungry, thirsty, and scared to death. Finally, the evening train arrived, and we boarded dead tired. When I arrived home, I was exhausted, worn out, and done with my evangelistic enthusiasm. I shared everything with my wife. She didn’t say much except that she was so sorry. That Wednesday, a few Christians from that group in the village came to our home. They said they had heard what had happened last Sunday and were very sorry. Yet they had come to ask me to please return as they said they needed me. I knew bet- I WAS ter than to listen. I was never going back to that village again. But I told them EXHAUSTED, I would think about it. WORN OUT, AND Saturday came, and my wife asked what I was going to do the next day. DONE WITH MY I said, “Well, we will go to attend our local church. I haven’t been there for EVANGELISTIC several Sundays.” ENTHUSIASM. Then she asked me a very unexpected question: “Are you not going to the village?” I was astounded. “That village?” “Yes. All those people will be expecting you. Some even came here to request you to come.” “I told you what happened the last Sunday, and you want me to go back there?” She said, “Yes. They are praying and trying to talk to the man. And many in our church are praying, and I am praying as well.” “I thought you loved me!” She said, “Yes, I love you, and I don’t want to see you quit as a loser. Please go back to them. The Lord will help you.” 130 Have I Been Made New? So my beloved wife persuaded me to do what I did not want to do at all! Despite my request, this time none of my friends were willing to go to that village with me. Very reluctantly, I traveled to the village alone. We held our service under a tree that day. And what I dreaded . . . happened. The man again came and stood on a small dirt mound watching. I preached about the forgiveness of sins through the blood of Jesus, as I had preached in previ- ous weeks as well. Toward the end of the message, the man raised his voice and said, “I have heard you saying before about God’s love and forgiveness. But you don’t know what kind of a person I am. Do you think God can ever forgive a person like me?” DO YOU THINK I responded, “I don’t have to know all about what you have done and what GOD CAN kind of a person you are. As for your question, I don’t think, but I know God will EVER FORGIVE forgive all your sins if you ask him and trust him.” A PERSON He thought for a moment. “Maybe God can forgive me for he is God. But can LIKE ME? you forgive me for all that I have done to you?” I couldn’t believe my ears. “If you are asking for it, I forgive you right now.” He said, “If you forgive me, would you baptize me now?” I had never imagined that I would hear anything like that from this man. Everyone present was in shock. I came to my senses, and said, “I sure will.” Tears welled up in us all! We walked together to the creek nearby, and the whole group along with several non-believers from the village also followed us. The man asked God for forgiveness, and in that dirty muddy water of the creek, I baptized him in Christ. He emerged that day crystal clean! That was the first baptism in that village. It was also a miracle in the truest sense. — Peter, India SUMMARY 1. We have two choices in life: stay in our sins and follow our own impulses or be forgiven of our sins and follow Jesus. 2. Jesus came to rescue us from our sins and inner brokenness. 3. We place our faith and demonstrate our faith in Jesus by repentance, confession, and baptism. 131

For further study on the topics in this chapter, we encourage you to check out the following resources: Tony Twist, Bobby Harrington, and David Young, Baptism: What the Bible Teaches (Renew.org, 2019), renew.org/ebook/baptism-what-the-bible-teaches/. pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook 3. What does this passage teach about God? 4. What does this passage teach us about the enemy (Satan)? 5. What does this passage teach us about humans? 6. What is one truth I will live out from this passage? 7. What truth from this passage will I share with someone? 134 99 WHAT IS MY SOURCE OF POWER? One of the promises in the New Testament is that when we place our faith in Jesus and are born again, we receive an amazing gift: God’s Spirit comes to live within us. One of the Scriptures we looked at in the last chapter was Acts 2:38, which says, “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins. And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.” So what does the Holy Spirit do inside us? As it turns out, the Holy Spirit does a lot of things, and we’ll look at those throughout this chapter. But one of the main characteristics of the Holy Spir- it is that he has power and can use that power in our lives. This means it is no longer just us using our own abilities to try to live life. We have God’s Spirit working powerfully within and through us. In Acts 1:8, when Jesus prepared his disciples to share the gospel throughout the world, he described the Holy Spirit this way: “You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on you.” One of the biggest ways the Holy Spirit works his power in our lives is by making us holy too. Holiness means that we are set apart from the sinfulness of our previous way of living so we can live the life God calls us to. Thus, it’s worth asking what is your source of power in trying to live a holy life? When it comes to your ability to say no to sin, are you following the Holy Spirit and leaning on his power, or are you relying on something else? Have you ever felt stuck in your sins? Like you can’t get past a particular sin—almost like an unbeatable level in a video game? When it comes to sin, maybe you’re stuck in the habit of getting angry and blowing up at people with whom you should be gentle. Perhaps you’re stuck in the hab- it of jealousy, one that grows and eventually ruins friendships. Maybe you’re stuck in the habit of getting on websites that paralyze your potential to be a faithful spouse in the future. Perhaps you’re stuck in unforgiveness, unable to move past how a person hurt you. In Romans 7–8, the apostle Paul described three levels in our fight against our own sin. These are all stages that take place here on earth; in heaven, we will be completely done with sin. Take a few minutes and ask yourself which stage you are in as you fight against sin. And as you look at 135

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook the options, remember that you are meant to move forward. Disciples of Jesus were never meant to stay stuck. Option 1: I’m not fighting it (Lust). Lust means to strongly desire something that is forbidden. At this level, it’s because you know you’re not supposed to have something that it feels like something you’d like to have. In Romans 7, Paul describes God’s law (think the Ten Commandments) and says that it’s because the law said not to do things that Paul decided he wanted to try them. (Think about the toddler who can’t wait to go ahead and put the fork in the socket because you told him not to.) In the Confessions, Augustine, the theologian and philosopher, confessed the sin of trespassing as a youth with his friends into a neighbor’s yard and stealing the neighbor’s pears. At the time he wrote Confessions, his guilt over this was tremendous. And we think, Augustine, it’s okay. It’s no big deal. You were probably just hungry. From Augustine’s writings, his answer is basically, “No, you don’t understand. I wasn’t hungry.” Oh, well, that’s okay. You must have just really liked pears. “Actually, we didn’t like them at all.” Maybe you were stealing the pears to give them to a needy person? “We flung them to fat hogs.” Well, if you weren’t hungry, and if you didn’t even like pears, then why in the world were you stealing them? “Ah, that’s the point. I didn’t like pears. I liked stealing.” Here are his actual words: “It was foul, and I loved it; I loved to perish, I loved mine own fault, not that for which I was faulty, but my fault itself. Foul soul . . .”20 How did we find ourselves in this stage? Well, we met God the Father, heard all his moral rules, and chose to rebel. We saw his rules as weights dropped on a soul that wants to float free. Who is he to tell me how to live my life? When Paul wrote autobiographically about his past feelings about God’s rules and his own sin, things got surprisingly dark: For when we were in the realm of the flesh, the sinful passions aroused by the law were at work in us, so that we bore fruit for death. (Romans 7:5) What shall we say, then? Is the law sinful? Certainly not! Nevertheless, I would not have known what sin was had it not been for the law. For I would not have known what coveting really was if the law had not said, “You shall not covet.” But sin, seizing the opportunity 136 What Is My Source of Power? afforded by the commandment, produced in me every kind of coveting. For apart from the law, sin was dead. (Romans 7:7–8) Option 2: I’m upset that I keep doing wrong (Disgust). How do we move past the stage of wanting something because we’re not supposed to have it? We move past the stage of lust by meeting someone else. We had met God the Father and felt like rebel- ling, yet after meeting this new Person, rebelling loses its thrill. We meet God the Son. Now when you sin, you’re not happy about it. You become disgusted by it. Why? Because you saw what your sin cost Jesus on the cross. It used to be that you were just rebelling against rules from a strict Father. But now when you sin, you’re hurting a friend. You’re betraying Jesus who went to all that trouble to save you from those sins. Paul described the stage of lust in past tense: “Sin . . . produced in me every kind of coveting” (Romans 7:8). When Paul later described his disgust toward his sin, he switched to present tense: “What I want to do I do not do, but what I hate I do. . . . For I do not do the good I want to do, but the evil I do not want to do—this I keep on doing” (Romans 7:15, 19). In this stage, Paul spoke as a Christian. And as a follower of Christ, what did he feel toward his sin? Disgust. Option 3: I’m allowing the Holy Spirit to make me holy (Trust). We don’t have to stay in the stage of lust. Why? Because we met God the Son and began to hate our sin. So is there a path that leads us out of consistently doing what we hate? Who can lead us out of the stage of sin and then disgust, sin then disgust? Here’s how: we meet someone else. God the Son introduces us to God the Spirit. When a person places faith in him, Jesus sends his Holy Spirit to indwell that person (Acts 2:37–38). Since I have the Holy Spirit, as a Christian, it’s no longer just me versus my sin anymore. And that’s a good thing, because fighting my sin doesn’t go well when it’s just me. Paul used “I” or “me” thirty times in Romans 7 as he described how he kept THE SPIRIT committing sin and feeling disgust over it. INTRODUCES How does the Holy Spirit give us victory over our sins? He does this US TO GOD THE by introducing us to someone else. Remember when you once saw God the FATHER YET AGAIN Father as a strict lawgiver who wanted to stifle your fun? The Spirit intro- AS SOMEONE duces us to God the Father yet again as someone who loves us immensely and WHO LOVES US whom we can trust wholeheartedly. IMMENSELY. 137

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook For those who are led by the Spirit of God are the children of God. The Spirit you received does not make you slaves, so that you live in fear again; rather, the Spirit you received brought about your adoption to sonship. And by him we cry, “Abba, Father.” The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are God’s children. Now if we are children, then we are heirs—heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ, if indeed we share in his sufferings in order that we may also share in his glory. (Romans 8:14–17) The Holy Spirit makes you holy by drawing you to greater trust in your Father. If you trust his good- ness, you can follow his lead. SELF-ASSESSMENT Here are my three main options when it comes to where I am in my fight against sin: 1. Lust: I’m not fighting it. 2. Disgust: I’m upset that I keep doing wrong. 3. Trust: I’m allowing the Holy Spirit to make me holy. When it comes to my fight against sin, here’s how I would describe where I am: When it comes to my fight against sin, here’s where I want to be and why I want to be there: In our fight against sin, we are made holy through the Holy Spirit. The rest of this chapter will explore who the Holy Spirit is and what he does in our lives. 138 What Is My Source of Power? Definition: Holy Spirit Definition: Prayer The third member of the Godhead. Sent out by the Talking with God. Among the many prayers re- Father and Son, he moves us toward Jesus through corded in Scripture, the book of Psalms records the Word, through power, and through deep con- 150 songs that are prayers to God from various viction, and he lives within us by immersing us in life situations (fear, joy, repentance, etc.). God and transforming us into the image of Jesus. Definition: Sanctification Definition: Fasting The process by which God brings disciples of The voluntary abstinence from food (or other things) Jesus to maturity through the work of the Holy for a season for the purpose of drawing closer to Spirit, thereby decreasing sin’s power over their God. The Bible describes various types of fasts based lives and restoring God’s glory in their lives. on length and types of food being abstained from. STUDY What should your source of power be? Here are some thoughts to help you as you wrestle with this question. How Does the Holy Spirit Draw Us Toward Jesus? One of the major things the Holy Spirit does is to draw us toward Jesus. We can resist him (Acts 7:51). But if we follow his lead, we will be drawn into relationship with Jesus. How does the Holy Spirit draw us toward Jesus? According to David IF WE FOLLOW HIS Young’s book Holy Spirit: Filled, Empowered, and Led, the Holy Spirit moves LEAD, WE WILL us to Jesus in three ways. Young takes his cue from 1 Thessalonians 1:4–5, BE DRAWN INTO which describes three ways the gospel comes to people: through words, pow- RELATIONSHIP er, and deep conviction. These are the three ways the Holy Spirit draws us WITH JESUS. to Jesus: • Word: “For prophecy never had its origin in the human will, but prophets, though human, spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21). • Power: “My message and my preaching were not with wise and persuasive words, but with a demonstration of the Spirit’s power, so that your faith might not rest on human wisdom, but on God’s power” (1 Corinthians 2:4–5). • Deep Conviction: “When [the Holy Spirit] comes, he will prove the world to be in the wrong about sin and righteousness and judgment: about sin, because people do not believe in me; 139

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook about righteousness, because I am going to the Father, where you can see me no longer; and about judgment, because the prince of this world now stands condemned” (John 16:8–11). How Does the Holy Spirit Make Us Like Jesus? The Holy Spirit draws us to Jesus and then makes us like Jesus. How does he do this? Young also describes four ways the Holy Spirit makes us more like Jesus: 1. Unites us with other believers: “Be completely humble and gentle; be patient, bearing with one another in love. Make every effort to keep the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace. There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called to one hope when you were called” (Ephesians 4:2–4). 2. Intercedes with the Father on our behalf: “The Spirit helps us in our weakness. We do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us through wordless groans. And he who searches our hearts knows the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for God’s people in accordance with the will of God” (Romans 8:26–27). 3. Produces the goodness of Jesus in our lives: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, for- bearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law. Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. Since we live by the Spirit, let us keep in step with the Spirit” (Galatians 5:22–25). 4. Equips us for the mission of Jesus: “There are different kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit dis- tributes them. There are different kinds of service, but the same Lord. There are different kinds of working, but in all of them and in everyone it is the same God at work. Now to each one the man- ifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good” (1 Corinthians 12:4–7). How Do We Seek the Holy Spirit’s Leadership? It’s a great idea to build “rhythms” into your schedule so you regularly connect with God and seek the Holy Spirit’s leadership in your life. Here are four core rhythms that are good to make into regular habits: 1. Prayer: Connecting with God by talking and listening to him. 2. Fasting: Going without something you usually consume so you can spend the time seeking God. For example, you might set aside a meal or two each week to go without food. 3. Bible reading: Regularly feeding yourself on the writings that the Holy Spirit inspired. 4. Serving: Using the abilities and opportunities the Holy Spirit has given you to serve your church and community. 140 What Is My Source of Power? How Do We Pray? It’s a great question. Jesus’ disciples recognized that even though they had learned a lot from Jesus, they were still beginners when it came to prayer. They asked him, “Lord, teach us to pray” (Luke 11:1). The result was a prayer that Jesus gave them: the “Lord’s Prayer,” given in Luke 11:2–4 and Matthew 6:9–13. The Lord’s Prayer shows us what disciples of Jesus pray about: Worship. “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name” (Matthew 6:9). When we call God “our Father,” we relate to him as a child relates to a loving father. We acknowledge that he pro- vides for us and protects us. We learn to live from his guidance. By “hallowed be your name,” we say, “Your name must be set apart as holy.” Thus, we ask for him to be famous, for his name to be glorified. God’s Kingdom. “Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10). Praying for God’s kingdom to come is to pray that his will be done here as it’s done in heaven. As we will explore in an upcoming chapter, the kingdom of God is the realm where God’s will is being done on earth as it is in heaven through the reign of King Jesus. We were able to see the beauty of God’s kingdom in action through the ministry of Jesus. His king- dom is already here, but it isn’t yet here in its fullness (as it will be when HIS KINGDOM IS Jesus returns). ALREADY HERE, Physical Help. “Give us today our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11). As we pray BUT IT ISN’T for our “daily bread,” we ask God to meet our day-to-day needs. If your needs YET HERE IN are already being met, you can still pray this, because the prayer says, “Our daily ITS FULLNESS. bread.” There are plenty of people around the world who are wondering where their next meal is coming from, and this can be a prayer for them as well. Confession. “And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors” (Matthew 6:12). When we ask God to forgive us as we forgive others, we both 1) confess our sins and ask for for- giveness for them, and 2) commit to forgiving others for their sins against us. Jesus followed up the Lord’s Prayer by saying, “For if you forgive other people when they sin against you, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you do not forgive others their sins, your Father will not forgive your sins” (Matthew 6:14–15). Spiritual Help. “And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one” (Matthew 6:13). As we pray this, we ask for help against spiritual temptation and our spiritual enemies. We acknowl- edge that we need God’s help and that we desire to be holy as he is holy (1 Peter 1:15). It is reassur- ing to know that God helps us when we need it. As mentioned earlier, “the Spirit helps us in our 141

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook weakness,” so that even when we don’t know the words to pray, he “intercedes for us through word- less groans” (Romans 8:26). SCRIPTURE What does each verse teach me about the Holy Spirit? “And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another advocate to help you and be with you for- ever—the Spirit of truth. The world cannot accept him, because it neither sees him nor knows him. But you know him, for he lives with you and will be in you.” (Jesus in John 14:16–17) “But you will receive power when the Holy Spir- it comes on you; and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.” (Jesus in Acts 1:8) Peter replied, “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgive- ness of your sins. And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. The promise is for you and your children and for all who are far off—for all whom the Lord our God will call.” (Acts 2:38–39) “And this is his command: to believe in the name of his Son, Jesus Christ, and to love one another as he commanded us. The one who keeps God’s commands lives in him, and he in them. And this is how we know that he lives in us: We know it by the Spirit he gave us.” (1 John 3:23–24) SNAPSHOT . . . FROM THE UNITED STATES With heavy hearts, we want to fill you all in on some news that we received about our son. A few weeks ago, we went in for a routine ultrasound, and they could not get clear enough pictures of the 142 What Is My Source of Power? baby’s heart, so we were referred to a high-risk specialist at the hospital. We had that appointment, and our world was turned upside down. We were told that our unborn son has hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS). If you’re a medical professional, you are probably familiar with this, but for those who aren’t, the summary is that one side of his heart isn’t developing properly. As a result, he will need a series of three open-heart surgeries as a young child. The first will likely come within the first week after birth, the second four to six months after birth, and the third eighteen to forty-eight months after birth. Unfortunately, all these surgeries are more to address the symptoms than the root cause, mean- ing there is a good chance he will also need to have a heart transplant at some point in his life. That then obviously presents its own set of challenges. As you can imagine, all throughout his early life he will need expert medical care. On the one hand, we mourn for our son as this was not the life that we have hoped and prayed for him to have, but we also mourn because if this diagnosis stays the natural course, the work that we felt sure God was calling us to in El Salvador no longer seems an option for us due to the level of care that will be required for our son. Since we I CAN’T HELP BUT received this news just days before we were to announce to the church our ASK, “WHY, GOD?” plans to move to El Salvador, I can’t help but ask, “Why, God?” I’m trying I’M TRYING NOT TO not to be so foolish as to think that I can understand the omniscient ways of BE SO FOOLISH AS God, but I am perplexed as to why he would lead us so far down this path TO THINK THAT I only for it all to fall apart now when we saw so clearly his plans for us in CAN UNDERSTAND El Salvador. THE OMNISCIENT I continue to pray to God for a miracle or that the doctors might possibly WAYS OF GOD. have gotten it wrong, both for my son’s future but also for all the lives that we had hoped might be forever changed in El Salvador. I know God has the strength to heal our son, but I also know this may not be what God has planned for our son. All I can do is petition the Lord for a miracle just as David did for his son whom Nathan said would die. Like David, I hold on to hope that God works in miraculous ways. However, I also pray that in whatever way God chooses to move that the Holy Spirit would pre- pare our hearts to accept that our Father is the giver of all good things, whose ways are far above our comprehension. — Dylan, US 143

One of the confusing parts of life is that there are so many good things to do with your life. Obvi- ously, you’re supposed to choose to do good (helping your grandma cross the street) over bad (pushing your grandma into the street). But what about when it comes to choosing one good choice over another good choice? That’s tricky. What is the mission we should dedicate our lives to? There are lots of good choices, but you can only pick one core mission to dedicate your life to. Here are some options. Take a couple of minutes and ask yourself which should be your main mission in life. Option 1: Make good grades and a lot of money. Doing well in school is great. Getting into a good job is too. When you have kids, you’ll want them to be successful in their studies and in their career. And having plenty of money means you’ll avoid poverty. You’ll also be able to buy some cool experiences, such as hobbies and vacations. Although it comes with its temptations and distractions, having money can mean an easier life, especially if it means having better access to healthy food and medical treatment. Because of all these benefits, some people make it their main goal in life to do well and make lots of money—especially since they’re going to spend most of their days working and earning a paycheck anyway. Option 2: Make a name for myself. Some people are driven to succeed so they can be famous. From social media “influencers” to his- tory’s inventors and conquerors, many people have chased after—and achieved—fame. To them, if this life is their one shot, they’re going to try to make a mark and become a recognized name. Option 3: Make a lot of great memories. God has made an amazing world full of breathtaking sights, inexhaustible learning opportunities, and fascinating people. Lots of fun times and meaningful moments are out there for us to enjoy. Because of this, some people make it their goal to live life to the fullest and make lots of memories. Even if you think the main purpose of life is something else, God’s world still offers some cool pos- sibilities for making great memories. 147

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook Option 4: Make the world a better place. For people who have a big heart, this can be a common main goal. To help poor people get out of their poverty. To help oppressed people find their voice. To make the environment a healthier, more sustainable place. These are great goals, but for them to be our main mission in life, we must assume this life is the only one that matters. Whoever you are, one of your goals in life should be to make the world a better place. But if this life is only the beginning (and there’s such a thing as eternal life), you must have a higher main goal for your life. After all, if you really want to make this world a better place, you must reckon with the sin at the root of our human problems, and that is one of your reminders of how much you need Jesus. Option 5: Be a disciple of Jesus who makes disciples. Jesus gives us the invitation to follow him, as his disciple, because following him is how we are restored to what God created us to be. Why did God create us? He created humans to bear his image, rule over his creation, and spread his glory. Sin marred God’s image in us. But Jesus came, bearing God’s image perfectly, and when we follow him in faith as his disciple, we relearn how humans are supposed to live. We resume our original mission. Being a disciple of Jesus means learning to love. From Jesus, we learn to love God and love people (the “Great Commandment”). We learn to do the BEING JESUS’ things Jesus did: serving the needy and sticking up for the lonely. We speak DISCIPLE MEANS truth in love. And we also learn to make more disciples like Jesus did. Jesus’ LEARNING TO LOVE. final words in the Gospel of Matthew were a command to his followers to make more disciples of all nations: All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Therefore, go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, to the very end of the age. (Matthew 28:18–20) This command is so important for Christians that we call it the Great Commission. Making dis- ciples of Jesus won’t be a matter of making a lot of money or making a name for ourselves, although it will make the world a better place and create a lot of great memories. But if Jesus is who he says he is (the saving and risen king), then being his disciple and making disciples are worth it. Notice that this is the path of multiplication (not just addition), because you make disciples who make dis- ciples who make disciples, and so on until Jesus returns. 148 What’s My Mission in Life? SELF-ASSESSMENT Here are my five main options when it comes to my main mission in life: 1. Make good grades and a lot of money. 2. Make a name for myself. 3. Make a lot of great memories. 4. pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook STUDY What should your mission in life be? Here are some thoughts to help you as you wrestle with this question. What Does It Mean to Be a Disciple of Jesus? All four Gospels and the book of Acts focus heavily on Jesus’ words of instruction, as he encouraged the early disciples to make it their mission to become more committed disciples themselves, and to concentrate on making disciples among others. To share the good news to those around us, we must be committed disciples ourselves. The Lord also desires that we become passionate about discipling others. To grow in our own walk with Jesus, we need to live for his mission, daily committed to sharing the good news of Jesus with others (evangelism) and helping them follow Jesus too (disciple making). DISCIPLES OF JESUS LIVE DAILY Being a Disciple FOR THE PURSUIT This is not just about attending church once a week or on Christmas and Eas- OF FOLLOWING ter, putting some surplus cash in the church offering every once in a while, HIM AS WELL or volunteering once a year at a youth event at church. Disciples of Jesus live AS MAKING daily for the pursuit of following him as well as making disciples of him. DISCIPLES OF HIM. They are totally committed. We need to follow the apostle Paul’s aspiration: I consider everything a loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord, for whose sake I have lost all things. I consider them garbage, that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ—the righteousness that comes from God on the basis of faith. I want to know Christ—yes, to know the power of his resurrection and participation in his sufferings, becoming like him in his death, and so, somehow, attaining to the resurrection from the dead. (Philippians 3:8–11) The Great Commandment Being Jesus’ disciple means caring about what he cares about. It means forming our lives around what he says is most important. And when asked the most important commandment from God we could follow throughout our lives, Jesus gave two: 150 What’s My Mission in Life? “The most important one,” answered Jesus, “is this: ‘Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.’ The second is this: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no commandment greater than these.” (Mark 12:29–31) As we relearn from Jesus what it looks like to be God’s image bearers, we find ourselves growing in love toward both God and people. It makes sense, since we love God and people, that we seek to connect the people we have grown to love with the God we have grown to love. That’s how Jesus’ Great Commandment leads us to follow Jesus’ Great Commission. The Great Commission If we want to grow in our maturity as a disciple, we are not only to trust and follow Jesus ourselves but also to follow him by daily joining his mission. One of the amazing aspects of being a disciple of Jesus is that our awesome, all-powerful God has made each of us his partner in the greatest vocation of all time: building his church by winning the world. Yes, that is the way he has set up his most critical mission of saving people from eternal destruction. It’s a partnership between Jesus and me, Jesus and you, working in a tight team to bring salvation to a lost world. What a privilege. God has chosen to rely on us as believers, empowered by his Holy Spirit. He could have cho- sen a myriad of ways to bring sinners to repentance; after all he is almighty God, capable of any- thing that goes according to his nature. However, his plan included us as his primary means of the unsaved hearing about and responding to the message of God’s love and forgiveness. Making disci- ples is what Jesus has left for us to do. Who, Me? Jesus has given the opportunity to every man and woman, young and old, regardless of position, social status, rich or poor, to join him on this great mission. God will get his mission done, but through his amazing grace he has given us the opportunity to be used by him for his glory. Is there any greater purpose that should bring us more joy? God specializes in using the ordinary to do amazing things, so don’t think for one minute you are not qualified or that this is for someone else. Jesus will use anyone who is open and willing. He can overcome IS THERE ANY our shortcomings, but he can’t overcome our unavailability. Jesus sees potential GREATER in you and wants to use you. PURPOSE THAT You need to ask yourself if you are open to being used by Jesus in his mission. SHOULD BRING The Great Commission reminds us that as we go to make disciples, we go in US MORE JOY? Jesus’ authority, in his name, and for his glory. When we become a committed disciple, our priorities change, and our calling changes. Jesus was clear that the 151

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook subject of his mission was people. Jesus commanded and commissioned his disciples to spread the good news of the love and grace of God to everyone: every tribe, every tongue, every nation. A Lot Bigger Than I The “going” (“Go and make disciples”) is about the commitment. It is being utterly available to God’s direction. To fully grasp the task, known as the Great Commission, we must first under- stand God’s mission. The mission exists because God exists. We must understand that our mission is rooted in God’s mission. It is easy to miss the grandeur of God’s mission: humans glorify God by knowing him, worshiping him, and making him known throughout the world. We are to be disci- ples who make disciples until Jesus returns or calls us home. If you love Jesus, you are to be his disciple and his disciple maker. Jesus has been calling his disci- ples for centuries to mission. It is our time as disciples to follow him, to do what disciples of Jesus do: make disciples who make disciples. It is a mission that never stops. It’s not a once-only occurrence. A Holistic Mission When we disciple others, it helps them grow spiritually, physically, socially, and intellectually in an integrated approach. In Luke 4, when Jesus launched his ministry, he introduced himself as the ser- vant of the Father, sent into the world with a mission. He claimed the authorization to bring into reality God’s longstanding plan for his people. In Luke 4, we see that Jesus came to meet the needs of all people: to proclaim good news to the poor, to proclaim freedom for the prisoners, recovery of sight for the blind, to set the oppressed free, and to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor. His min- istry went on to meet people’s spiritual, intellectual, physical, and social needs. In giving us his Great Commission, Jesus was declaring that his work is now our work. In Acts 1:8, we read, “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on you; and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.” IN GIVING US Do you notice a word repeated in this verse? Three times the word “you” HIS GREAT appears. A lot of centuries have passed since Jesus said this, but even today, he COMMISSION, means you. It is personal. God’s mission is directed to you. JESUS WAS Thus, he gives every disciple the power of the Holy Spirit. The Spirit is per- DECLARING THAT sonal and active in the life of every disciple, and he gives us the power, ability, HIS WORK IS strength, giftings, and words to be witnesses for Jesus. Jesus said we are to be NOW OUR WORK. his witnesses (to make disciples) in Jerusalem (our local community in which we live), Judea (our region), Samaria (nearby regions and nations), and to the ends of the earth (globally). This is the greatest mission on the planet. 152 What’s My Mission in Life? SCRIPTURE What does each verse teach me about being a disciple of Jesus? “As Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon called Peter and his brother Andrew. They were casting a net into the lake, for they were fishermen. ‘Come, follow me,’ Jesus said, ‘and I will send you out to fish for peo- ple.’ At once they left their nets and followed him.” (Matthew 4:18–20) “Therefore everyone who hears these words of mine and puts them into practice is like a wise man who built his house on the rock.” (Jesus in Matthew 7:24) “When he saw the crowds, he had compassion on them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. Then he said to his disciples, ‘The harvest is plentiful but the work- ers are few. Ask the Lord of the harvest, there- fore, to send out workers into his harvest field.’” (Matthew 9:36–38) Then [Jesus] said to them all: “Whoever wants to be my disciple must deny themselves and take up their cross daily and follow me. For whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for me will save it.” (Luke 9:23–24) SNAPSHOT . . . FROM SOUTHEAST ASIA Being a believer in my village is not easy. I remember my very first experience of church. I was only four years old, and all the believers in the village came to have fellowship and worship together at my house. The gathering resulted in persecution as Hindus and Buddhists came from all over the 153

They did not want us meeting together to praise and worship Jesus and they forced all the believers to leave the village. Growing up, I planned to become an army officer. That is all that I ever wanted to do. Sadly, that was not God’s plan for my life. My dream of becoming a soldier was not fulfilled because I had an illness. No matter how much medicine I took, my stomach problem did not get better. I thought my story was over. I thought God’s plan for my life was not to get better. I did not know what to do as I was just not getting better. One day I repented and prayed to the Lord that if I was healed, I would serve him. The Lord heard my prayer, and I was healed. My story was not over! I went to discipleship school and after receiving Bible training, a few months later, I went back to the place where I was born and raised. I planted a church, and now I share Jesus with my village. — Bhagyaman, Southeast Asia SUMMARY 1. God is on mission to redeem and restore people, and he wants to use us in his mission. 2.
