pages.content: Page intentionally left blank 1111 WHAT KINGDOM HAS MY ALLEGIANCE? It’s odd that the Bible’s amazing news is of yet another kingdom (Mark 1:14). The track record of kingdoms is awful. Biblical history tells the story of kingdom after kingdom that all turn out to be disasters. One way to outline biblical history is to tell the story of seven kingdoms, and most of the story is bloody and tragic. Yet, thankfully, the end of the story makes up for the dark chapters. The final kingdom is the good news the rest of the story made us long for. In order of appearance, here are the seven main kingdoms narrated in biblical history. As you think through what kingdom will have your ultimate allegiance or loyalty, these are the types of kingdoms you’ll be able to choose from. Take a few minutes and consider the options of what kind of kingdom you want to participate in. HERE ARE THE Option 1: Kingdom of Egypt SEVEN MAIN The first major kingdom we meet in biblical history is Egypt. True, at times in KINGDOMS ancient history, Egypt was friendly to God’s chosen people, the Jews. Yet for cen- NARRATED turies in early Jewish history, the relationship was one of cruelty. The Jewish peo- IN BIBLICAL ple had migrated to Egypt to survive a famine, but when they stayed and grew HISTORY. in number, the Egyptian king feared their potential and made them slaves. To further neutralize the threat, the king instituted gender-based infanticide, where it became official policy to dump baby boys in the Nile River. What image comes to mind when we think about the kingdom of Egypt? Babies in the river. Option 2: Kingdom of Israel After centuries of slavery, God miraculously delivered the Jewish people out of Egypt. Now no lon- ger slaves, they were led through the wilderness to the land God had promised their forefathers. This promised land, once called Canaan, was a sliver of land at the intersection of three continents: 159

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook Africa, Asia, and Europe. When the Jews entered the land, Jewish leaders called “judges” led them at first, followed soon after by Jewish kings. With the Jews being God’s chosen people, one could assume this kingdom would be the ideal. Yet most of the Jewish kingdom saw one disaster after another. Because of infighting, the kingdom split in two after just three kings. In both the Northern Kingdom and South- ern Kingdom, kings often led the people into following other gods. God sent MOST OF THE his prophets to both now-separate nations, yet most of the time, the kings per- TIME, THE KINGS secuted these prophets and did not listen. Here’s the unfortunate image that PERSECUTED comes to mind when we think about the ancient kingdom of Israel: prophets in THESE the dungeon. PROPHETS AND DID NOT LISTEN. Option 3: Kingdom of Babylon Both sections of Israel’s divided kingdom collectively rejected the God of their forefathers and followed other gods. As a result, both were conquered by other kingdoms. First, the kingdom of Assyria took over the Northern Kingdom. Then, the kingdom of Babylon took over the Southern Kingdom, destroying their temple and burning Jerusalem to the ground. Thanks to prophets like Jeremiah, Daniel, and Ezekiel, the Bible gives us a close-up view of the kingdom of Babylon, including events that took place there. The prophet Daniel also narrates visions from God that give us heaven’s view of the kingdom of Babylon. According to one vision, Babylon is the “head of gold” on a grand statue. According to another vision, Babylon is a proud lion with the wings of an eagle. As with most kingdoms, Babylon was obsessed with its own glory, and on one occasion Baby- lon punished three Jews for not bowing before a massive statue by throwing the three into a fiery furnace. Although God protected them and they survived, the image that comes to mind when remembering the kingdom of Babylon is this: God followers in the furnace. Option 4: Kingdom of Persia Within a century of conquering a crescent from the Red Sea to the Persian Gulf, the kingdom of Babylon was overtaken by the kingdom of the Medes and Persians. This kingdom was friendlier to the Jewish people than the Babylonians had been. For example, it allowed the Jews to return home and rebuild the homeland that Babylon had destroyed. According to one vision in the book of Dan- iel, the vision of the grand statue, this kingdom was the statue’s chest and arms of silver. Yet another vision pictured it as a flesh-eating bear. The most memorable story of the Jews under Persian rule unfolded when a Persian law made it illegal to pray to anyone other than the king for thirty days. When the prophet Daniel didn’t stop praying to God throughout the thirty days, his fellow administrators ratted on him, and he was sentenced to be thrown into a den of lions to be 160 What Kingdom Has My Allegiance? torn apart and eaten alive. Although God protected Daniel from death, the image that most comes to mind when we remember this kingdom is this: God follower in the lions’ den. Option 5: Kingdom of Greece Amid an ongoing rivalry, the kingdom of Greece eventually beat the kingdom of Persia, and the Macedonian Alexander the Great went on to expand Greek civilization from Egypt to India. Dan- iel’s vision of the grand statue depicts this kingdom as a belly and thighs made of bronze. Another vision depicts this kingdom as a leopard with four heads and four wings. After Alexan- der died, his kingdom was divided among his four generals. Two of these generals are worth men- tioning because they factor into the history of the Jewish people: Ptolemy over Egypt and Seleucus over West Asia. The Jewish people in Israel were caught between these two divisions of the Greek Empire until eventually the Seleucids gained the upper hand and proved to be tyrants. One Seleucid king, Antiochus IV Epiphanes (the “God Manifest”), persecuted the Jews and forced Hellenization (Greek culture) on them so heavily that the Jews rebelled in what is known as the Maccabean Revolt. This war for independence was successful, and Jews celebrate it today with the holiday called Hannukah. Yet the horrors of the Seleucid reign were forever branded in Jewish memory, most notably in an act of unthinkable sacrilege: Antiochus IV Epiphanes entered the Jewish temple and sacrificed a pig to Zeus on the altar. For the ancient Jewish people, this kingdom is most encapsulated in this image: pig on the altar. Option 6: Kingdom of Rome After a century or so of independence due to the Maccabean Revolt, it was becoming clear that even an independent nation ruled by descendants of the original revolutionaries (the Maccabees) wasn’t a guarantee of peace or civility. Bitter infighting between two Maccabee brothers led both brothers to ask Rome to intervene. The emerging empire of Rome was glad to oblige, and soon the Jewish people were under the kingdom of Rome. Daniel’s visions picture Rome as the most vicious kingdom of all: it has THIS KINGDOM legs of iron built for crushing opponents. It is a terrifying, powerful beast with ADVANCES BY iron teeth and ten horns. This kingdom advances by crushing, trampling, and CRUSHING, devouring anything in its path. TRAMPLING, The kingdom of Rome commonly made use of a form of execution that AND DEVOURING combined torture and humiliation: crucifixion. Although many atrocities are ANYTHING IN associated with this kingdom, for students of biblical history, the image that ITS PATH. most comes to mind for Rome is this: Messiah on the cross. 161

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook Option 7: Kingdom of God The kingdom of Rome devastated the Jews even more brutally than Babylon had centuries before. In the early AD centuries, two significant Jewish rebellions took place against Rome. After the first (AD 66–70), Rome destroyed Jerusalem, including its temple, and after the second (AD 132–136), Rome scattered the Jews out of their homeland, removed all Jewish influence, and reestablished the country in a pagan mold. Rome also tried to crush a new movement that began out of Judaism, a movement that start- ed with a carpenter-turned-teacher named Jesus of Nazareth. When comparing the meek group of Jesus’ disciples to Rome’s legions, the odds were obviously in Rome’s favor. Yet they weren’t—and it shouldn’t surprise the student of biblical history. Prophets had long foretold of a new kingdom on its way that would outlast and overpower even Rome. After describing the vision of the grand statue, Daniel offers a twist: While you were watching, a rock was cut out, but not by human hands. It struck the statue on its feet of iron and clay and smashed them. Then the iron, the clay, the bronze, the silver and the gold were all broken to pieces and became like chaff on a threshing floor in the summer. The wind swept them away without leaving a trace. But the rock that struck the statue became a huge mountain and filled the whole earth. (Daniel 2:34–35) Daniel’s vision that depicts the four kingdoms as four beasts ends similarly: In my vision at night I looked, and there before me was one like a son of man, coming with the clouds of heaven. He approached the Ancient of Days and was led into his presence. He was given authority, glory and sovereign power; all nations and peoples of every language worshiped him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that will not pass away, and his kingdom is one that will never be destroyed. (Daniel 7:13–14) This was the kingdom that Jesus excitedly announced in his first recorded words in the Gospel of Mark: “The time has come. The kingdom of God has “HIS DOMINION IS come near. Repent and believe the good news!” (Mark 1:15). It might seem AN EVERLASTING like we should be tired by now of kingdoms. But then we learn what this new DOMINION kingdom is like. A kingdom ruled by love and holiness? A realm where rejects THAT WILL NOT find a home of grace and compassion? A king who sacrifices his life to save PASS AWAY.” former enemies? Sign me up. By now, we are exhausted and disillusioned by kingdoms that promise peace yet bring horrors like these: 162 What Kingdom Has My Allegiance? • Babies in the river • Prophets in the dungeon • God followers in the furnace • God follower in the lions’ den • Pig on the altar • Messiah on the cross What makes the kingdom of God the kingdom we’ve longed for is that although countless kings have come before and demanded our wor- ALTHOUGH ship, we’ve finally found a king worthy of it. The vision we get of his king- COUNTLESS KINGS dom, in contrast to the selfish, treasure-gobbling self-glorifying of former HAVE COME BEFORE kingdoms, is bizarre and beautiful: “A Lamb, looking as if it had been AND DEMANDED OUR slain, standing at the center of the throne. . . . And they sang a new song, WORSHIP, WE’VE saying, ‘You are worthy’” (Revelation 5:6, 9). FINALLY FOUND A The one we can trust is on the throne. The one who loves us also KING WORTHY OF IT. reigns over us. Jesus is king. What a relief! For the image that best fits the kingdom of God is this: Lamb on the throne. SELF-ASSESSMENT You’re not likely rooting for the ancient kingdoms of Babylon, Persia, or Rome. But even in the twenty-first century, numerous kingdoms compete for our allegiance. Political parties and popu- lar ideologies want your complete buy-in. When they say “jump,” they want you to robotically ask, “How high?” They want to wow you with their ultimate vision of how the world should be. Yet Jesus invites you to a kingdom in which he is king. In his kingdom, he writes the rules. He calls the shots. So are you: 1. Placing your highest hopes and ultimate allegiance in building your own personal kingdom (of success, popularity, etc.)? 2. Placing your highest hopes and ultimate allegiance in a political party or popular ideology of this world? 3. Placing your highest hopes and ultimate allegiance in the kingdom of King Jesus? 163

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook When it comes to what “kingdom” has my ultimate allegiance, here’s how I would describe where I am: When it comes to what “kingdom” has my ultimate allegiance, here’s where I want to be and why I want to be there: Definition: Kingdom of God Definition: Love The realm where God’s will is being done on A cross-shaped action that glorifies God earth as it is in heaven through the reign of King and benefits someone else. It is the ac- Jesus. Sometimes it is called the “kingdom of tion that best models King Jesus. heaven.” Even though most kingdoms move for- ward through tyranny and tribalism, God’s king- dom moves forward through love and holiness. Definition: Holiness Definition: Church A lifestyle of separation or “set-apart-ness” An assembly or gathering of kingdom-people who from the ways of the world so you can be display the reign of God through King Jesus. dedicated to God and his kingdom. STUDY What kingdom should have your allegiance? Here are some thoughts to help you as you wrestle with this question. The Church Displays the Kingdom of God . . . Really? The kingdom of God is the realm where God’s will is being done on earth as it is in heaven through the reign of King Jesus. And where do we see the kingdom of God at work most clearly? The church. The church is an assembly or gathering of kingdom-people who display the reign of God through King Jesus. Right? 164 What Kingdom Has My Allegiance? Sometimes, we read about the kingdom of God in the Gospels—a kingdom of forgiving, peace- making, righteousness-pursuing people who are light in the darkness (see Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount)—and we think back to times we have seen the church filled with this sort of self-sacrificial, God-honoring activity. Yet sometimes we read about the THE CHURCH IS kingdom of God—and we realize the church we attend falls way short. A GATHERING OF What does it look like to display God’s kingdom reign? The best place to KINGDOM-PEOPLE discover what God’s kingdom reign looks like is Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount WHO DISPLAY (Matthew 5–7). Sadly, a serious look at Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount can THE REIGN OF make it painfully clear just how far short of kingdom living churches can fall. GOD THROUGH Here’s a quick tour of the sermon: KING JESUS. • Disciples of Jesus are humble, meek, merciful, and hungry for righteousness and justice (Matthew 5:3–10). • Disciples of Jesus are the light of the world and salt of the earth, bringing light into darkness all the while preserving their distinctiveness as followers of Jesus (Matthew 5:13–16). • Disciples of Jesus avoid hatred, anger, lust, divorce, and dishonesty; they reconcile quickly with people and love their enemies (Matthew 5:17–48). • Disciples of Jesus give to the needy, pray, and fast in order to connect with God and bring him glory—not to be admired by people (Matthew 6:1–18). • Disciples of Jesus seek God’s kingdom and his righteousness, storing up treasures in heaven and rejecting worry and greed (Matthew 6:19–34). • Disciples of Jesus reject judgmentalism and do for others what they want done for themselves (Matthew 7:1–12). • Disciples of Jesus refuse to listen to false teachers, put Jesus’ words into practice and do God’s will, and are content following the less-traveled road that leads to life (Matthew 7:13–27). Sometimes, you’ll look at your church and recognize these sorts of values and behaviors in action. Other times, the church won’t look like this, and you will feel discouraged. How should we view the church when we are discouraged about how it falls short of displaying the reign of God’s kingdom? First, we view the WE VIEW THE church through the lens of what Jesus said about it. Second, we view the CHURCH THROUGH church through the lens of what Jesus did for it. THE LENS OF What did Jesus say about church people? In Matthew 13, Jesus told WHAT JESUS some parables that help explain why churches sometimes fall short of dis- SAID ABOUT IT. playing God’s kingdom reign. Here is a summary of these parables and what they teach us about church people: 165

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook • The Parable of the Soils. Jesus told a parable in which a sower scattered seeds on different types of soil: the path, rocky soil, thorny soil, and good soil. According to this parable, not everybody who hears God’s Word (and by extension, not everybody who comes to church) has a heart that receives the Word and acts on it. Merely hearing the Word doesn’t cut it (Matthew 13:3–23). • The Parables of the Fish and the Wheat. Jesus told a couple of parables that show not everybody who looks like a disciple of Jesus is one. In the fish parable, a fisherman catches all kinds of fish in a net, but has to sort the good from the bad. In the wheat parable, an enemy sows weeds in a field of wheat, and the farmer waits until the harvest to separate the wheat from the weeds. Merely looking like a Christian and going to church doesn’t cut it (Matthew 13:47–50; 13:24–30). • The Parables of the Mustard Seed and the Leaven. Jesus told a couple of parables that show how the kingdom of God starts out small and then grows. In these parables, a mustard seed grows into a large tree and flour works its way eventually through a whole lump of dough. In the same way, merely starting out as a Christian doesn’t cut it. If we don’t allow God’s kingdom to work its way throughout our lives and churches, we will fall short of displaying God’s kingdom reign (Matthew 13:31–33). • The Parables of the Treasure and the Pearl. Jesus told a couple of parables describing the cost that comes with being a citizen of his kingdom. Both parables describe somebody finding something inestimably valuable and selling all they have to get it. In the same way, we must figure in the cost of discipleship. Merely window-shopping doesn’t cut it (Matthew 13:44–46). From these parables, we see four reasons why church people can fall short of displaying God’s kingdom reign: • Some church people merely hear the Word. • Some church people merely look like Christians. • Some church people only start out following Jesus. • Some church people aren’t interested in the cost of discipleship. All of these are not reasons to give up on church. It’s true that sometimes there are reasons to leave a particular local church and join a different one—if the church leaders are no longer teaching biblical truth in the spirit of love. But most of the time, it’s not time to leave one church for another. Rath- er, these realities we’ve looked at are reasons to step up in your mission: to be a disciple who makes disciples. As you and others do that, the church will more and more display God’s kingdom reign. 166 What Kingdom Has My Allegiance? How should we view the church when we are discouraged about how it falls short of displaying the reign of God’s kingdom? Again, first, we view the church through the lens of what Jesus said about it. Second, we view the church through the lens of what Jesus did for it. WE VIEW THE What did Jesus do for the church? How do you love a church you won’t CHURCH THROUGH always like? We remind ourselves what Jesus did for it. THE LENS OF WHAT The apostle Paul talked with the church leaders (specifically the elders) JESUS DID FOR IT. he had appointed in the city of Ephesus, because he was leaving for Jerusa- lem and was not going to see them again. He gave them final directions and encouragement, and one of the instructions he gave was this: “Be shepherds of the church of God, which he bought with his own blood” (Acts 20:28b). Did you catch how much Jesus paid to create the church? “The church of God, which he bought with his own blood.” Apparently having the church was worth God’s blood. Nothing is more valu- able on the planet—if it’s worth the Son of God shedding his own blood. Church may some days be disappointing as church people fail to display God’s kingdom reign in their lives. But if the church is worth God’s blood, then surely it is worth our time and love and effort. Am I a Loving Person? Holiness and love characterize the kingdom of God. Holiness is a lifestyle of separation or “set- apart-ness” from the ways of the world so we can be dedicated to God and his kingdom. Love is a cross-shaped action that glorifies God and benefits someone else. When asked the most important commandment we can spend our lives pursuing, Jesus brought it down to love: “The most important one,” answered Jesus, “is this: ‘Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.’ The second is this: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no commandment greater than these.” (Mark 12:29–31) So if you are a citizen of God’s kingdom, it’s worth asking yourself, Am I a loving person? THERE IS NO You know the I Love NY mug (with I + a heart + NY)? If you own this mug, COMMANDMENT it usually means you went to New York City, and the trip was really enjoyable. GREATER I (Daniel) have a friend who has an I Love NY mug, but she has a differ- THAN THESE. ent reason for having the mug. As New York City reeled from COVID-19, the 167

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook city needed medical personnel. At the time, my friend worked in another state as a surgical nurse. Her hospital wasn’t doing elective surgeries because of COVID-19, so she wanted to go to New York City where they needed help. She chose to go work in New York City for no pay instead of continuing not to work for pay. Her workplace had basically told her, “If you go, we’re letting you go.” (In other words, “We’re letting you go from the company.”) As a result, she left her job, went to a field hospital in New York City, and worked a couple of weeks straight of twelve-hour shifts. When the COVID-19 numbers went down, the field hospital closed, and she returned to her home state. But before she left for home, she decided to do one touristy thing: she bought an I Love NY mug. So her mug says more than, “I went to New York City, and the trip was really enjoyable.” It means something a lot deeper, doesn’t it? When God says, “I love you,” he’s not saying, “I find this person is always enjoyable and always follows each of my commands predictably and perfectly. I just really love this person because this person never disappoints me with bad decisions.” No, God’s love goes a lot deeper than that, and we should all be very grateful. Why? Because we know the truth about us isn’t always something we’re proud of. Praise God that his love for us doesn’t go up and down depending on our lovability. It’s constant because it’s based in his faithfulness. As Psalm 118:29 puts it, “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good; his love endures forever.” How about you? Again, the most important commandments Jesus gave us are to love God and to love other people (Mark 12:30–31). Is your love based on how much you’re enjoying the relation- ship at the time? Is how well you love based on how well you feel at the moment? Or is your love based on something solid? Our love can be faithful and devoted even when don’t personally feel like it. How? We love in response to something that never fails us: “We love because he [God] first loved us” (1 John 4:19). 168 What Kingdom Has My Allegiance? SCRIPTURE What does each verse teach me about the kingdom of God? “For to us a child is born, to us a son is given, and the government will be on his shoulders. And he will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. Of the great- ness of his government and peace there will be no end. He will reign on David’s throne and over his kingdom, establishing and upholding it with justice and righteousness from that time on and forever.” (Isaiah 9:6–7) “From that time on Jesus began to preach, ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near.’” (Matthew 4:17) “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. . . . Blessed are those who are persecuted because of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” (Jesus in Matthew 5:3, 10) “So do not worry, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ For the pagans run after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them. But seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well.” (Jesus in Matthew 6:31–33) 169

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook SNAPSHOT . . . FROM EAST ASIA Policemen leapt over the gate of my house in the middle of the night. This was a few days after my wife had just had surgery delivering our newborn baby girl. Several policemen wanted to enter my home, and several others remained outside. The police commander of a nearby police station led them. My wife, who had only been discharged from the hospital prior the incident, heard the knock on the door. When she heard the policemen knocking at the door, she looked at them through the door peephole, and asked, “Who are you?” They responded, “We are the police. Open the door!” After that, my wife woke me up, explain- ing who was knocking on our door. When I opened the door, five policemen and one policewoman entered the house. They ordered us to stand by as they took photos of us, even while I was still shirtless and my wife could barely stand due to having just given birth. The police wanted to know where our bedroom was, and they went in and searched it as if they had been given instructions of where to search. They then told me to sit down on the bed, and they asked for my cell phone, which I gave them. Then they asked me for my second cell phone. It was then that I realized the police had been tipped off since they were asking such specific questions. They searched my bedroom, and they found a second phone, a lap- top, the wedding photo album, documents, and a Christian book in English. They then told me to follow them into different rooms as they searched them all. They discov- ered an Arabic-language book about the gospel. After finishing their search, they told my wife and me to go with them. They put us into one of the three cars they were driving. We did not know where the police were taking us. When we arrived at the criminal investigation department, the police checked me in while my wife was taken to another police station. I was taken in to be interviewed and asked about the possessions they took from my home. After that, they relocated me to another place that was well-fortified with thick doors, and the lights inside were extremely bright. The officers interrogated me. “Why did the police arrest you?” they asked. I responded that I did not know the reason. The tiny cell they put me in had no window, and the only source of light was a single bulb. There was a bunk bed, with the lower bed made of concrete, and a toilet in the corner. This was to be my new home for a while. One morning, I overheard the guards speaking about me. One asked, “For what reason was this man arrested?” 170 What Kingdom Has My Allegiance? The other responded, “He is a Christian, and the court may sentence him to one year in jail. Or the court may release him, so let’s add poison to his food.” After that, I stopped eating food at all for fourteen days. I only drank water. One of the first nights I was there, the police took me to the office where I was first interrogat- ed, and they asked me, “Did you know why you got arrested?” I said I didn’t. They explained that I had been arrested because I was spreading Christianity. They asked if that was true. I responded that it was not true, and I told them to provide the evidence. So they asked, “What do you believe? Are you a Christian or a Muslim?” I said, “I am a Christian.” When I said that, they read a verse to me out of the Quran and left me alone for a while. Eventually, the police took my wife and me to a court to notify us of the rea- son we were arrested and to tell us that our case was under investigation. While I SAID, “I AM A inside the court, we both confessed our faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, knowing CHRISTIAN.” it would not make the process easier for us. Every week the police took us back to court until the allotted time limit of the police investigation ended, which was three months. They only had three months to hold us by law, but even after the court appearanc- es, our time in confinement lasted much longer. Several others whom we knew were also arrest- ed and brought to jail. All the while, the police kept asking me and my wife many questions and pressuring us. The months that went by were extremely tough and stressful. They did not give me my basic rights of water or exercise each day. The police told me that these basic rights and services were only available to Muslims, and I had no rights in this regard. Another source of stress was that the police chief threatened to kill me, saying he would behead me, and that because I was a citizen, I could not be deported to another country. Sometimes when the police threatened me, I truly thought they were about to kill me. It was hard to be there. The specific section of the jail I was in was designated to arrest terrorists, of which I was not. After several months, the police brought us to the court. They once again accused us of spread- ing Christianity. But by God’s unfailing grace, eight months after being arrested, my wife and baby and I were released from prison. The judge announced we had committed no crime and were inno- cent. We are so thankful to God that he was with us in every circumstance that we went through, and he continues to be with us, whether we are in prison for Christ’s sake or are free. We are determined to stay in our country as we want God’s kingdom to be advanced in our country, and we want to show our people the truth. They are in darkness, and the devil has blinded them. We must remain in our country, serve our people, and show the light of the Lord Jesus Christ. So many of our people have never heard the good news of Jesus Christ, and the majority have never 171

Right now, most do not love us or hate us, but I believe that if they know our God-given morals and ethics, their thinking will change. — Mo, East Africa SUMMARY 1. pages.content: Page intentionally left blank 1122 AM I OKAY WITH BEING DIFFERENT? Whether you believe in God or not will have a huge effect on your religious life (if you go to church, if you read the Bible, etc.). But does it have much of an effect on your everyday life? The truth is whether you believe in God or not has a massive influence on how you see the whole world (your “worldview”). Some people’s worldview includes God at the center, and other people’s worldview puts God off to the side or removes him altogether. Here are five examples of things you will see very differently depending on whether you believe in God in your core or not: • Human life • Marriage/sexuality • Ethnicity/race • Sex/gender • The earth If you choose to believe in God and trust that he created us, some people are going to look at you as if you are from another planet. They won’t get why you have such different views than they do on such basic parts of life. Are you okay with being seen as crazy by mainstream culture? Take a few minutes and consider the options listed below. Option 1: I choose to accept what my culture teaches about these topics. Both of us, Daniel and Andrew, live in the global West. So the answers you’ll see here are com- mon answers you’ll get from the modern Western culture, a culture that has largely moved past Judeo-Christian philosophy and come up with its own answers to these big-picture questions. Yes, there are other ways of thinking within modern Western culture, but at this cultural moment, these are helpful summaries of mainstream secular teaching on these topics: 177

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook If I accept what my culture teaches about these topics . . . Human life Humans are a highly evolved species of animal that over time has developed sophisticated tools such as language, morality, and self-reflection. Essentially the result of matter + time + undirected natural processes, humans aren’t created for a specific purpose. They aren’t valu- able because they are somehow “made in God’s image.” Rather, a human life is valuable inso- far as it can survive, contribute to the sustainability of the planet and the advancement of the species, and live an authentic life true to its deepest desires. Sometimes, this means the lives of less important humans are discardable for the sake of more important humans (e.g., in the cases of abortion, infanticide, and involuntary euthanasia). Marriage Although marriage was once primarily a matter of security (a secure way to form core relation- ships and perpetuate one’s genetics), marriage is now more adaptable. Whereas it used to be common to see marriage as between a man and a woman, or between a man and multiple women or a woman and multiple men, it has evolved to where men can marry men and wom- en can marry women. Marriage is something that will continue to evolve to fit human needs and desires. For example, consider the case of “open marriages,” in which the spouses agree that extramarital romantic relationships are permitted. In the same way, a particular marriage that a person is in may evolve to where the partners fall out of love; in cases like this, divorce makes good sense. And gender “roles” assigned in marriage, as in the biblical teaching of the husband as the Christlike head in the home, are outdated and unnecessary. Race It has been common in Western culture to speak in terms of many races of humanity. Seeing one race as more evolved than another was at one time popular in Western culture. For exam- ple, some white Westerners saw themselves as genetically superior to black Africans, so they felt justified in using black people as their slaves. More recently, it is popular in Western culture to see white people as morally inferior and inherently racist because of injustices committed in the past (e.g., the system of slavery in pre-1865 southern United States) and racial inequity in the present (e.g., comparing education, poverty, crime, etc., statistics from one racial group to another). Gender In modern Western culture, the standard has become to make a distinction between a per- son’s sexuality (are you biologically male or female?) and a person’s gender (do you identify as male or female?). In this way, gender has become something that humans discover for them- selves by looking within and being authentic to their truest self. As such, a person can identify as numerous types of genders (transgender, bigender, genderfluid, genderqueer, polygender, etc.). What’s important isn’t whether you are biologically male or female but that you know yourself and identify as your most authentic self and that other people treat you accordingly. To be authentic to yourself, you make your body align with what you feel inside at whatever level feels most authentic, even up to surgical gender-affirming procedures. The earth Our planet remains habitable to life, but that could change. Earth is not the special focus of a Creator. Rather, we are here, alive, thanks to a series of happy accidents that make this planet life-permitting. Because we aren’t guaranteed survival in the future, we need to do everything we possibly can to ensure that our planet survives. Because our planet is in our hands, we can’t be too anxious about making sure it stays safe. 178 Am I Okay with Being Different? Option 2: I accept what my Creator teaches about these topics. If I accept what my Creator teaches about these topics . . . Human life God created humans in his image (imago dei). This is why we are unique in areas such as written language, culture making, being able to make moral decisions that contradict basic instinct, and being able to have a personal relationship with our Creator. Humanity’s identity as being made in God’s image is also the reason God made it a horrendous crime to take another human’s life. God created humans for the purpose of overseeing the planet he entrusted to them. As God put it, “Let us make mankind in our image, in our likeness, so that they may rule over the fish in the sea and the birds in the sky, over the livestock and all the wild animals, and over all the creatures that move along the ground. So God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he cre- ated them; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:26–27). Because all humans, great and small, are made in God’s image, God regularly reminds his people through the Bible to defend the defenseless and lift up the oppressed. Marriage Marriage is something that God created to give humans faithful companionship and deep oneness, and to provide a healthy environment for the raising of children. Here is how God described mar- riage: “A man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). This profound oneness between a husband and wife is why God is grieved when spouses get divorced. Throughout the Bible, versions of sexuality and marriage that fall outside one man-one woman marriage are frowned upon. This goes for sexual relations before marriage and outside of marriage, homosexual sexuality, and sexual relations with another person’s spouse; and whenever we see polygamy in the Bible (multiple spouses), it’s predictably a disaster. God also created marriage to give us a picture of his own love for and relationship with the church. In marriage, the husband is called to love his wife sacrificially, and the wife is called to respect her husband, submitting to his leadership (Ephesians 5:25–33). Race Since God created humans in his image from one ancestral pair of humans, the Bible doesn’t speak of multiple races. It speaks of multiple ethnicities (people groups) scattered throughout the world, but they all share the image of God. Thus, even though racial tension and tribalism have been part of our world for millennia, the biblical authors continue to call God’s people to show empathy toward the foreigner, seek justice for the oppressed, and to reach people of all nations with the good news of Jesus. When it comes to the multiethnic nature of the church, the apostle Peter explained what God had taught him: “I now realize how true it is that God does not show favoritism but accepts from every nation the one who fears him and does what is right” (Acts 10:34–35). The apostle Paul explained that salvation is offered to everyone: “Here there is no Greek or Jew, circumcised or uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, or free; but Christ is all, and in all” (Colossians 3:11). Where there is injustice from one ethnicity to another, Christians seek justice. Where there is resentment between ethnicities, Christians seek reconciliation. 179

pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook Gender If I believe reality is something that humans create, then I should be able to give myself whatever identity best fits my sense of my true self. On the other hand, if reality is something that God cre- ated, then I’m not able to define myself; I’m already what God created me to be. As Genesis 1:27 puts it, “So God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them.” If I am created one way, but I reject my createdness to give myself my own identity, I do so to my own loss. On the other hand, if God created me as a biological male and I experience gender dysphoria, having discomfort accepting my maleness, I follow God in this area by seeking to align what I feel inside with how God has created me. The Bible describes the different ways in marriage and the church in which men and women use their complementary gifts to serve each other, but God has also given qualified men pastor/elder roles for leading the church and protecting her from false teachings. The earth By all accounts, our planet was perfectly placed for the emergence of life. To say this was just a happy accident is naïve. The truth is if we’re just looking at probability alone, we shouldn’t have a universe in the first place, let alone a life-permitting universe or a life-permitting earth with actual life. First and foremost, as people who believe in God, we don’t look at our earth as accidental in any way. This was God’s idea. Thus, we shouldn’t have an obsessive anxiety about whether we’ll be able to keep our earth surviving calamity (it’s his earth, not ours). At the same time, manmade environmental disasters have occurred throughout history, and God created humans to be his wise stewards over the earth. Therefore, we shouldn’t waste our world, nor should we worship it. We should watch over it well. SELF-ASSESSMENT Here are your two main options when it comes to views on major cultural topics: 1. I choose to accept what my culture teaches about these topics. 2. I choose to accept what my Creator teaches about these topics. When it comes to my views on major cultural topics, here’s where I am: When it comes to views on major cultural topics, here’s where I want to be and why I want to be there: 180 Am I Okay with Being Different? We are called to be panionship, and propagation of humanity. wise, diligent stewards over what God has given us. STUDY Should you be okay with being different in order to follow Jesus? Here are some thoughts to help you as you wrestle with this question. How You’ll Be Enticed to Leave Jesus Behind Apple has two ways of encouraging people to buy new iPhones. On the one hand, older models lose their compatibility with newer updates. Eventually, incom- patibility forces you off your older model. When Apple introduces a new operating system, chances are that iPhones from a few years back won’t be compatible with it. On the other hand, newer models are advertised enticingly as being significantly better than models from even half a year before. If you’re into Apple products, the ads are pretty hard to resist. In short, Apple encourages us to buy their iPhones using both a have-to and a want-to approach. We are both 1) forced into it by incompatibility and 2) enticed into it by their irresistibility. Let us be clear. We’re not trying to be negative about iPhones. The marketing is brilliant, and the product is satisfying. 181

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook But think about the iPhone’s forced incompatibility and its fashionable irresistibility. These both provide a fascinating illustration of a couple of timeless themes we find in the Bible’s last book: the book of Revelation. In Revelation is one main Satan-figure, the dragon, and the dragon has three puppets that do his will: two beasts and a harlot. In the beasts and harlot, we’ll see Satan’s strategies of “forced incompatibility” and “fashionable irresistibility.” Tactic 1: Forced Incompatibility Revelation 13 describes a “beast out of the sea” who blasphemes God and persecutes God’s follow- ers. It wages war against God’s people and tries to force them to worship itself. A second “beast out of the earth” forces everyone to worship the first beast and allows them to buy and sell only if they are marked with its name. The two beasts rule by trying to THE TWO BEASTS force people off one type of worship (worship of God) and onto another (wor- RULE BY TRYING ship of the beast). They dominate through showing the incompatibility of fol- TO FORCE lowing God with their system of government. The way of the beast is a have-to PEOPLE OFF approach by which we are forced to reject God because of God’s incompatibil- ONE TYPE OF ity with the world’s ways. WORSHIP AND Tactic 2: Fashionable Irresistibility ONTO ANOTHER. Revelation 17 describes a different tactic to get the same result. Here, we find a harlot, dressed up in glittery purple and scarlet. She is skilled in adultery. Although she doesn’t herself seem to be the one killing the people of God, she gets drunk on their blood. This harlot appears to be the personification of an affluent city, which the book of Revela- tion calls “Babylon.” A harlot is a seducer, and the book of Revelation depicts this woman, or regime, as having seduced many of the kings of the earth. When the great city is finally destroyed, the book of Rev- elation pictures the kings of the earth feeling a great loss, for they had shared her luxury and prof- ited from her riches. The way of the harlot suggests a want-to approach by which we are enticed to reject God because of the irresistibility of the world’s ways. When it comes to the actual identity of Revelation’s beasts and harlot, it’s easy to have more questions than answers. But when it comes to Satan’s strategies of getting you and me to stop fol- lowing Jesus, it’s clear that he uses both ways to great effect. But it gets worse. 182 Am I Okay with Being Different? A Third Strategy Satan doesn’t just use “you have to” and “you want to” to get people to stop following Jesus. As we mentioned, the beast out of the earth tries to get everyone to worship the first beast. But do you know how he does this? He does this by looking like our Messiah. He is disguised to look like Jesus. Revelation 13 tells us he looks like a lamb (think the “lamb of God”) and even performs miracles, yet when he speaks, he speaks with the voice of the dragon. So this beast is particularly frightening because he deceives people into thinking he’s good and right. In other words, the way he gets people to stop following Jesus is by saying, “You ought to.” Let’s say you’re a young Christian growing up in a culture already experiencing the iPhone effect when it comes to sexuality and gender. Your biblical beliefs about sexuality and gender are increas- ingly incompatible with the culture around you, especially when it comes to what your university teaches or what your workplace celebrates. At the same time, you catch yourself wanting to fit in and flow with the cultural tide. All the while, you’re able to withstand the temptation and the hostility, even if barely, because you know that what you’re doing is right. Even if it costs you, you’re going to do the right thing. You’re going to follow the path of morality and justice. It’s what it means to be faithful to Jesus. THEN ALONG Then along comes the beast dressed as a lamb. “You ought to.” COMES Mentored from multiple angles in a post-Christian worldview, you find your- THE BEAST self thinking, You know, maybe I was wrong. I’ve always wanted to be a moral per- DRESSED AS son. I want to care about justice. I want to help people who are hurting. I want to be A LAMB. “YOU an agent of compassion and not condemnation. And, after all, Jesus is all about love. OUGHT TO.” Compassion. Acceptance. In fact, the Jesus of love sure doesn’t look much like those Christians who talk about sin. Maybe they’re the ones reading the Bible wrong. I think we should read the Bible in a way that helps people, especially marginalized people, instead of reading it in a way that could further marginalize them. For a lot of Christians, “You ought to” is the straw that punctures their fidelity to historic Chris- tianity. It’s just too tempting to equate Christianity with niceness and Christian love with affirma- tion, and then read the Bible through those lenses. It’s too easy to paint Jesus with wide, cultural brushstrokes, slopping over Jesus’ many countercultural (i.e., unpopular) teachings. Satan tries to get us to stop following God using three approaches. Don’t fall for them: • You have you. • You want to. • You ought to. 183

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook To beware Satan’s schemes, we need to be aware that he comes at the people of God from all three directions. He tries to entice us away from Jesus while forcing us off Jesus as well as pos- ing as Jesus. Satan is master tempter (Genesis 3), prowling lion (1 Peter 5:8), and angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14). For the sake of our salvation and the salvation of others, we must stay alert, guard our souls, and hold tight to “the faith that was once for all entrusted to God’s holy people” (Jude 1:3). When Christianity Isn’t Cool . . . Mr. and Mrs. Donner welcome a newborn son, and right away they notice two things about him. One thing is not surprising, and another thing is very surprising. First, they notice their son is a reindeer. This is not surprising because Mr. and Mrs. Donner are also reindeer. This story is set in the 1964 Christmas classic Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer. Mr. Donner is one of Santa’s reindeer; he helps pull his sleigh. Second, they notice their son has a strange-looking nose. It’s red instead of black. Sometimes it gets really bright and sort of squeals. Everyone who sees this little reindeer’s nose knows he’s in for a rough time. Santa will look at that nose and say, “That won’t work for my sleigh team.” Donner will look at that nose and say, “And to think, a son of mine.” Mr. and Mrs. Donner think it best to take some dirt, form a clump, and put it over the nose. That should do it. So little Rudolph goes out to play with the other reindeer. He makes a friend named Fireball. He meets a cute girl reindeer named Clarice. He gets excited about Clarice, and he jumps up and down, up and down. And wouldn’t you know, the clump of dirt comes loose. Now everyone’s eyes are squinting, and their ears are ringing. What in the world is that light and that sound? Then they see it. It’s coming from Rudolph’s nose. Fireball leaves to find other reindeer to play with. Clarice’s dad tells her that Rudolph is not a rein- deer she can play with. Rudolph has no other choice but to find other misfits to hang around with. Rudolph meets Hermey, the elf who wants to be a dentist. Society wants neither Rudolph nor Hermey, so they decide to run away. They meet up with a gold prospector named Yukon Cornelius. But even this arrangement isn’t going to work out, again, because of Rudolph’s nose. The Abomi- nable Snowman will be attracted to his glowing nose, and Rudolph doesn’t want to endanger his friends. So Rudolph has no other choice than to leave his HIS NOSE IS friends behind and set out all alone. EMBARRASSING. And it all goes back to that nose. It’s the reason for all the troubles Rudolph will face for a long time. His nose is embarrassing. 184 Am I Okay with Being Different? What Makes Christians Strange? Often, disciples of Jesus have their own “Rudolph nose” to deal with. Here’s what we mean. A string of churches in the country of Turkey (back then, the region was called Asia Minor) once felt insig- nificant. They didn’t have church buildings; instead, they met in homes. Most of the Christians in these churches were poor, and many of them were foreigners who had moved there from other countries. Many were slaves. They were trying to survive inside an empire that wasn’t hospitable to them. This was the same empire (the Roman Empire) that had crucified their leader, Jesus, and now the empire persecuted his church. As the apostle Peter wrote a letter to these churches to encourage them, he used words like “fiery ordeal” and “suffering for doing good” to describe their situation. What caused this suffering? What was their Rudolph nose? It was their faith. They believed in a God who told them true from false and right from wrong. Their belief in God made them THEIR BELIEF look very strange to the culture around them. IN GOD MADE And when Peter wrote this letter to them, they were only about to the “San- THEM LOOK ta-says-you’re-probably-not-going-to-get-to-pull-the-sleigh” stage. They still had VERY STRANGE yet to hear all their friends laughing at them. Clarice’s dad? That was still in the TO THE CULTURE future. They hadn’t even caught a glimpse of the Abominable Snowman yet. AROUND THEM. In other words, it was going to get a lot worse for these churches. The Christians to whom Peter wrote wouldn’t see circumstances get better in their lifetimes. In fact, Peter himself ended up on a cross. Centuries passed before the churches started experiencing widespread religious freedom. Advice for Rudolph? So what advice do you have for Rudolph? Should he keep covering up his nose? After all, it’s going to cause him a lot of suffering. Yet we all know something else about Rudolph’s nose: the source of his suffering will also give his story its happy ending. With his nose, he’ll light his way to find his family being held captive by the Abominable Snowman. Also with his nose, he will lead Santa’s sleigh through a snowstorm. The churches to whom Peter wrote felt shellshocked by the hostility around them, and it was just going to get worse. Again, what was their “Rudolph nose”? It was their faith. So should they try to hide their faith? Be embarrassed by it? Try to blend in and be like everybody else? After all, their faith made a lot of people squint and complain about them. Yes, their faith caused them suffering. But, no, they shouldn’t be embarrassed by it or try to hide it. Why? Because their faith was the most precious thing they had. Peter said their faith was “of greater worth than gold” (1 Peter 1:7). Because, as Peter put it, the “end result of your faith” was 185

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook the “salvation of your souls” (1 Peter 1:9). As the apostle Paul also put it, “For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith” (Ephesians 2:8). When It Gets Tough . . . As a disciple of Jesus, you will have moments when you are made to feel weird, even a cultural her- etic, because of your faith and what your faith teaches you to believe. It’s going to be clear in those moments that: Your faith + people knowing about your faith = some kind of suffering You will be tempted to make a clump of dirt and pack it down over your faith to where it’s still in there but not visible. It won’t cause people to squint. And you won’t suffer for it. You won’t be publicly shamed for believing this or that unpopular Christian belief. But if Peter were writing you a letter, he would say something like this: “Don’t for a moment see your faith as embarrassing. Your faith is the most precious thing you’ve got. It’s more precious than gold. After all, the end result of your faith is salvation.” Is Peter just bad with math? No, Peter gets it. He knows your faith + people knowing about your faith = some kind of suffering. It’s just that Peter takes it a step further (notice the extra equals sign): Your faith + people knowing about your faith = suffering = you get blessed Here’s how Peter put it: “But even if you should suffer for what is right, you are blessed” (1 Peter 3:14a). Was he crazy? No. He just took his cue from his friend Jesus, who had told him and the other disciples, “Blessed are you when people insult you, persecute you and falsely say all kinds of evil against you because of me. Rejoice and be “BLESSED ARE glad, because great is your reward in heaven, for in the same way they perse- YOU WHEN cuted the prophets who were before you” (Matthew 5:11–12). PEOPLE INSULT YOU, PERSECUTE Deciding What to Value YOU AND FALSELY SAY ALL KINDS OF I (Andrew) remember when I was young that I really dreaded Sundays. My EVIL AGAINST YOU parents made me dress nice for church (our “Sunday best”), which always felt BECAUSE OF ME.” awkward and uncomfortable. There I was, wearing clothes I didn’t want to wear and with a perfect combover. 186 Am I Okay with Being Different? I remember my dad always sat in the car, with it running, about thirty minutes before we had to even leave to make sure we made it to church on time. He sat in the car and waited, and waited . . . with it running until we all were loaded in. Then came the part that I dreaded all week: Dad backed out of the garage and down the drive- way, through the neighborhood, on our way to church—which exposed and declared to all my friends that the Jit family was off to church! You see, my neighborhood friends didn’t have to get dressed up and go to church. No, they got to play. At this stage in my life, I got really good at learn- ing how to do the electric slide down in my seat to minimize the damage of not being spotted by anyone! Being seen going to church was so embarrassing. Looking back, I am truly grateful that my parents instilled in me the importance of church attendance, and taking me every week, even when I thought it wasn’t cool or trendy. I feel this way now because being in church has shaped me and grown my faith in incredible and unspeakable ways. But in the moment, being seen as different because of our faith was not easy. When Christianity isn’t cool, value your faith. It really is the most precious thing you’ve got. Nothing else is as important. SCRIPTURE What does each verse teach me about living counterculturally? “But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s special possession, that you may declare the praises of him who called you out of darkness into his wonderful light.” (1 Peter 2:9) “You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt los- es its saltiness, how can it be made salty again? It is no longer good for anything, except to be thrown out and trampled underfoot. You are the light of the world. A town built on a hill cannot be hidden. Neither do people light a lamp and put it under a bowl. Instead they put it on its stand, and it gives light to everyone in the house.” (Jesus in Matthew 5:13–15) 187

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook “For the time will come when people will not put up with sound doctrine. Instead, to suit their own desires, they will gather around them a great number of teachers to say what their itching ears want to hear. They will turn their ears away from the truth and turn aside to myths. But you, keep your head in all situations, endure hardship, do the work of an evangelist, discharge all the duties of your ministry.” (2 Timothy 4:3–5) “Dear friends, I urge you, as foreigners and exiles, to abstain from sinful desires, which wage war against your soul. Live such good lives among the pagans that, though they accuse you of doing wrong, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day he visits us.” (1 Peter 2:11–12) SNAPSHOT . . . FROM THE UNITED STATES I’ve always thought my story wasn’t all that interesting. I grew up in a very loving Christian home and have always been supported by my whole family to pursue my faith and the callings God has given me. That doesn’t mean my life has been without hardships or complications. I’ve dealt with anxiety, being hurt by others, hard dynamics with coaches and friends, and the craziness that comes from living in a broken world. But the one constant in life has been Jesus. Through all the good and bad, he has been my safe space and biggest support system. Knowing and growing in my faith in Jesus gave me hope and purpose when I had none. Growing in my faith has always looked like seeking out new opportunities to learn who God is and how he can use me. This has taken the form of participating in youth group, serving in chil- dren’s ministry, finding community on my college campus, pursuing a career in healthcare, and joining a missions organization (MiT Global). I have always wanted to know God better, why he says the things he does, how to best grow the kingdom in my heart and community, and what living a life in pursuit of Jesus should look like for me. These are all massive, complicated, and wisdom-re- quiring questions that I often could not have answered on my own. That is where wise communi- ty comes in. I am convinced God uses his people to talk to us by giving people the right words to say when we need to hear from him. I’ve seen this so evidently in my own life as well as in the lives 188 Am I Okay with Being Different? of so many others. My greatest faith growth has come when I have been surrounded by a healthy, authentic, and wise community. I stayed connected to my faith through high school because I really needed to. I learned early on that life sucks sometimes—that’s just the truth of living outside of heaven. Jesus is the only access we have to perfection, the only thing that is truly confident, dependable, and steadfast. I STAYED I don’t know how people get through a day without believing in God. CONNECTED What do they gauge good and evil with? What gets them out of bed in the TO MY FAITH morning? How do they make decisions without seeking out peace from the THROUGH God who holds the universe and knows the future? Maybe these sound like HIGH SCHOOL silly questions, but once you’ve tasted life with Jesus and been inhabited with BECAUSE I REALLY the Holy Spirit, life without seems void of purpose and full of fear. Staying NEEDED TO. connected to my faith in high school gave me solid ground despite all that I encountered, and I don’t know where I’d be today if I hadn’t had that. Another important aspect for me of staying connected to Jesus in high school was finding com- munity. It is so hard to pursue your faith by yourself. God wired us to crave community. Living and thriving with Jesus is difficult when you are walking that road alone. My advice is to find commu- nity—youth groups, small groups, ministries within your school. If you can’t find it, create it. Find a trusted, wise counsel to come alongside you and help you study the Bible. It only takes a few, but those few can bring so much strength. Ecclesiastes 4 talks about strength in numbers, even if they are few: “A cord of three strands is not quickly broken” (Ecclesiastes 4:12). Find your one or two “cords” to do life with, and you will be much harder to break. Learn accountability early and take it seriously. Creating healthy community not only strengthens your own faith, but it also creates an environment that welcomes people who are curious about Jesus. Living counterculturally means living and loving in a way that reflects our Savior. If you think about it, nothing about Jesus’ behavior makes sense from a worldly perspective. He was selfless, full of mercy, abounding in grace, and held no one’s faults or debts against them. He was and is the antithesis of everything the world claims we should be to be “successful” or “happy.” Living coun- terculturally means reflecting him in how we live. That does not mean we are expected to be the people’s Messiah—and thank goodness for that. Pretending to be perfect is missing the whole point of the gospel: that Jesus came and paid for our sins even though he was without blame because he knew we were incapable of living perfectly. I am utterly imperfect, and thanks to the grace of God and sacrifice of Jesus, it’s not me whom I must place my faith in. Living counterculturally doesn’t mean that you are the perfect Christian; it just means that you follow Jesus with all your heart and mind. You live and love as an outpouring 189

pages.title: [CHAPTER] Real Life Theology Handbook
pages.content: Real Life Theology Handbook of the life and love that the Holy Spirit provides in you. He makes the right connections and gives you the right words when you need them. People don’t come to Jesus through hatred and judgment; they see Jesus in people, recognize there is something different about them, and want to know what that is. YOU LIVE AND As someone pursuing global missions, I’ve been asked a lot how I know LOVE AS AN that I’m following the calling God has for me, and in all honesty, I don’t OUTPOURING OF think I’ve quite figured out how to put it in words for myself, much less oth- THE LIFE AND ers. I can say, however, that it is a certain peace that surpasses my understand- LOVE THAT THE ing. No matter how dangerous, hard, or crazy my future plans sound, under HOLY SPIRIT my worldly fears and disappointments, I always have an immovable peace PROVIDES IN YOU. when I think about my future. This is because I always know who is in con- trol of it. God is the author of every chapter of my life, and I am merely fol- lowing in hopes of being used to glorify him and grow his kingdom. I know that anything the Lord leads will be fruitful, and I’m honored he gives me the opportunity to be a part of it. — Reagan, US SUMMARY 1. God is the Creator and sustainer of all things. 2. Believing in God influences how we see the world and live everyday life. 3. Keeping the faith is more important than fitting in with the culture. SELF-REFLECTION AND DISCUSSION 1. When it comes to topics such as human life, marriage, and sexuality, do you tend to believe what your surrounding culture teaches or what the Bible teaches? 2. What is your biggest fear when it comes to trying to be a Christian when it’s not cool culturally? 190 Am I Okay with Being Different? 3. The apostle Peter said, “But even if you should suffer for what is right, you are blessed” (1 Peter 3:14a). Do you believe this? Why or why not? 4. Jesus said, “You are the light of the world,” (Matthew 5:14). What are some ways you are trying to be light in the darkness? 5. What are the most precious things in your life? If you’re being completely honest, does your faith in Jesus make the list? STUDY MORE For a deeper dive into this chapter’s topic, see the Real Life Theology book dedicated to this topic: Carol M. pages.content: Page intentionally left blank 1133 AM I PREPARED FOR THE END? William Shatner, who played Captain Kirk on Star Trek, made the news for going up into space for real in the spaceship Blue Origin. Even apart from his fictional USS Enterprise and real- life Blue Origin flights, Shatner’s biography is legendary. His career includes starring in numerous movies and TV shows, recording eight albums, voice acting, book writing, horse breeding, hosting awards shows and Miss America pageants, and even participating in professional wrestling. He’s in numerous “halls” and “walks” of fame. His personal biography includes three kids, four wives, and at least five autobiographies. Yet nothing in his colorful career—not even simulating space flights for a living on Star Trek— prepared him for what he would experience on the real-life Blue Origin flight. It was a 10-minute flight that went only 66.5 miles up (just past the Kármán line, the basic boundary between earth’s atmosphere and outer space). But it was enough of an experience that it reduced Shatner to an emo- tional post-flight interview in which he just couldn’t get over the stark dichotomy with which the experience presented him.21 Commenting on the ominous space he entered and the fragile, life-giving blueness he left, Shat- ner said, “That was death and this was life. And everything else just stood still for a moment. I was overwhelmed . . . I was overwhelmed with the experience, with the sensation of looking at death and looking at life.”22 Although Shatner has written over thirty books and thousands of pages, mostly on the topic of space flight, he knew what happened in those ten minutes was way bigger than he could capture in words: “Everything I thought might be clever to say went out the window.” Shatner, who many felt overacted his part on the USS Enterprise, didn’t overact when he emerged from the Blue Origin. Fighting back tears, he explained: To see the blue cover whip by! Now you’re staring into blackness. . . . This comforter of blue that we have around us. We think, Oh, that’s blue sky. And then suddenly you shoot through 195

Is that the way death is?”23 Spiritually speaking, most people want options. They want latitude to customize their spiritual- ity like they create an avatar or order a latte. The idea that in the end there’s a stark “either-or” strikes them as rude. But it’s true. In the end, it’s either life or death. Multiple decades of Shatner’s acting and speculating and writing—all IN THE END, reduced to “either-or” clarity. Many people live cluttered lives that periodically IT’S EITHER LIFE collide with clarity. But disciples of Jesus don’t have to wait for life’s Blue Origin OR DEATH. events before we find clarity. We have received God’s “either-or” statements in writing. In the end, these “either-or” statements are inescapable. It’s salvation or destruction. Light or darkness. Life or death. Heaven or hell. In the end, life is a lot like what we read in Deuteronomy 30:19: This day I call the heavens and the earth as witnesses against you that I have set before you life and death, blessings and curses. Now choose life, so that you and your children may live. SELF-ASSESSMENT My two options when it comes to whether or not I am prepared for the end are: 1. Yes 2. STUDY Why should you be prepared for the end? Here are some thoughts to help you as you wrestle with this question. We’re Scared of Death We are often afraid of death, aren’t we? The fear of lying there helpless. The fear of being in pain. The fear of being separated from those we love. Even the fear of being ashamed before God at a life we know we could have lived so much better. The thought of death often terrifies us. And because of our fear of death, we sometimes think, You know, if Jesus really beat the devil, how come there is still such scary stuff down here? Why the terrifying headlines? The auto accidents. The homicides. The short caskets. The lonely cemetery. Why all the tragedies?
